Dominican prosecutors say they arrested 28 people in 37 raids on Friday, 18 September 2026, in the Senasa 2.0 case. This time prosecutors are focusing on doctors and other health providers, not only on former managers.

What Senasa is and how the case began

Senasa, short for Seguro Nacional de Salud (National Health Insurance), is the Dominican Republic’s public health insurer. It covers more than 70% of the population.

The original case, called Operación Cobra, came to court in December 2025. Prosecutors accused former director Santiago Hazim and others of running a structure that diverted public funds.

On 14 December 2025, a court ordered 18 months of pretrial detention for Hazim and six others. Three more defendants were placed under house arrest, and a court later upheld the detention orders.

Prosecutor Mirna Ortiz said the alleged fraud could reach about 15 billion Dominican pesos (US$255 million). That uses about 58.9 Dominican pesos to the dollar, at 19 September 2026 rates.

No one in the case has been convicted. All defendants are presumed innocent until a court rules otherwise.

What prosecutors say happened in the Senasa 2.0 raids

The new operation is called Operación Cobra 2.0-A. The Public Ministry says 45 prosecutors and 200 police officers took part.

Wilson Camacho, deputy attorney general and head of prosecutions, led it with Mirna Ortiz. She works in Pepca, the special prosecutor’s office for administrative corruption.

Judge Ana Lee Florimón authorized the operation at the prosecutors’ request, Listín Diario reported. Prosecutors say they seized cash, vehicles and firearms.

The Public Ministry says those held include former Senasa employees, doctors and private individuals. Prosecutors describe the doctors and providers as the operational part of the alleged network.

Specialties named in the warrant include gynecology, general surgery, cardiology, gastroenterology and internal medicine, Diario Libre reported.

The seven schemes under investigation

Diario Libre listed seven schemes that the Public Ministry is investigating. The first three are large-scale bribes, double billing, and charges for services or medicines never delivered.

Prosecutors also cite fake medical seals and altered financial statements. The last two are the sale of donated medicines and digital sabotage, including theft of files.

Prosecutors allege that some doctors billed for fake consultations and then shared the money. In one example, men appeared in records as receiving gynecology consultations.

Prosecutors also describe a call-center scheme that approved fake surgeries and consultations from January 2021 to September 2024. They estimate it caused about 40 million Dominican pesos (US$679,000) in losses.

Senasa itself filed a complaint about irregular medical authorizations on 28 November 2024, Listín Diario reported.

How Senasa 2.0 differs from the first phase

The first phase centered on Senasa’s former top managers and a small group of associates. In Senasa 2.0, prosecutors say they are moving down to the people who provided and billed the services.

The Public Ministry lists possible charges in the wider case, including bribery, fraud against the state, embezzlement, forgery and money laundering. These are accusations that a court has not tested.

Prosecutors also link the case to Operación Onco14 in June 2026. It led to three arrests over alleged fraud at the Patronato Cibaeño Contra el Cáncer, a cancer charity.

Late on Friday, 20 of the detainees were taken to the Palace of Justice in Ciudad Nueva, Santo Domingo. Diario Libre counted eight women and 12 men in that group.

The Public Ministry presents the operation as part of Attorney General Yeni Berenice Reynoso’s firm stance against corruption. The wider Senasa inquiry remains open.

Why this matters for expats and investors

Because Senasa covers most Dominicans, many private clinics, laboratories and pharmacies rely on its payments. A fraud case of this size reaches the same private providers many foreign residents use.

Investors in Dominican clinics, labs or pharmacy chains could face closer checks on billing and more questions from partners. Careful records and clear contracts with insurers matter more now.

Senasa’s finances are also under strain. Its director since August 2025, Edward Guzmán, reported finding a deficit of about 14.7 billion pesos (US$250 million).

For expat patients, the case is a simple reminder to keep itemized bills. It also helps to check what any insurer is charged in your name.

What is not known yet

The Public Ministry has not released the names of the 28 people held in this phase. It has also not said exactly how many of them are doctors.

On Saturday morning, 19 September, prosecutors had not yet asked a judge for pretrial measures, Diario Libre reported. The constitution gives them 48 hours after an arrest to do so.

It is not yet clear whether any detainee will be released, placed under house arrest or held in custody. Prosecutors have also not said whether more arrests will follow.

The coming hearings should give the first clear picture of who the detainees are and what evidence prosecutors hold.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Senasa?

Senasa is the Dominican Republic’s public health insurer, the Seguro Nacional de Salud. It covers more than 70% of the population.

Has anyone been convicted in the Senasa 2.0 case?

No. Former director Santiago Hazim and others from the first phase are in pretrial detention, and all defendants are presumed innocent.

What happens next for the 28 detainees?

Prosecutors are expected to ask a judge for pretrial measures. The judge then decides whether each person stays in custody.

Sources: Public Ministry of the Dominican Republic (Procuraduría General de la República) statements, 18 September 2026 and earlier; Diario Libre; Listín Diario; El Caribe; El Día.

World.title: Mexico: Michoacán Prosecutor Resigns After Morena Names Him Coordinator
World.content:
MEXICO · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Carlos Torres Piña resigned as Michoacán’s state prosecutor on 18 September 2026, sending his letter to the state Congress.

— The context Four days earlier, Morena named him its Michoacán coordinator, seen as a step toward the 2027 governor race.

— Why it matters The move removes doubt on the 90-day rule, leaving a caretaker atop the prosecutor’s office.

— The catch Congress must still vote to accept the resignation, and he is not yet Morena’s registered candidate for governor.

— Who it affects Foreign residents and businesses in Michoacán, who report crimes to that office, and investors watching the 2027 governor race.

— What comes next Congress will vote on the resignation, then pick ten candidates and elect a new prosecutor to a full nine-year term.

Four days after Morena chose him to lead its work in the state ahead of 2027, Carlos Torres Piña asked Congress to accept his exit.

Morelia Cathedral in the capital of Michoacán state, Mexico (Photo: Adavyd, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The Michoacán prosecutor resigns: Carlos Torres Piña sent his resignation to the state Congress on Friday 18 September 2026. Four days earlier, Morena named him its state coordinator, a role widely seen as the path to its governor candidacy.

What the resignation letter says

Torres Piña addressed his letter to Baltazar Gaona García, who presides over the Michoacán Congress. He asked lawmakers to approve his definitive exit from the Fiscalía General del Estado, the state prosecutor’s office.

In the letter, he called the step “una reflexión personal y responsable sobre la siguiente etapa de mi vida pública”. That means a personal and responsible reflection on the next stage of his public life.

He wrote that his time in office showed him the pain many Michoacán families face. He added that every institution must put human dignity at the centre of its decisions.

He also said that respect for the office’s independence meant he should leave it for good. The resignation is not yet in force, because the Congress must first meet and vote on it.

What Morena named him to do

On Monday 14 September 2026, Morena named Torres Piña its Michoacán coordinator for the defence of the transformation and national sovereignty. Party president Ariadna Montiel and elections chief Citlalli Hernández handed him his certificate in Mexico City.

The title is an internal party post, not a government job or a registered candidacy. Latinus, Infobae and other Mexican outlets say it makes him Morena’s likely candidate for governor.

Morena chose him over several other hopefuls, including senators Raúl Morón and Reyna Celeste Ascencio. La Razón reported that party surveys decided the outcome.

Why the Michoacán prosecutor resigns now

Torres Piña had already stepped away from the prosecutor’s office on temporary leave since June 2026. He used two leaves to take part in Morena’s internal selection.

On 15 September, Gaona said Torres Piña could still legally return to the post. His second leave, he added, expired on 18 September — the day the resignation arrived.

After the party announcement, Congress president Gaona said the most honest step would be a full resignation. He warned that keeping the option to return would send a negative signal to citizens.

Local reports also note that state rules require a prosecutor to leave office at least 90 days before running for governor. The resignation removes any doubt on that point.

Who he is

Torres Piña became Michoacán’s Fiscal General in July 2025. Before that, he twice served as the state’s secretary of government under Governor Alfredo Ramírez Bedolla.

He has also served twice as a federal deputy. Infobae lists these posts in his profile after the Morena announcement.

How a new prosecutor is chosen

Under the state constitution, Congress first issues a public call and picks ten eligible candidates. The governor then has ten days to choose three names from that list.

Congress elects the new prosecutor by a two-thirds vote of its members. The winner serves a full nine-year term, not just the rest of Torres Piña’s period.

Until then, the law lets a vice-prosecutor cover the post. Vanguardia and Quadratín report that Israel Vega Rodríguez has been doing so.

His record in office

In his exit report, Torres Piña highlighted rising results between mid-2024 and mid-2026. Arrest warrants carried out rose from 212 to 477, according to figures carried by Mi Morelia.

Compensation recovered for victims rose from 38.5 million pesos (US$2.2 million) to 74.9 million pesos (US$4.4 million). Those figures use about 17.2 Mexican pesos to the dollar, at 19 September 2026 rates.

The office also reported 223 extortion investigations and 85 arrests. These are the office’s own figures and have not been independently checked.

What this means for expats and investors

The state prosecutor’s office handles criminal cases such as extortion, theft and property crimes. For foreign residents and businesses in Michoacán, it is the main door for reporting a crime.

A long search for a new prosecutor could slow decisions at the top of the office. Day-to-day work continues under the vice-prosecutor, so filed cases should keep moving.

For investors, the bigger story is the 2027 governor race, which Mexican media say is set for June 2027. Until then, the prosecutor’s office stays in the hands of a caretaker.

What is not yet known

It is not known when Congress will vote on the resignation, or when it will issue the public call for candidates. No names for a permanent successor have been announced.

Governor Ramírez Bedolla has said the Congress will decide on the replacement. His own role comes later, when he picks three names from the list of ten.

It is also not confirmed that Torres Piña will be Morena’s registered candidate for governor. Formal registration comes later under electoral rules.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Carlos Torres Piña resign as Michoacán’s prosecutor?

Yes. He sent his resignation to the state Congress on 18 September 2026. It takes effect once Congress approves it.

What did Morena name him to do?

On 14 September 2026, Morena named him its state coordinator in Michoacán. Media see this as the step before a governor candidacy in 2027.

Who runs the prosecutor’s office now?

Vice-prosecutor Israel Vega Rodríguez is covering the post. Congress will later choose a permanent prosecutor by a two-thirds vote.

Sources: Torres Piña’s resignation letter to the Michoacán Congress, 18 September 2026; Morena national leadership announcement, 14 September 2026; Quadratín; Vanguardia; Latinus; Infobae; La Razón; Mi Morelia.

World.title: Colombia Enforces JEP FARC Sanctions on Seven Ex-Leaders
World.content:
COLOMBIA · JUSTICE

Key Facts — What happened On 18 September 2026, Colombia’s JEP court began enforcing restorative sanctions on seven former FARC leaders.

— The context The JEP is the court created by Colombia’s 2016 peace deal to judge the worst conflict crimes.

— Why it matters It is the first time the FARC leadership’s kidnapping sentence moves from ruling to enforcement.

— The catch These are not prison sentences; the men live at fixed homes, work set hours and wear electronic monitors.

— Who it affects The seven ex-commanders, kidnapping victims awaiting redress, and anyone judging whether Colombia’s peace deal is enforced.

— What comes next Five of the men start a cemetery search in Pitalito, Huila, running from 21 to 30 September.

Seven former guerrilla commanders must now live where the court says, work set hours and wear electronic monitors — without going to prison.

Plaza de Bolívar in Bogotá, with Colombia’s Capitol building behind (Photo: szeke, CC BY-SA 2.0 via Flickr)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesWhat this means, and what's next › RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. × Economy impact Key players Stability What's next Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Colombia’s JEP FARC sanctions moved into enforcement on 18 September 2026, when the tribunal ordered their execution. The seven men sanctioned are former members of the last FARC-EP Secretariat, held responsible in Case 01 for mass kidnapping.

What the JEP decided on 18 September

The Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) is the court created by Colombia’s 2016 peace agreement to judge the worst conflict crimes. On 18 September 2026, its first-instance section for cases where defendants admit responsibility took charge of executing the sanctions.

The sanctions themselves were set earlier. The first-instance ruling came on 16 September 2025, and the JEP says the appeal decision became final on 1 July 2026.

Work was meant to start on 15 August 2026. It was delayed while requests to clarify the ruling were settled on 24 August, according to El Tiempo and El Universal.

Case 01 covers hostage-taking and serious deprivation of liberty by the former FARC-EP guerrilla. The JEP says the seven men are most responsible for more than 21,000 kidnappings between 1982 and 2016.

The seven men and their terms

Rodrigo Londoño Echeverri, long known as Timochenko, and Pablo Catatumbo Torres Victoria each received eight years. Jaime Alberto Parra Rodríguez received seven years, ten months and two days.

Milton de Jesús Toncel Redondo received seven years, eight months and 25 days. Pastor Lisandro Alape Lascarro received six years, 11 months and 22 days.

Julián Gallo Cubillos received six years, and Rodrigo Granda Escobar five. The first-instance ruling had given all seven the maximum eight years.

The appeals section found that three men did not deserve the maximum. It said they took part in only one or two of three kidnapping policies, or had no command over troops.

How the JEP FARC sanctions work in daily life

These are not prison sentences. The men must keep a fixed home in the area assigned for each phase.

They must do restorative work from Monday to Friday, 08:00 to 17:00. They cannot leave their assigned department without authorisation, or leave Colombia except in exceptional cases the court approves.

Each must wear an electronic monitoring device at all times. The JEP says the men will carry out 79 restorative projects in seven regions, in phases running into 2034.

The projects include rural roads, demining, environmental work, historical memory and the search for missing people.

The first tasks

From 21 to 30 September, Londoño, Granda, Alape, Parra and Toncel will support a cemetery search in Pitalito, Huila. They will help dig under the Search Unit for Disappeared Persons.

Catatumbo and Gallo were not assigned to the Huila work. El Tiempo reports that they begin memory activities in Bogotá instead.

Why this is a test for transitional justice

This is the first time the JEP has moved the FARC leadership’s kidnapping sentence from ruling to enforcement. That makes it a practical test of a model built on repair rather than prison.

The appeal ruling tightened the rules by adding fixed schedules, set locations and monitoring. It also dropped a slavery conviction on due-process grounds, while punishing the same acts as torture and cruel treatment.

The JEP has said the sanctions only work if the state pays for them. It asked for about 121,858 million pesos (US$39.0 million) to start its first two restorative sentences.

The previous government initially set aside 20,000 million pesos (US$6.4 million), the JEP says. Those figures use 19 September 2026 rates, about 3,128 Colombian pesos to the dollar.

What expats and investors in Latin America should watch

For foreigners living in Colombia or holding Colombian assets, this is a rule-of-law signal rather than a market event. It shows the peace court can carry a ruling through appeal and into practice.

The bigger question is political: President Abelardo de la Espriella took office on 7 August 2026. Parties in his government have since filed two proposals affecting the JEP.

On 17 September, senator Enrique Gómez Martínez proposed moving 100,000 million pesos (US$32.0 million) out of the JEP’s 2027 budget. The JEP says the plan has the president’s backing and threatens its work.

A separate reform in the Senate would let military courts review JEP rulings against members of the security forces. Anyone weighing legal predictability in Colombia should follow both debates.

What is still unclear

It is not yet known whether Congress will approve the budget cut, or how any cut would affect the restorative projects.

The JEP has not publicly detailed what would happen to a sanctioned man who breaks the rules. The names of the magistrates supervising the execution have also not been confirmed.

The longer view

Under the 2016 peace deal, those who tell the truth and admit responsibility get five to eight years of restorative sanctions. This case is the clearest test of that bargain so far.

How the work goes over the coming years will shape how Colombians judge the peace deal. The next milestone is the Pitalito search, which ends on 30 September.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

Are the seven former FARC leaders going to prison?

No. They received restorative sanctions of five to eight years. They must live where the court says, work set hours, wear electronic monitors and carry out repair projects.

What is Case 01 about?

It covers kidnapping and serious deprivation of liberty by the former FARC-EP guerrilla. The JEP counts more than 21,000 kidnappings between 1982 and 2016.

Why did enforcement start only now?

The appeal ruling became final on 1 July 2026. A planned 15 August start was delayed until clarification requests were settled, and the execution order came on 18 September.

Sources: Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) statements of 1 July, 7 July, 14 July and 18 September 2026; El Espectador; El Tiempo; El Universal; Infobae; CNN en Español.

World.title: United States Third-Country Deportation Ruling Upheld in Boston
World.content:
UNITED STATES · IMMIGRATION

Key Facts — What happened A US appeals court in Boston upheld a ruling that migrants must get notice before third-country deportation.

— The context The court reviewed 2025 DHS guidance allowing removals with as little as 24 hours notice.

— Why it matters Under the ruling, Latin American migrants sent to Mexico and the Caribbean must learn their destination and object first.

— The catch This is a process right only; it grants no new status and people can still be removed.

— Who it affects Mexico received about 20,000 of more than 25,000 third-country deportees, mostly Cubans, Venezuelans, Guatemalans, Hondurans, Salvadorans and Nicaraguans.

— What comes next The government may seek Supreme Court review; the ruling is not yet in effect.

The First Circuit says migrants must be told where they are being sent — and get a real chance to say they fear harm there.

The Moakley federal courthouse on Boston’s waterfront, seat of the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit (Photo: 4300streetcar, CC BY 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesWhat this means, and what's next › RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. × Economy impact Key players Stability What's next Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

A US federal appeals court in Boston has largely upheld a third-country deportation ruling against the Trump administration. On Friday, 18 September 2026, it said migrants need notice and a fair chance to object before such removals.

What the court decided

The case, number 26-1212, is D.V.D. v. US Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Judges Lara Montecalvo, Jeffrey Howard and Seth Aframe heard it. Judge Aframe wrote the unanimous opinion.

The panel affirmed a 25 February 2026 judgment by US District Judge Brian Murphy of Massachusetts. He had set aside the DHS guidance on third-country removals as unlawful under federal administrative law.

The core holding is simple. Before any third-country removal, a person must get effective notice and a meaningful chance to claim fear of persecution or torture.

The right to object “means little if one does not receive prior notice of the intended removal destination.”

The person also needs “a meaningful opportunity to contest that destination,” Judge Aframe wrote. The court said DHS’s reading would deny that protection to “a substantial swath of noncitizens.”

The panel did overturn one part of the judgment. On standing grounds, it dropped the rule that DHS first try the home country or a country the migrant chose.

The policy behind the case

DHS issued the guidance on 30 March 2025. With credible diplomatic assurances from a country, it said, people could be removed “without the need for further procedures.”

The appeals court said the guidance generally allowed only 24 hours of notice or less. A July 2025 memo from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) allowed as little as six hours in some urgent cases.

The Supreme Court paused an earlier injunction in this case in June 2025. The First Circuit also paused Judge Murphy’s February judgment while the appeal was heard.

What the third-country deportation ruling means for Latin American migrants

Latin Americans are among those most affected. The opinion describes a Guatemalan plaintiff removed to Mexico, which then deported him to Guatemala.

CBS News reported that recent flights to Liberia carried people from Brazil, Colombia, Guatemala, Honduras and Venezuela. Under the ruling, such people must learn the destination in advance and be able to say they fear it.

For a Cuban or Venezuelan facing removal, this means time to object before boarding a plane.

It is a process right, not permission to stay. It grants no new status, and people can still be removed once their fear claim is fairly heard.

What it means for Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean

Mexico is by far the main receiving country. The Third Country Deportation Watch, run by Refugees International and Human Rights First, counts about 20,000 of more than 25,000 cases there.

Refugees International says Mexico received at least 12,983 non-Mexicans from the US in 2025. Most were Cubans, Venezuelans, Guatemalans, Hondurans, Salvadorans and Nicaraguans.

The group says Mexico’s migration institute buses most of them south to cities such as Villahermosa and Tapachula. Many Central Americans are then sent on to their home countries.

The tracker says El Salvador, Costa Rica, Panama, Guatemala, Honduras, Belize, Dominica, St Kitts and Nevis, and St Lucia received deportees. Jamaica, the Dominican Republic, the Bahamas, Grenada, and Antigua and Barbuda have signed agreements.

If the ruling takes effect and survives review, flights to these countries could slow. Each person would need time to receive notice and raise a fear claim first.

Why this matters for expats and investors

Governments in Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean have made deals with Washington that depend on this policy. A slower process could change how many people arrive and how much planning and money they need.

For businesses in border cities and southern Mexico, fewer or slower transfers may ease pressure on shelters and local services. For families with mixed immigration status, the extra notice gives more time to find a lawyer.

What is not known

It is not known when the decision will take effect. DHS General Counsel James Percival said the policy “continues, as the First Circuit’s ruling is not currently in effect.”

It is also unclear how many hours of notice will count as effective, since the court set no fixed number. The government has not said publicly whether it will seek Supreme Court review or rewrite the policy.

What to watch next

The first thing to watch is a government petition to the Supreme Court, which could decide the rule for the whole country. The First Circuit’s decision binds courts in Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Puerto Rico.

People facing removal should keep their papers in order and speak to an immigration lawyer. The coming months should bring a clearer answer on how much notice migrants will get.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the First Circuit rule?

It said DHS must give migrants effective notice of a third-country destination and a meaningful chance to raise fear of persecution or torture there.

Does this stop all deportations to third countries?

No. Removals can continue after proper notice and a fair chance to object, and DHS says the ruling is not yet in effect.

Why does it matter for Mexico?

About 20,000 of the more than 25,000 people sent to third countries went to Mexico, according to Third Country Deportation Watch.

Sources: US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit opinion in D.V.D. v. DHS, 18 September 2026; CBS News; ABC News; The Spokesman-Review; Refugees International and Human Rights First’s Third Country Deportation Watch.

World.title: Costa Rica Raises El Niño Alert as Rainfall Shortage Deepens
World.content:
Costa Rica has placed 23 municipalities under an orange alert as months of below-normal rainfall linked to El Niño deepen concerns over water supplies, agriculture, livestock and environmental conditions in several areas. Another 51 municipalities are under a yellow alert, leaving most of Costa Rica covered by one of the two warning levels as authorities monitor a rainfall deficit that has become particularly serious in the North Pacific.

In that area, rainfall has been running about 37% below normal, which is a significant shortfall for an area that is already more vulnerable than much of Costa Rica to extended dry periods and water shortages. The orange alert covers municipalities in the North Pacific, Central Pacific and Los Santos areas, including several communities that are important to our tourism industry, such as Liberia, Nicoya, Santa Cruz, Carrillo, Monteverde, Garabito, Quepos and Puntarenas.

Keep in mind, the alert does not mean travel has been restricted or that normal activities have been suspended, but it signals that authorities believe the accumulated lack of rain has reached a level that requires greater attention and preparation. The concern is less about whether it rains on any particular afternoon and more about how much rain has fallen over a longer period.

Costa Rica can still experience strong thunderstorms, localized flooding and heavy downpours while remaining in an overall rainfall deficit, because a few intense storms do not necessarily replace the amount of water that has been missing over weeks or months. That is likely to be especially noticeable this weekend, when Tropical Wave 45 is expected to increase rainfall and thunderstorms across several areas as it interacts with the Intertropical Convergence Zone.

For those of use that live here, that can create what appears to be a contradiction: authorities may warn about possible flooding and landslides during a period when areas are also dealing with drought-like conditions. Both can happen at the same time. Short bursts of heavy rain can overwhelm drainage systems, swell rivers and trigger landslides, while the broader rainy season still produces less water than normal for reservoirs, groundwater, farms and ecosystems.

The North Pacific remains one of the main areas of concern because the rainfall shortage there is already substantial and because Guanacaste traditionally becomes much drier toward the end of the year. That raises questions about how water supplies could be affected if the deficit continues into the normal dry season, particularly in communities where tourism, agriculture and residential development all place heavy demand on available water.

Hotels, restaurants and other tourism businesses are not currently facing widespread restrictions because of the alert, but a prolonged shortage could become more important as Costa Rica approaches the high tourism season. Agriculture and livestock are also vulnerable because less rainfall can reduce water availability for crops, pasture and animals, while rivers and wetlands can experience lower water levels that affect fish and wildlife.

El Niño is a climate pattern associated with unusually warm waters in the tropical Pacific Ocean and can influence weather across much of the world. In Costa Rica, it often contributes to drier-than-normal conditions along parts of the Pacific slope. The current alert is therefore focused not just on immediate weather but on the accumulated effect of the rainy season so far.

Authorities here are expected to continue watching rainfall levels, water availability and conditions in the most affected areas as September and October progress. Those months will be important because they normally form part of the wetter period of the year across much of Costa Rica, giving a limited window to reduce the rainfall deficit before the dry season begins.

For the moment, those in affected areas are being encouraged to use water carefully and follow local updates, while authorities monitor whether upcoming rains are enough to improve conditions or whether the shortage continues into the final months of the year.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Juan Santamaría Airport Keeps Highest Passenger Experience Accreditation
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Juan Santamaría International Airport has renewed the highest level of an international passenger experience accreditation, placing the country’s main airport among just 12 worldwide holding the distinction in 2026. The airport, operated by AERIS, received Level 5 accreditation for the second consecutive year under the Airports Council International Customer Experience Accreditation program. Level 5 is the highest of five levels in the program.

The distinction does not simply rank airports based on how much passengers like them. Instead, ACI examines how well an airport has built the passenger experience into the way it operates, including how it listens to travelers, trains employees, measures service, uses technology and coordinates the different companies and government agencies working inside the terminal.

Juan Santamaría is one of only 12 airports worldwide currently holding Level 5 accreditation. Quito’s Mariscal Sucre International Airport in Ecuador is the other Level 5 airport in the Americas. “Renewing Level 5 represents for us an achievement as important as reaching it for the first time, because it demonstrates that we have managed to maintain a culture of service over time and that the passenger experience is part of the decisions we make to continue transforming the airport,” AERIS CEO Ricardo Hernández said.

AERIS has expanded its passenger service programs over the past year, including an Excellence Program aimed at improving customer service across the airport community. The airport also strengthened its Customer Experience Committee, which brings together airlines, airport operators, businesses and government agencies to identify problems and coordinate improvements.

About 500 employees from AERIS and other organizations working at Juan Santamaría participated in training, workshops and passenger service activities during 2025. Travelers have also begun seeing more technology designed to reduce waiting times and make moving through the terminal easier.

The airport is using LiDAR technology to anonymously monitor passenger flows around passport control and security in the international departures area. According to AERIS, Juan Santamaría is the first airport in Latin America to use the technology for this purpose. Other projects include automated eGates for immigration, self-service baggage drop systems and new scanning technology at security checkpoints. The airport began operating its first four eGates in the arrivals area on September 8.

Accessibility has also become part of the effort. Juan Santamaría joined the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower program, an international system that allows travelers with non-visible disabilities to discreetly signal that they may need extra time or assistance. The airport has also achieved Level 1 in ACI’s Accessibility Enhancement Accreditation program.

Recent passenger surveys indicate that the changes are being noticed. At the end of June 2026, Juan Santamaría scored 4.44 out of 5 for overall passenger satisfaction and 4.38 for overall experience under ACI’s Airport Service Quality program. Its satisfaction score was slightly above the worldwide average of 4.38 for airports handling a similar number of passengers.

The accreditation comes as Juan Santamaría continues a broader modernization program. The airport currently connects Costa Rica with 42 destinations and is served by 26 international airlines and two domestic carriers. For travelers, the Level 5 renewal does not mean every trip through Juan Santamaría will be trouble-free.

Lines, flight disruptions and busy travel periods remain part of airport travel. What the accreditation indicates is that passenger experience has become part of the airport’s formal management system rather than a collection of individual customer service projects. For Costa Rica, that carries added importance because Juan Santamaría is the first and last impression of the country for millions of international visitors each year.

World.title: Video of Orcas Spotted Near Costa Rica’s Cocos Island in Rare Encounter
World.content:
A group of orcas has been spotted near Costa Rica’s Cocos Island, giving park rangers a rare look at one of the ocean’s most recognizable predators in waters where the species is only occasionally reported. Between four and five orcas were observed around midday yesterday near Manuelita Islet, just off Cocos Island.

Park rangers found them while carrying out routine monitoring in the waters surrounding Cocos Island National Park. Several of the orcas appeared to be juveniles, raising the possibility that the animals were traveling as part of a family group. The encounter was captured on video.

While orcas can travel enormous distances and have previously been documented in Costa Rican waters, they are not considered regular visitors around Cocos Island. The remote national park is much better known for marine species that are routinely encountered there, including hammerhead sharks, whale sharks, manta rays and dolphins.

Scientific records show just how unusual an orca encounter around the island can be. A study examining Costa Rican Pacific sightings between 1990 and 2020 identified 31 reported orca encounters involving 105 animals throughout the country’s Pacific waters. Only four of those sightings, involving a total of 10 animals, were recorded around Cocos Island.

The South Pacific accounted for the largest number during the study period, with 17 sightings involving 56 animals. Researchers have not established that the latest appearance represents any broader change in the distribution of orcas around Costa Rica. Orcas are highly mobile animals capable of traveling long distances while searching for food. Their movements can be influenced by prey availability as well as changing ocean conditions.

The waters surrounding Cocos Island provide an unusually rich marine environment. Ocean currents and underwater mountains help concentrate nutrients and marine life around the island, supporting large populations of fish and other animals that can potentially attract top predators.

Orcas are opportunistic hunters with diets that vary significantly between populations. Depending on where they live and the group involved, they can feed on fish, rays, sharks, sea turtles and marine mammals. Their presence in Costa Rica is not unprecedented.

Occasional sightings have been documented for decades along the country’s Pacific coast, with previous reports occurring in the northern, central and southern Pacific as well as around Cocos Island. However, researchers still know relatively little about the orcas that pass through tropical waters compared with populations studied in areas such as the Pacific Northwest, Norway and Antarctica.

That makes individual sightings potentially useful for understanding when the animals appear in Costa Rican waters and where they travel. The latest encounter also highlights the extraordinary marine biodiversity surrounding Cocos Island, located approximately 550 kilometers (342 miles) off Costa Rica’s Pacific coast.

Its isolation and surrounding protected waters have made the island one of Costa Rica’s most important marine conservation areas and an internationally known destination for experienced divers.

For now, yesterday’s encounter appears to be another uncommon visit rather than evidence that orcas are becoming regular residents around the island. But for the park rangers conducting their routine monitoring, it provided a rare encounter with a species that can pass through Costa Rican waters without being seen for long periods.

World.title: Costa Rican TikTok Star Julián Valverde Reported in ICE Custody
World.content:
Costa Rican content creator Julián Valverde, known online as Julián Valjota, is in the custody of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. A source close to the case confirmed his custody, and said the 26-year-old, whose full name is José Julián Valverde Meneses, is being processed by US immigration authorities.

Costa Rican journalist Elías Alvarado confirmed on Thursday night that Valverde was detained on Wednesday, in Orlando, and the reasons have not been made public. Alvarado said people close to Valverde told him that Orlando police stopped the creator while he was driving.

Alvarado also said no official information yet establishes the circumstances of the detention, Valverde’s current immigration status, or whether he faces a final order of removal from the United States. Before the custody confirmation, Alvarado had said Valverde did not appear in ICE records.

The detention became public yesterday through fellow content creator Christopher Araya, known as Araya Vlogs. In a video, Araya said Valverde had been held for nearly 24 hours and had not yet appeared before a judge. He added that the group was in contact with Valverde’s attorney and with lawyers who specialize in immigration.

Araya said Valverde had asked him to share the news in order to head off rumors. Valverde’s last social media post, published Wednesday night, was a video recorded inside his car with a patrol vehicle visible behind him. Costa Rica’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it is following the case. The ministry’s Consular Department and the Consulate General in Miami said they are aware of the situation and are making inquiries with US immigration authorities to learn more about the citizen’s circumstances.

The case also reached the Legislative Assembly. Frente Amplio lawmaker Joselyn Sáenz called on the Foreign Ministry to act to protect Valverde and all Costa Ricans held by ICE in the United States. She also criticized ICE over what she described as alleged inhumane, degrading and discriminatory treatment.

Valverde has lived in the United States for more than five years and left Costa Rica in search of work opportunities. He has frequently joked in his content about a possible deportation, though those remarks do not establish his current immigration status or explain this week’s detention.

Costa Rica is among the countries whose citizens are subject to mandatory consular notification when arrested or detained in the United States. US authorities must therefore notify the relevant Costa Rican consulate without delay.

The next steps depend on facts not yet made public. If a final removal order exists, ICE could move ahead with his departure, including arranging travel documents. If he has an open immigration case, a pending protection claim or another legal avenue to challenge removal, his attorneys could pursue those remedies.

World.title: International News:  Trump to meet Venezuela’s Interim President Delcy Rodriguez in New York
World.content:
International News: Trump to meet Venezuela’s Interim President Delcy Rodriguez in New York

By Zoila Palma: US President Donald Trump is set to meet Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez in New York on Tuesday, marking the first in-person meeting between the two leaders since Washington ousted former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January.

The meeting is expected to take place on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz confirmed the meeting during a briefing on Friday, saying Trump will host a reception for UN General Assembly leaders.

“The president will host a UN General Assembly leaders’ reception. There, he’ll participate in a pull-aside with the acting president Rodriguez of Venezuela,” Waltz said.

The meeting comes amid closer US-Venezuela engagement following the change in leadership.

Last month, the two countries signed an energy agreement that would allow the United States to take partial control of Venezuela’s vast oil reserves, with American companies expected to play a role in efforts to revive the country’s energy sector.

World.title: Tonight’s September Fest block party to bring music, food and community spirit to Burns Avenue
World.content:
Tonight’s September Fest block party to bring music, food and community spirit to Burns Avenue

By Zoila Palma: For the first time, Burns Avenue in San Ignacio will come alive with a Grand September Fest Block Party tonight as residents and visitors are invited to celebrate Belize’s 45th anniversary with an evening of music, food, entertainment and community spirit.

The event is being organized by San Ignacio and Santa Elena Town Councilor Aaron Mai and sponsored by Cayo North Area Representative Michel Chebat.

The block party is scheduled to run from 6:00 p.m until midnight and will feature live steel band performances, patriotic Belizean music by a DJ, food and drinks, and local vendors showcasing a variety of products.

Come out and support our local businesses!

World.title: Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital marks 31 years of service with expanded units
World.content:
Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital marks 31 years of service with expanded units

By Zoila Palma: The Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital (KHMH) is celebrating 31 years of service to Belize, highlighting the doctors, nurses, physical therapists and support staff who continue to provide critical healthcare to patients from across the country.

Anniversary activities began with a church service and include raffles, giveaways and fellowship, with the celebrations culminating in an official ceremony, staff awards and karaoke.

As part of the anniversary activities, Prime Minister John Briceño joined hospital staff for the official opening of two new units, including an expanded Hemodialysis Unit.

Hemodialysis Unit Manager Michelle Casimiro said the additional space is necessary as KHMH serves patients from across Belize. “KHMH is a national referral hospital. We serve the whole entire public. We serve the whole entire country, so every patient that is affected by kidney failure, some sort of renal insufficiency, we have to see those patients, and so the space was necessary.”

The expanded unit now has 8 dialysis machines, with space to add 7 more as demand increases.

Meanwhile, KHMH’s Physiotherapy Department continues to treat between 20 and 30 patients daily, including people recovering from gunshot injuries, road traffic accidents, illnesses and other trauma.

Physical Therapist Noel Avila said the department’s five staff members face limitations in accommodating the demand. “We can’t see everybody all at once and we can only afford patients twice a week. If we had more staff, maybe we could facilitate more sessions for patients.”

KHMH Chief Executive Officer Sherine Reyes said the 31st anniversary is also an opportunity to recognize the hospital’s workforce while working to improve the institution’s relationship with the public. “We’re trying to change the image of the institution. We’re trying to have the public see us in a different light. Some of those staff has been the contributory factor to some of the changes that we’re having and we’re hoping that the public can also contribute in terms of giving us their feedback.”

Special guest Prime Minister John Briceño planted two trees just outside the hospital’s entrance marking the milestone.

World.title: International News: Armed groups escalate drone attacks across Colombia, Ombudsman reports
World.content:
International News: Armed groups escalate drone attacks across Colombia, Ombudsman reports

By Zoila Palma: Drone attacks by armed groups in Colombia increased by 146 percent during the first five months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, according to the country’s Ombudsman’s Office.

The attacks killed 21 people and injured 145 others, including children, as the use of explosive-laden drones becomes an increasingly prominent feature of Colombia’s armed conflict, Yahoo reports.

Ombudsman Iris Marín warned that the impact extends beyond those directly injured or killed, saying the constant sound of drones has created fear among communities in conflict-affected areas.

Homes, schools, petrol stations and other infrastructure have been targeted, while attacks and the threat of further strikes have contributed to displacement and restricted residents’ ability to travel, work in fields and access healthcare.

Armed groups commonly use improvised drones equipped with explosives for attacks and surveillance, including against rival groups and government forces and to monitor illegal coca-growing areas. The Ombudsman’s Office said the attacks have also restricted humanitarian missions and complicated efforts by displaced communities to return and remain in their territories. Human Rights Watch has separately reported that children are being trained in drone warfare and recruited by armed groups through social media.

The Colombian government is also using unmanned aircraft in its military operations, while authorities announced a $1.68 billion project in January to develop an anti-drone defense system.

World.title: Enrique Martinez & Sons brings Veslee car care products to Belize
World.content:
Enrique Martinez & Sons brings Veslee car care products to Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belizean motorists looking to keep their vehicles clean and protected can check out a range of Veslee car care products available through Enrique Martinez & Sons Ltd.

The product lineup features a variety of automotive cleaning, detailing and maintenance products designed for different areas of a vehicle.

The range shown includes products for cleaning and caring for vehicle interiors and exteriors, including the dashboard, upholstery, tires, glass and painted surfaces.

There are also several sprays, cleaners, polishes and other detailing products available for motorists who prefer to maintain their vehicles at home.

Enrique Martinez & Sons Ltd. continues to expand its automotive product selection, giving Belizean vehicle owners access to products for routine cleaning and vehicle care.

Customers looking to give their vehicle a fresh appearance can visit Enrique Martinez & Sons Ltd. and ask about the Veslee car care product lineup.

World.title: Military leaders arrive in Belize for 45th Independence celebrations
World.content:
Military leaders arrive in Belize for 45th Independence celebrations

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Belize Defence Force is hosting senior military leaders and representatives from several countries as Belize celebrates the weekend leading up to its 45th anniversary of Independence.

The international delegation includes Brigadier Carlos A. R. Lovell, Chief of Staff of the Barbados Defence Force; Brigadier General Miguel Maldonado Castro, Director of Human Resources for the Honduran Army; Brigadier Mahatma Williams, Acting Chief of Defence Staff of the Jamaica Defence Force; and Colonel Donald Henley, Defence Attaché of Canada in Mexico.

The official programme began Friday night with a Welcome Cocktail Reception at Grand Resort and Residences in Belize City, bringing together the visiting military representatives and Belizean dignitaries.

Today, Saturday, the programme continues with the JWIC Graduation Ceremony.

On Sunday, the international guests are expected to participate in a Cultural and Heritage Excursion to Caye Caulker, giving them an opportunity to experience Belizean culture and heritage.

The delegation is also expected to attend the Independence Eve Flag Raising Ceremony on Sunday night as Belize prepares to officially mark 45 years of Independence.

The activities will conclude on Monday, September 21, with Belize’s Independence Day celebrations and a parade in Belmopan.

The Belize Defence Force says the visit reflects the friendship and partnership shared between Belize and its international defence counterparts.

World.title: Verdes FC announces management changes after disappointing Concacaf and PLB results
World.content:
Verdes FC announces management changes after disappointing Concacaf and PLB results

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Verdes FC has announced that changes are coming at the managerial level after the club conducted what it described as a comprehensive assessment of its recent Concacaf Central American Cup campaign and its performance in the 2026/2027 Premier League of Belize Opening Season.

In an official statement, the club acknowledged that recent results have fallen below its standards and the expectations of supporters.

“We share that disappointment, and we take responsibility,” Verdes FC stated.

The club said its Concacaf campaign exposed areas requiring improvement, including squad depth, coaching continuity, training facilities, competitive preparation, player integration and overall football operations.

Verdes also revealed that it was unable to extend agreements with some key members of the coaching staff that guided the team to the 2026/27 Closing Season championship.

According to the club, approximately 12 to 14 Verdes players have also been involved in national team preparations and activities at different periods, creating additional workload alongside domestic and Concacaf competition.

Verdes said approximately nine players are currently dealing with varying degrees of injury, making recovery and rehabilitation a priority.

Following its internal assessment, the club said decisions have been made at the managerial level and that it will introduce “new and proven leadership” supported by a more centralized football structure.

The changes will focus on player management, workload monitoring, recovery, technical preparation, performance management, communication, accountability, tactical consistency and football operations.

Despite its recent struggles, Verdes says its objective remains unchanged.

“We intend to defend our championship,” the club stated.

World.title: International News: Google reveals Gemini AI gained unauthorized access to 3 outside systems
World.content:
International News: Google reveals Gemini AI gained unauthorized access to 3 outside systems

By Zoila Palma: Google has disclosed that its Gemini artificial intelligence model gained unauthorized access to three external computer systems during a security test in May, marking what the company described as the first known instance of its AI software carrying out an undirected computer hack.

The disclosure comes amid growing concerns about AI systems taking actions beyond the intentions of their human developers, NBC reports.

According to Google, Gemini accessed the systems after either guessing login credentials or finding credentials in a public repository. Google Vice President for Security Engineering Heather Adkins said the model believed the outside systems were part of the test. However, Gemini stopped before carrying out any further actions after gaining access.

Google said it does not consider the incidents to represent “misalignment,” a term used in the AI industry to describe systems acting contrary to their instructions or objectives. The company characterized the incidents as a case of mistaken identity, saying Gemini believed it was operating within a controlled test environment when it was actually connected to the real internet. Google said its investigation found no evidence of damage.

The incidents were discovered in July after cybersecurity company Irregular reviewed its testing of Gemini following similar disclosures by other AI companies.

Google said it subsequently investigated the incidents, notified the organizations operating the affected systems and informed federal authorities.

World.title: Anger in Cooper’s Pen
World.content:
Tents on the site of demolished houses in Cooper’s Pen, Trelawny (Horace Hines)

COOPER’S PEN, Trelawny — Residents here whose homes were demolished on August 11 say they are being forced to choose between accepting relocation grants they have not yet received and moving their tents and belongings temporarily to a site in New Town, Salt Marsh, for two weeks, with no clear indication of what will happen afterwards.

The residents, who have lived in tents since their homes were demolished, say they had been told by government officials to leave by today, Saturday, September 19. They have opted for the grants but insist they will not move until the money is deposited into their accounts.

The Government’s response to the demolition initially included humanitarian assistance for approximately 44 affected families, with the Ministry of Labour and Social Security, the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management, and other agencies providing emergency support.

Among those affected are Shane Ricketts, Moesha Richardson, and a woman who identified herself only as Tia.

Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer that he had signed for a $500,000 grant but would not leave before receiving it.

Richardson explained that residents were given the choice of accepting the grant or moving to the temporary location for two weeks. She questioned the practicality of relocating families for such a short period without a plan for their accommodation afterwards.

“Two weeks from now I still cannot find somewhere to live,” Richardson said. She said although she would accept the grant, she would have preferred a more permanent housing solution from the Government.

Richardson said Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness had previously given residents the impression that they would receive assistance with housing and eventually have an opportunity to acquire land.

Following Holness’s August 28 visit to Cooper’s Pen, the Government announced that land had been identified for eligible residents and that the intervention would include serviced lots and relocation grants. Holness said the lots would form part of a properly planned subdivision with roads, water, and electricity, while beneficiaries would contribute to the cost of the land and utilities according to their circumstances. He said he intended to oversee the process and hoped relocation could begin by December.

Meanwhile, Tia said her name was not on the grant list, leaving her uncertain about what assistance she would receive.

“I am feeling bad because I don’t know what’s happening for me because my name didn’t come down on the list,” she said, adding that she has lived in the community for a very long time.

Her house was demolished, and she said she and her baby had been separated, with the child staying with someone else while she remained in a tent. She said she would prefer a house or parcel of land.

“If I get a house option or a land option I’ll definitely choose the land or the house,” she said.

Tia said residents were unwilling to move to Salt Marsh for two weeks without knowing where they would go afterwards.

“No one is willing to go to Salt Marsh for two weeks and then we’re going to get kicked off,” she said.

Richardson, who has three family members in her household, including a three-year-old child and a 14-year-old nephew, said residents were particularly concerned about being required to move before receiving the grants.

“They are saying we have to move before we get the grant. So we have to take up our stuff before we get the grant,” she alleged.

She also questioned what she described as unequal treatment between residents whose homes were destroyed and those whose houses remain standing. Richardson said residents whose homes were not flattened were being considered for relocation to land, while those who lost their homes were being offered money to relocate.

“Our houses are demolished, and our businesses are demolished. So I don’t know why they’re not giving us back land as well,” she said.

Richardson said officials were expected to return earlier in the week to collect copies of documents residents had signed and provide arrangements for the grants, but no one had done so at the time of the

Observer interview on Friday.

Tova Hamilton, the Member of Parliament for Trelawny Northern, told the

Observer that the affected residents had opted for the grants and that the Government was proceeding with the relocation process.

“The Government is working with them to provide them with grants,” Hamilton confirmed.

She said development of land for the original Cooper’s Pen residents was also under way, including site clearing and preparations for roads, lot preparation, and other infrastructure. The Government said land was being surveyed for the first group of displaced families, with civil works expected to follow.

World.title: ‘He never lost his humble touch’
World.content:
Pall-bearers carry the remains of George Soutar out of the University Chapel on Friday. (Joseph Wellington)

MEMBERS of the legal, religious, business, and political fraternity gathered at the University Chapel on Friday to wish farewell to renowned attorney-at-law and political stalwart George Soutar.

Soutar, who served for years as legal advisor to the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP), died on August 10 after battling illness for an extended period. He was 81 years old.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer following the sermon, held at the University Chapel on the Mona campus of The University of the West Indies Mona (The UWI), Minister of Culture, Gender Entertainment, and Sport Olivia Grange remembered Soutar for his support when she took on the role of Member of Parliament for St Catherine Central.

“George was someone who was loved by those whose life he impacted, and I am one of those. When I entered representational politics, the late Edward Seaga, former prime minister, asked Mr Soutar to give me the support that was needed and to assist in raising funds as well. He brought a team of individuals in business together to give me the support in a seat that was considered the roughest seat in the island.

“With his support, and the structure that he put in place, I came through in flying colours, because everyone knows Spanish Town is not an easy place. Many individuals in the constituency benefited from his guidance, he was a no-nonsense person as well, he did not encourage antisocial behaviour or disrespect. He was a good person to have beside me in a constituency that was known to be a difficult one,” said Grange.

According to Grange, despite Soutar’s battle with his rare illness, national matters remained a priority for him.

“He was still very alert, we spoke frequently. He was always enquiring about what was happening, keeping abreast, and making recommendations and suggestions which I passed on to the prime minister. He was passionately loyal to his country. As much as he achieved the highest in his profession as a King’s Counsel and honoured by Jamaica, he never lost his humble touch,” said Grange.

Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness lauded Soutar for what he described as, “a critical role played by him in the transition of leadership in the Jamaica Labour Party”.

According to Holness, Soutar’s contribution to the Jamaica Labour Party was equally substantial and extended across many years.

“He served as legal advisor to the party, as chairman of its disciplinary committee, and as a trustee. In each of these roles, he brought not only his considerable legal knowledge, but also his deep understanding of the party, its history and tradition. George represented an important link between generations.

“There are those who would say that George was a non-elitist [and that] he served the [party] leader, and they misunderstood. George was an institutionalist; he served the institution, whomever the leader may be. And in that way, he protected the party. He protected what the party stood for. And so today, the party, I would say, is stable because of the actions of people like George. His advance was therefore vital not only because he knew the law, but because he understood context. When difficult or complex matters arose, his counsel could be relied on,” Holness told mourners during his tribute.

King’s Counsel Peter Champagnie shared that he was sponsored by Soutar when he was called to the Bar.

“I am forever grateful for his teachings. He was a mentor. There were moments when I would go to court, while he was in active practice — shortly after he had stopped going to court — and I would indicate to the judge that I am here holding a matter. And I was told, or would be told, yes, have a seat, wait your turn, essentially. And the moment I had it, I would call Mr Soutar,” said Champagnie.

Soutar was admitted to the Jamaican Bar in 1973.

He was appointed King’s Counsel in 2012 and awarded the Order of Distinction at the rank of Commander in 2017.

He also served as president of the Advocates’ Association of Jamaica and practised criminal, civil and company law for decades.

Soutar also chaired several major boards, including the Sports Development Foundation, the Public Broadcasting Corporation of Jamaica, and the Betting, Gaming and Lotteries Commission.

He also served on boards of the Jamaica Bauxite Mining Institute, Private Security Regulation Authority, and Aeronautical Telecommunications.

World.title: Dated merger plan drives family services shake-up
World.content:
Minister of Education, Skills, Youth and Information Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon

MINISTER with responsibility for youth Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon says the current leadership shake-up at the island’s two primary State family services agencies results from the activation of a dated Cabinet decision to merge the two entities.

The Jamaica Observer on Wednesday reported that the ministry had cut ties with the heads of the Child Protection and Family Services Agency (CPFSA) and the National Parenting Support Commission (NPSC) to undertake a major shift in their operations.

Consequently, the contract of CPFSA Chief Executive Officer Laurette Adams-Thomas — who took the helm of the agency in October 2023 — has not been renewed. She demits office next month.

Similarly the Observer has confirmed that the contract of NPSC head Kaysia Kerr — who took the reins of the agency in 2017 — had also not been renewed and she is no longer with the entity.

Responding to questions from the Observer following the weekly post-Cabinet media briefing on Wednesday, Morris Dixon said the planned merger is in keeping with the ongoing rationalisation of the public sector which has been placed in the hands of the Transformation Implementation Unit.

“So many years ago, long before my time, there would have been efforts to look at how we can rationalise the public sector, and there were certain entities that were flagged for merger, and these two entities were flagged for merger many years ago, and so the ministry is implementing that plan.

“The permanent secretary is doing the day-to-day work and working with the Ministry of Finance on that merger in keeping with the rationalisation of the public sector,” Morris Dixon explained.

She said, as a consequence, the posts of the two agency heads were impacted.

“In terms of both cases, they have contracts that came to an end and, in terms of the CPFSA, we will be going to market momentarily to advertise that post through the Public Services Commission. In terms of the National Parenting Support Commission, that was also a contract that came to an end and there was already a Cabinet decision to say both agencies should merge,” Morris Dixon said.

She pointed out that since the Cabinet decision the youth ministry has been working with the Ministry of Finance in terms of how to merge the two entities.

The CPFSA, an executive agency, is already an amalgamation having been formed from the merger of the Child Development Agency and the Office of Children’s Registry in 2017.

At the time then minister with responsibility for youth Fayval Williams indicated that, “There is still another step to go in terms of merging the CPFSA and the NPSC for a more holistic and coordinated approach to all the services that our children who are in State care will need.”

Williams said it was intended that an islandwide audit of children’s homes and places of safety, which was under way at the time, would identify the needs of the institutions.

“While we are going through that reform, we also started an audit of all our children’s homes to set a beginning point for the homes to identify what are the gaps and to give us a holistic view of what is on the ground, so we can make those reforms that are necessary,” Williams said then.

The audit was conducted within State-run and private facilities. There are more than 40 childcare facilities across Jamaica.

World.title: CUPS back on The Rock
World.content:
Mark Golding (second right), leader of the Opposition, engages with (from left) CUPS promoters Dane Lynch, Keisha Smith, and Tamark Bailey on a recent courtesy call to discuss Greatness Weekend 2026.

After approximately 11 years of building its reputation on New York’s entertainment scene, CUPS returns to Jamaica for its second staging on the island, bringing its signature immersive experience to Greatness Weekend 2026.

CUPS: Château Blanc takes place on Sunday, October 18, from 10:00 a m to 4:00 p m at BOJ Lawn in Kingston, offering patrons a premium blue-and-white, food-inclusive breakfast party.

For promoter Tamark Bailey, Jamaica was a natural choice for a brand whose growth in New York has been strongly supported by Jamaican and wider Caribbean audiences.

“Jamaica was a natural next chapter for CUPS. Our New York audience has always included a strong Jamaican and wider Caribbean community, so the connection between the brand and Jamaica has existed from the beginning. Greatness Weekend presented the perfect opportunity to bring that connection home while introducing the CUPS experience to a broader audience,” Bailey said.

Since its inception, CUPS has evolved from a social gathering into a premium lifestyle event known for creative themes, immersive décor, fashion, music, and high-energy entertainment.

Bailey said the team has deliberately elevated its production and hospitality while remaining focused on creating memorable experiences.

“Our patrons are not simply attending a party. From the moment they arrive, they enter a carefully curated environment where the décor, music, fashion, and energy work together seamlessly,” he said.

That approach will be central to Château Blanc, which will feature multiple breakfast stations, striking décor, and quality entertainment.

“Our goal is to engage every sense. We want guests to enjoy exceptional food, connect with great people, appreciate the décor, dance to outstanding music, and leave knowing they experienced something genuinely special,” Bailey explained.

Château Blanc forms part of the four-day Greatness Weekend, which runs October 16-19 in Kingston and features a series of entertainment and lifestyle events across Heroes’ weekend.

Bailey also views the Jamaican staging as an opportunity to deepen collaboration between the diaspora and the local creative sector. The event will utilise Jamaican caterers, entertainers, DJs, production professionals, hospitality workers, and other local businesses.

“Bringing CUPS to Kingston allows us to strengthen that relationship and create a meaningful bridge between our New York audience and patrons in Jamaica,” Bailey added.

World.title: ‘A profound betrayal’
World.content:
x

A district constable who was allegedly caught while trying to hide $400,000 she stole from a colleague was granted bail in the sum of $500,000 when she appeared in the St Andrew Parish Court on Thursday.

The district constable, 31-year-old Shaneek Plummer of Innswood Village, St Catherine, is charged with simple larceny and possession of criminal property.

Reports are that between 6:00 am and 6:30 am on Monday, a constable stationed at the Firearms and Narcotics Investigation Division (FNID) temporarily left a bag containing more that $650,000 cash in his office to use the restroom.

When he returned, he discovered that a portion of the cash was missing. Supervisors were notified and an internal investigation was launched.

Plummer, who was based at FIND, was subsequently arrested on the compound after she was reportedly caught attempting to conceal the cash. The funds were fully recovered and verified as the exact amount reported missing.

A file was prepared and submitted to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, which advised that Plummer should be charged.

Addressing the breach of trust, the director of FNID Superintendent of Police Patrae Rowe declared that the division holds its personnel to the highest operational and ethical standards.

“FNID handles some of the most sensitive investigations in Jamaica. That demands absolute and unshakable integrity from every member who walks through our doors,” Rowe stated.

“Stealing from a colleague is a profound betrayal of the JCF [Jamaica Constabulary Force]. We do not hesitate to investigate our own, as criminality has no place within these walls,” added Rowe.

World.title: THINKING AHEAD
World.content:
Rudolph Speid (centre), Jamaica football interim head coach, oversees a practice session at Verde Valle training centre in Zapopan, Mexico, on March 30, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

Although appointed on an interim basis, Reggae Boyz Head Coach Rudolph Speid says he’s already thinking about the 2030 FIFA World Cup Qualifying campaign, after naming the squad for the upcoming Concacaf Nations League campaign.

On Friday, the 24-man squad was revealed for the four games in the September to October international window, which kicks off next Friday against Guatemala at the National Stadium. The national senior men’s team will then host Honduras the following Monday before travelling to El Salvador on October 2 and Honduras on October 5.

Ten players who were not part of last September to November’s unsuccessful Concacaf World Cup qualifying campaign have been selected including winger Leon Bailey, who recently made his debut for Greek club Olympiakos. Only one, though, will be set for a debut in defender Miguel Freckleton who plays for Austrian League champions LASK.

The 23-year-old England-born centre back acquired his Jamaican passport earlier this month, having been tracked by the technical staff for close to a year. He played with Reggae Boyz defender Richard King last season at Scottish club St Mirren before moving to LASK this summer where he made his debut in the UEFA Champions League.

Speid, who the Jamaica Observer had reported will be in charge of the national team until December, believes he will be a great addition to the squad.

“We have been looking at him from last year, but his paperwork has now come through, so he’s eligible to represent Jamaica, so we can actually invite him,” he said.

“We were looking at him from last year when we scout our initial squad of players to play in the World Cup qualifiers, but he wasn’t ready to play for us yet. It’s his body of work over a particular period [that impressed us].”

Other notable call-ups are Israeli-based striker Javon East who last played for Jamaica in 2022 and American-born defender Tayvon Gray who last played in the 2024 Nations League.

Captain Andre Blake, Vice Captain Damion Lowe, defender Joel Latibeaudiere and midfielders Isaac Hayden and Kasey Palmer are among the experienced names in the squad. Mount Pleasant Football Academy goalkeeper Shaquan Davis and Cavalier’s Christopher Ainsworth are the only local players in the squad.

The team consists of several players aged 23 and under, including forward Kaheim Dixon and relatively newcomers Andre Brooks, Brandon Cover and Courtney Clarke who are all based in England.

While aiming to be competitive immediately, Speid says the current squad is also being built with the future in mind.

“The selection criteria is different from when we last played the World Cup qualifiers. This time we’re looking at player form and also looking at player trajectory. So we look at where they are now and where we think they will be when the qualifiers come around, plus where we think they will be when the [2030] World Cup will be played,” he said.

“As everyone knows that at the World Cup, the teams that do well is somewhere in the [age] range of about 27 to 27 and a half, so we have deliberately reduced the age by three years in line with keeping with what will be required for the World Cup qualifiers. So we’re planning short term, medium term and long term, so some of these selections are based on those forward planning.”

Jamaica will need to finish in the top two of the group if they are to advance to the quarter-finals where they will join top-ranked Concacaf nations USA, Mexico, Canada and Panama.

World.title: $1.6b for long-overdue fixes at three west Kgn high schools
World.content:
Member of Parliament for Kingston Western Desmond McKenzie hugs his Cabinet colleague, Minister of Education Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon on Thursday, following her announcement that $1.6 billion is being allocated to three secondary schools in his constituency.Garfield Robinson

A total of $1.6 billion is being allocated to three high schools in the Kingston Western region for long-overdue upgrades, Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon told their principals on Thursday.

Morris Dixon, who made the disclosure at the Kingston Western Principals’ Awards function, identified the three schools as Denham Town High, Kingston High, and St Andrew Technical High (STATHS).

Morris Dixon said Kingston Western Member of Parliament Desmond McKenzie had long advocated the need for educational support in the constituency. Now, Denham Town High is set to receive funds to assist with the rebuilding of its facilities.

“Denham Town High School, your Member of Parliament has talked non-stop to my ministry about that project; it is currently at the Public Procurement Committee, which is its last step before going to Cabinet,” she said, adding that rebuilding would start within two years after Cabinet approval.

The news delighted Principal Yvette Richards-Thompson who said the rebuilding will allow teachers to provide quality service.

“The building that was proposed has been a long time coming. It is an administrative building which includes vocational areas and some other essential areas. With this now we will be able to cater more to our students’ needs,” Richards-Thompson said, adding that the new facilities will make the learning environment more comfortable.

“One of our main buildings was damaged by the earthquake two years ago, and that building housed four classrooms plus two science labs, and so that is a significant loss. And considering also safety, we do not want buildings that would pose a risk to our students,” she said.

Denham Town High is experiencing a major revolution, with the results of its students in external examinations improving rapidly while instances of misconduct have declined sharply.

The school recorded an 88 per cent pass rate in mathematics in the Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) this year, up from 11 per cent last year, with its overall pass rate at the CSEC level improving from 48 per cent last year to 73 per cent this year.

On Wednesday Richards-Thompson told the Jamaica Observer that the improvement was the result of deliberate strategic planning, including providing extra classes and identifying and addressing students’ learning gaps.

Meanwhile McKenzie, at Thursday’s function, said there is a need for improved buildings at Denham Town High School, and this has impacted learning for a long time.

“Now [that] we have reached to the stage where these issues will be solved, I am looking forward to it, and all of this will only enhance our education,” he said, adding that the school has faced these challenges for more than 40 years.

The funds being allocated to Kingston High School will be used to build a perimeter wall.

Morris Dixon said that after Cabinet approval the building of the wall would take six to nine months.
