Kingston High Principal Jermaine Loutin said the school has been without a wall for over 20 years.

“We’re happy that it is now in a state that it’s going to be [built]. This will now help our safety and security. It was a serious issue when we have our community functions, when we have our sports day, the entire community comes and we’re not able to keep the children as safe as we can,” Loutin said.

At STATHS the funds will be used to construct a new lab.

“A lot of STATHS labs look like they were there from a long time ago, and we need to update,” Morris Dixon said, adding that the school will be outfitted with “a state-of-the-art renewable energy lab”.

Principal Dr Worrel Hibbert said the school has explored options for building the skills needed to understand renewable energy.

“It is a wonderful idea; we have already put together a curriculum so essentially we are just waiting on the minister and the lab to be built… We have been doing renewable energy classes; we already started those at the school,” Hibbert said.

Morrison Dixon also told the principals the education ministry intends to create two performing arts schools within the next two years, one of which will be in the area.

“We’re not building it new, we’re using an existing school and converting it into a performing arts school, changing its curriculum, and then adding the state-of-the-art auditorium where they can do performances,” Morris Dixon said.

World.title: US$45,000 undeclared cash lands man in court
World.content:
MONTEGO BAY, St James — A man who entered the island with US$45,000 (approximately $7 million) in cash which he allegedly failed to declare, has found himself before the courts facing a charge of possession of criminal property.

The accused, Robert Tong, arrived in Jamaica on a flight from Miami with the cash allegedly concealed in a an envelope.

Under the law people entering Jamaica with in excess of US$10,000 in cash, cheque or otherwise, need to declare this on the online Customs and Immigration C5 form.

When Tong appeared before Judge Natiesha Fairclough-Hylton in the St James Parish Court on Wednesday, the court was told that after the money was found in his possession he told authorities that the US$45,000 represented his savings and that he had brought the money to Jamaica for a property-related purpose.

However, he was reportedly unable to provide sufficient documentation at the time to satisfactorily back-up his account for his possession of the cash.

The matter took on further significance after Tong’s cellular phone was seized during the investigation.

Conversations allegedly found on the device between Tong and another man reportedly included discussions about sending money on several occasions, including references to bringing money to Jamaica and instructions concerning how the funds should be received.

The cash was subsequently seized, and Tong was arrested and later charged.

Under caution, Tong allegedly sought to explain the legitimacy of the funds, telling authorities: “My money is legit, it is from my trust.”

Wednesday Tong’s attorney Henry McCurdy provided the court with further context regarding the origin and intended purpose of the money as he made a bail application.

According to McCurdy, the money formed part of a family trust from which Tong receives a specified amount each month. He further told the court that his client had supplied documentation to Customs officers in relation to the money.

“My client has provided proof to the Customs officers. They went through six months of the bank statements where they saw where money went in and came out and were satisfied that he had accounted for the money,” McCurdy said.

McCurdy also told the court that Tong is married to a Jamaican and has three properties in Jamaica.

He said the US$45,000 was intended to facilitate payment to a contractor for refurbishing work on one of those properties, which had reportedly suffered damage during Hurricane Melissa.

The court, having heard the bail submission, granted Tong bail in the sum of $700,000, with provision for up to three sureties. Tong was also made subject to reporting conditions, requiring him to report to a specified police station on designated days. In addition, a stop order was imposed against him at all ports of entry and exit.

He is scheduled to return to court on October 28.

World.title: France’s National Rally criticizes Russia in rare rebuke
World.content:
But the statement also came after French President Emmanuel Macron chaired a rare crisis meeting Friday at which the country's political leaders, including Bardella, were briefed on the threats posed by Russia’s war in Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East.



Le Pen and Bardella also cited the August drone attack at Leipzig airport, which German authorities attributed to Russia. "No provocation, clandestine operation, or destabilization effort could lead France to facilitate Russia’s achievement of its war aims in Ukraine," the far-right leaders write.

The statement marks a rare show of unity within a party that has been divided over whether to treat the Kremlin as the enemy. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 exposed fault lines within the movement.

Le Pen has historically taken a warmer stance toward Russia; she has met Russian President Vladimir Putin in the past and her party took a €9.4 million loan from a Czech-Russian bank with links to the Kremlin, which has been repaid since. Bardella, a member of the European Parliament, has been more eager to portray Russia as a threat to France and Europe.

Le Pen, who hopes to succeed Macron as president next year, is open to supplying military equipment to Ukraine but has ruled out providing additional financial assistance as Kyiv continues to fend off Russia's ongoing assault.

"Firmness in the face of hostile actions and the pursuit of a diplomatic resolution to the war are not contradictory," reads the statement.

The National Rally is expected to release its campaign platform before the end of the year, potentially clarifying its positions on Ukraine and Russia.

World.title: Germany’s top general to lead NATO’s highest military authority
World.content:
Breuer will take over from Dragone next July and will serve a three-year term.

The rest of the votes were kept secret to avoid the risk of breeding disloyalty and divisions over the result, said one NATO official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely.

The German four-star general beat Canada's chief of defense Jennie Carignan for the role. He was seen as the favorite given Berlin's status as Europe’s top defense spender and implicit backing from Washington. Breuer had campaigned on Germany's leading role in defense spending as European allies come under U.S. pressure to take control of their own defense.

Carignan, Ottawa’s top general since 2024, made her pitch about reinvigorating the role of the military committee and signaling enduring transatlantic unity inside NATO. Strained bilateral ties between Canada and the U.S. were seen by NATO officials as making Carignan’s case more difficult.

The result underscores Berlin's growing role in the alliance, as it takes over senior military roles and assumes greater operational responsibility for protecting frontline states with a regional army command focused on Estonia and Latvia and a permanent deployment in Lithuania.

The chair of NATO’s military committee is expected to give honest military advice to allies — helping assess the feasibility, financing and capabilities of operations. They oversee dozens of working groups of NATO military staff, and broker consensus on formulating military advice.

World.title: NATO ‘ready’ for potential Russian false flag attack, alliance’s top general says
World.content:
NATO is ready to respond to a potential Russian escalation on Europe’s eastern flank, the alliance's top general Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone said Saturday, amid growing warnings of a possible staged attack by Moscow.

“The alliance is ready, the structure is ready, the soldiers … the weapons are ready,” Dragone told reporters during a regular meeting of the alliance’s 32 top generals in Copenhagen, adding that NATO was continuing its work in “increasing” these forces “in number … and also in sophistication.”

The remarks follow growing warnings by European leaders about a possible Russian escalation in Europe. On Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Moscow could send drones or missiles into a frontline NATO country in “the next few months” in a staged provocation to test the alliance — a risk that was later echoed by France and the Netherlands.

World.title: Smoke and flight delays at Riyadh airport after air raid alert
World.content:
Residents said they heard explosions during the first air raid alert issued for the Saudi capital.

A large plume of black smoke was seen near Riyadh’s main airport on Saturday after an overnight air raid alert, amid an escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

Reuters footage showed black smoke rising and flames near Riyadh’s King Khalid airport, while residents told AFP they heard explosions before Saudi’s civil defense issued an all-clear on Saturday morning.



Flight-tracking website FlightRadar24 rated the airport at Level 5 on its disruption index, indicating a very high likelihood of delays or cancellations.

Saudi authorities have not commented on the reported incident. The Saudi ministry of defense and Riyadh’s airport authorities did not immediately reply to requests for comment.

The first air raid alert for the Saudi capital came amid escalating attacks between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed rebel group. The Houthis tightened their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb strait last week by seizing the Red Sea port of Mokha and Mayyun Island, also known as Perim.

On Monday, Yemeni and Houthi officials said they captured the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands, though those claims have not been independently verified. The roughly 30-kilometer-wide strait carries about 8.7% of global seaborne trade, according to UN figures.



Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called U.S. President Donald Trump twice last week to seek U.S. strikes on Houthi targets, but Washington has so far resisted direct military intervention.

World.title: Germany cuts fuel tax as Middle East conflicts send prices soaring
World.content:
Germany will lower tax on petrol and diesel by 17 cents per liter in a relief package worth €2.5 billion, the German government announced Friday.

"Those who rely on their cars every day are reaching their financial limits. ... The relief package of €2.5 billion is no small sum in times of strained budgets," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said. The tax discount is to be implemented next month.

The measure, brokered between Germany's federal and state governments, is part of the package promised by Merz as fuel prices continue to climb in response to the war in Iran and the escalating conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

Two weeks ago, a key oil benchmark reached $100 a barrel for the first time since July following the latest escalations in the Middle East, sending pump prices soaring all over Europe.

The Merz government also plans to introduce a temporary fuel price cap on petrol and diesel modeled on similar policies in Luxembourg and Belgium. The price cap would take into account price moves on the oil markets, transportation and distribution costs, and retailers’ profit margins. Berlin aims to introduce the measure by Jan. 1, 2027.



Germany, through the voice of its Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, is among the EU member countries calling for a bloc-wide windfall tax on oil companies that have reaped billions of euros in excess profits since the start of the war. The topic is high on the agenda at an informal meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday and Saturday.



Ahead of the meeting on Friday, Klingbeil has called on the European Commission to present a proposal by the end of October.



“Several member states have been calling for models for a long time,” Klingbeil, from Germany's Social Democratic Party, told reporters. “People can see how oil companies are exploiting the situation, overcharging and significantly increasing their profits.”



But Merz's conservatives have pushed back on the proposal. Germany's Economic Affairs and Energy Minister Katherina Reiche said a windfall tax would only make sense in case of abusive price increases, she told Handelsblatt.



“The fact that eleven refineries are producing in Germany makes us less dependent on foreign countries; that must not be put at risk,” Reiche said.

World.title: Inside the secret race to become NATO’s next top general
World.content:
Although little-known, NATO’s military committee is the alliance’s most senior military authority, with the chair expected to give honest military advice to allies — helping assess the feasibility, financing and capabilities of operations. They oversee dozens of working groups of NATO military staff, and broker consensus on formulating military advice.

The position is a “highly complex role,” said Eleonora Russell, the spokesperson of former chair Adm. Rob Bauer, because it requires simultaneously gaining the trust of both the military and the political leadership across the alliance — and not taking sides.

Such a role is particularly challenging today given enduring transatlantic tensions, she said, and important as sensitive talks on NATO’s next four-year war planning cycle will kick off in October. “The trick is you have to be … an extremely good listener,” Russell said, “but then you have to also have a very strong backbone.”

Germany’s Breuer, who Berlin announced as a candidate in February, is seen as the front-runner, according to one NATO diplomat and two European national security officials, who were granted anonymity to speak freely about the sensitive matter.

Berlin is now Europe’s leading defense spender, the officials said, and the U.S. has previously nudged Germany toward leadership roles in the alliance as it seeks to reduce its military engagement on the continent. Strained bilateral ties between Ottawa and Washington might also make Carignan’s case more difficult, the officials said.

That support was on display in Washington on Jul. 23, when Breuer briefed Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby on Germany’s new military strategy. Colby later called the strategy “historic” and “highly laudable” and said Germany was positioning itself as “a key leader of Europe’s conventional defense” in a post on X.

World.title: A ticking 'mercury bomb'? Ancient Nazi U-boat lies off Norway
World.content:
Around 150 metres below the water's surface, west of the Norwegian island of Fedje, a fragment of German wartime history lies on the seabed. A submarine called U-864 has been resting there for more than eight decades, broken into two parts, surrounded by sediment and a cargo that still poses an environmental problem today.

 

U-864 is an exceptional case: according to historical records, large quantities of mercury were probably on board, with a Japanese order mentioning 1,867 containers.

If the entire shipment had been loaded, that would correspond to between about 65 and 67 tonnes. However, the exact loading documents have not survived, so the actual quantity cannot be definitively established. The only certainty is that mercury is still stored in the wreck.

A final voyage with a deadly end

By February 1945, the war was in its final phase. Even so, U-864 was still on a special mission. The German submarine was supposed to travel via Norway to Japan. On board, in addition to military and technical equipment, were specialists and material intended for Japan’s armaments industry. But the voyage ended off Fedje.

The British submarine HMS Venturer had decrypted German radio transmissions and tracked down U-864. On 9 February 1945, Venturer fired a torpedo. It hit the German submarine and destroyed it. U-864 sank to a depth of around 150 metres. All 73 people on board were killed. The attack is considered the only known case in which one submerged submarine sank another.

After that, the wreck was forgotten for decades.

It was not found until 2003

Only decades later did U-864 return to the spotlight: clues about the special cargo ultimately led to investigations off the Norwegian coast.

In 2003, the wreck was located by the Norwegian naval vessel KNM Tyr. It became clear that the submarine had not remained intact on the seabed. The two parts of the wreck lie separated from each other at a depth of about 150 metres.

The problem with the cargo is that mercury does not simply disappear. Mercury can remain in the environment for a very long time because, unlike many organic pollutants, it is not broken down biologically.

How long mercury persists in the environment depends on its chemical form and the prevailing environmental conditions. In contaminated sediments, it can remain for decades, in some cases even for centuries. The US environmental agency EPA points out that mercury can be released from soils for potentially hundreds of years.

Particularly problematic is the fact that micro-organisms can convert mercury into methylmercury. This especially toxic form accumulates in the food chain, especially in fish.

New images from the depths

New images released by the Norwegian Coastal Administration Kystverket (source in German) show what the wreck looks like today.

In May 2025, Kystverket had the wreck examined using remotely operated underwater vehicles. Among other equipment, WROVs (remotely operated underwater vehicles connected to a ship by cable), 4K cameras, photogrammetry and acoustic measurement techniques were deployed. The recordings were also used to create a three-dimensional model of the wreck and the surrounding seabed.

The submarine lies far below the surface of the water, partly embedded in sediment on the sea floor.

Dangerous cargo

Many of the presumed 1,867 containers are likely to have been damaged when the submarine sank.

A recovery operation could remove some of the mercury from the wreck, but the work itself could also stir up contaminated sediments and release pollutants.

This is exactly what the Norwegian authorities experienced during investigations and salvage work in 2026, when 22 containers were recovered from the wreck. Initial examinations showed that around 80% of the containers were damaged and leaking. Around half a tonne of mercury was brought ashore. At the same time, according to the Norwegian Coastal Administration, mercury was also released into the water from the working area.

Recover it or seal it for good?

Norway is therefore facing a dilemma. Should it try to retrieve the dangerous cargo from an 81-year-old wartime wreck lying at a depth of 150 metres? Or should the wreck and the contaminated seabed be permanently covered?

This question has been fiercely debated for years. In 2026, after its experience with the operations, Kystverket again recommended covering the wreck. In the authority’s assessment, a large-scale recovery could ultimately release more pollutants than it would remove.

Covering the wreck would not be a simple, final solution either: the cover would have to be monitored over the long term.

The people of Fedje live with the knowledge that just a few kilometres off their coast lies a German submarine whose cargo still raises questions. And while decades later, technology can now look deep inside the wreck, the crucial question remains unresolved: what should be done with it?

The Norwegian authorities have, incidentally, been analysing fish and shellfish from the region for years. So far, there appears to be no reason for undue concern: the tests have so far shown stable or low mercury levels.

World.title: Flames and smoke spotted at Riyadh's King Khalid airport after overnight air raid alert
World.content:
Residents of the Saudi Arabian capital Riyadh reported seeing flames and black smoke at the city's King Khalid International Airport on Saturday, hours after local authorities issued an air raid alert.

 

Video footage circulating on social media appears to show a towering column of smoke rising from the airport, which flight tracking site Flightradar24 says is experiencing "major problems."

A journalist for the AFP news agency also reported seeing firefighters working to extinguish a burning fuel truck close to the site.

Saudi Civil Defense had sent an alert to residents in several parts of the country overnight, warning of potential danger and advising people to remain indoors and away from windows. It later gave the all clear.

"I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," a 27-year-old Riyadh resident living in the north of the city told AFP.

"It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this," they added.

It comes amid an uptick in attacks from Yemen's Houthi rebels, which declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in July.

The Houthis, whom the US has designated as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation, have since been increasingly targeting Saudi cities and shipping, further heightening tensions in the Middle East - which is already reeling under the effects of the Iran war and tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia has hit back with its own strikes on the group - which has seized vast stretches of territory in Yemen this month in a lightning offensive - but has failed to stop its advance.

“Developments around the Bab al-Mandab Strait underline the urgent need to prevent Yemen’s conflict from further threatening the security of the Red Sea and this vital international maritime route,” Khaled Khiari, the UN assistant secretary-general for the Middle East, Europe, the Americas, Asia and the Pacific, said earlier this week.

“What is needed now is sustained engagement that reduces tensions, prevents further escalation and safeguards freedom of navigation," he added.

World.title: Contrast in Tehran as unveiled women race marathon alongside regime military display
World.content:
Tehran saw two very different scenes unfold at the same time on Friday, as in one part of the city, many women raced a marathon without a headscarf, and in another part, a regime military display took place with thousands of women in hijab showing their loyalty with machine guns in their hands.

 

The state-organised rally brought together 300,000 supporters of the Islamic Republic. The "Jan-Fada" (Self-Sacrificers) marched from Imam Hossein Square toward central Tehran. Among these, the image of a woman in a full chador with a baby wrapped in a keffiyeh perched behind a machine gun stood out as particularly striking.

On the other hand, female runners joined a sporting event and competed in a track-and-field race. During the event, women whose clothing, according to published images, did not comply with Iran’s mandatory hijab rules were featured.

A woman holding a baby behind a machine gun" Photo: Mostafa Tehrani / Tasnim News Agency AP Photo

The Tehran 10-kilometre marathon was held at Velayat Park, with men and women competing in separate divisions.

According to the official schedule, the women’s race started at 5:30 AM, followed by the men’s at 7:00 AM. Published photos showed some female participants running without headscarves and wearing standard athletic gear, including long-sleeve tops and track pants.

This event proceeded despite the cancellation of the "Mahan Run" in the city of Kerman just days earlier, which had been scheduled for 5km, 10km, and 21km distances.

Kerman's seminary had demanded the cancellation, citing co-ed participation and concerns over "religious values", ultimately leading authorities to withhold a permit.

Similarly, in December 2025, images of unveiled women running in a Kish Island marathon sparked widespread backlash from conservative figures and led to legal actions against the organisers.

Meanwhile, the Tehran Prosecutor's Office has announced the opening of a judicial case against the organisers of the Tehran Marathon over what it described as a "failure to observe legal and religious standards," HRANA (Human Rights Activists News Agency) reported.

Pro-regime rally

A short distance away, in a markedly different atmosphere, central Tehran hosted the "Jan-Fada-ye Iran" (Iran's Self-Sacrificers) drill. The event featured Basij forces, campaign volunteers, and several senior military and political figures, including Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. State media claimed an attendance of 313,000 people.

The procession moved from Imam Hossein Square toward the city centre, showcasing military hardware, drones, and organised Basij units.

"Jan-Fada-ye Iran" is a campaign launched following the outbreak of armed conflict. Islamic Republic officials initially claimed over 30 million enrollments, later updating the figure to around 32 million, and asserted that 32% of registrants are women and 68% are men.

Given Iran's population of roughly 90 million, 32 million would represent nearly 35% of the country's total population.

However, this statistic relies solely on the organiser's claims and cannot be independently verified.

What is the law, and where is the contradiction?

Under Iranian law, women are required to wear the hijab in public. However, four years after the start of the “Woman, Life, Freedom” movement, an increasing number of women have openly refused to comply with the rule.

This trend has continued despite the two recent wars involving Iran against Israel and the US.

A similar change has also been evident at pro-government rallies in recent weeks and months. Images from several events have shown women attending without headscarves or wearing them in ways that do not fully comply with the official dress code.

At the same time, some voices within the Iranian establishment have argued that women who support the Islamic Republic should still be considered supporters of the system, even if they do not fully comply with the mandatory hijab rules.

What defined Tehran on Friday morning was the juxtaposition of these two realities: on one side, thousands of mobilised forces gathered for a state military display focused on "comprehensive defence"; on the other, men and women took part in an athletic event that presented a distinctly different picture of women's presence in Iranian public life.

These paradoxes play out against a heightened political and security backdrop inside Iran following the start of US and Israeli military strikes on February 28.

Even as state rallies and pro-regime demonstrations fill the streets, reports indicate an ongoing crackdown marked by detentions of protesters and state executions.

According to Human Rights Watch, the Islamic Republic executed at least 29 people between March 18 and the end of August who had been arrested in connection with the January protests.

World.title: The keg is tapped: Munich springs to life as Oktoberfest returns
World.content:
By late morning, it was clear: the Wiesn was back. Decorated horse-drawn carriages, brass bands and festival hosts made their way towards the Theresienwiese, while growing crowds gathered around the fairground. Munich had dressed up for the occasion, and apparently nobody intended to worry about details such as calories, footwear or the weather forecast – not least because Bavaria was enjoying glorious sunshine and temperatures just above 20 degrees Celsius.

 

The Theresienwiese was already filling up earlier in the day. At around 10:35 a.m., the traditional procession of the Wiesn landlords got under way. Around 1,000 participants, including festival hosts, showmen, musicians and waiting staff, made their way through central Munich to the Theresienwiese in decorated carriages and horse-drawn wagons.

People in traditional Bavarian dress during the Oktoberfest parade at the 191st Oktoberfest in Munich, Germany, on Saturday, 19 September 2026. AP Photo

Beer only after the keg is tapped

The festival tents had already opened at 9 a.m., initially serving non-alcoholic drinks and light snacks. Beer could only be served after the official tapping of the first keg. The fairground rides also started operating only afterwards.

The big moment finally came at exactly noon in the Schottenhamel festival tent. Munich’s new mayor, Dominik Krause, took the mallet and, for the first time in his term of office, tapped the first keg. After the traditional “O’zapft is!” and the twelve cannon shots fired from the Bavaria, the monumental bronze statue and landmark of the Free State of Bavaria, it was clear: there was no turning back. The beer could flow.

The Bavaria statue, unveiled in 1850, towers over the Theresienwiese and is considered a symbol of Bavaria, with the Hall of Fame in the background. Rudolf Simon CC BY-SA 3.0

As the first one-litre stein made its way to Bavarian Minister-President Markus Söder, the most important question of the day on the Theresienwiese was probably already being asked: Where can we still find a seat?

People celebrate after the opening of the 191st Oktoberfest in Munich on Saturday, 19 September 2026. AP Photo

Millions of visitors expected

The Wiesn is one of the largest folk festivals in the world and attracts millions of visitors from Germany and abroad every year. According to Bavarian public broadcaster BR, around 6.5 million people attended the last Oktoberfest.

This year, a Maß of beer costs between €14.80 and €15.90, depending on the tent, meaning visitors once again have to dig a little deeper into their pockets. A large pretzel at the Wiesn costs around €5 to €6.

For getting to the festival, the city recommends using public transport. The Theresienwiese can be reached via several U-Bahn and S-Bahn stations. Anyone travelling by car should be prepared for an extremely difficult search for a parking space around the fairground.

World.title: Thousands of migrants return to beaches in Ceuta after new port facility runs out of space
World.content:
More than 2,000 migrants in Ceuta had to return to the beaches after there was not enough space to accommodate them at a new facility located in the autonomous city's port.

 

Thousands of migrants had been moved from the territory's Trampolín and Benítez beaches on Friday morning, escorted by officers from Spain's Civil Guard and National Police towards the new temporary reception centre, which is designed to accommodate 1,700 people.

However, there were over 4,000 people coming from the beaches, meaning many had to return after the new camp filled up. According to government sources, around 3,000 migrants remain on the city’s streets in total.

Police had struggled to maintain order on Friday as people fought to secure a spot at the new site after weeks of living on the beaches and streets, with officers firing warning shots into the air in an attempt to contain the crowd. No serious incidents were recorded, however, according to local authorities.

The migrants' return meant a clean-up operation that had been planned for the beaches once they were cleared also had to be put on hold.

As a result, Trampolín still looks much as it had in recent days, with makeshift tents and shacks strewn across the sand.

The Ceuta migrant crisis began in late July when more than 70,000 people crossed into the Spanish exclave from Morocco.

People walk on a beach after attempting to cross from the Moroccan northern town of Fnideq to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, July 31, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Kissy Chandiramani, a member of Ceuta's autonomous government, has described the port transfer as chaotic and said that neither the city government nor port authorities had been given advance warning.

Chandiramani also called for procedures to return the migrants to be speeded up, warning that otherwise, Ceuta risked becoming "the great CETI of North Africa," in reference to the Temporary Immigrant Reception Centres.

She noted that around one hundred migrant cases were being processed each day and that, with more resources, the process could be completed in 15 days.

If the current pace continues, she warned, the situation "is going to drag on forever."

World.title: Sweeping raids leave Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community fearing what comes next
World.content:
Turkey has jailed dozens of people pending trial as a sweeping crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups widens, prompting international condemnation and protests outside Turkish embassies on Friday.

Advertising

By Thursday, courts in several provinces had jailed at least 82 people following raids on LGBTQI+ organisations, clubs, cafes and homes.

The cases include LGBTQI+ activists and members of rights groups as well as people accused of prostitution, drug offences and other crimes. Not everyone jailed is accused of gay rights advocacy.

The United Nations human rights office has called on Turkey to uphold human rights without discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity and to immediately release anyone arbitrarily detained.

Protests were held outside Turkish embassies in cities including Paris, Brussels, London, Oslo and Washington on Friday.

The crackdown began on Saturday, when police carried out coordinated raids targeting nine LGBTQI+ organisations. Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said legal action was being taken against 162 people, nine associations and 13 businesses in 15 provinces.

Turkey arrests dozens in ongoing crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups

Mass detentions

The raids prompted protests across Turkey, including outside Istanbul’s main courthouse on Tuesday. Police broke up the demonstration and detained more than 100 people, including journalists. They were later released.

“I am here because I want to say that LGBTQ+ friends are not alone in this country,” said Ayse, a protester who asked to be identified only by her first name.

“I want to support them and to stay in solidarity with them, which is not easy these days in Turkey, but they are not alone, and we are not alone, and we will be here until the end.”

Opposition DEM Party parliamentarian Ozgul Saki remained at the protest, protected from arrest by parliamentary immunity.

“This oppression against LGBTQ+ people is an attempt to compress society into a single type; to build an Islamist, Turkish, racist society,” Saki said. “Those who are here say, 'No! Society will live equally, freely and honourably with all its diversity,' and that's why they were all detained.”

The operations have been defended by Gurlek, from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s conservative Justice and Development Party (AKP).

“No criminal organisation, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated,” Gurlek posted on social media.

Among the organisations affected was Istanbul-based SPoD, which provides psychological support to LGBTQI+ people.

“As a community, we were expecting that such an operation would come one day. But we didn't imagine it as that violent, that much unlawful,” said a SPoD representative who asked to remain anonymous.

“They raided our office; I think four or five have been detained, and they are still in custody. What will happen to the LGBTQ+ community after this day? Like they can implement a kind of informal criminalisation upon our community, so my personal feeling is an immense feeling of uncertainty.”

Surge in anti-LGBTQ disinformation targets Pride in Europe

Obscenity allegations

Homosexuality has been legal since the foundation of the Turkish republic in 1923, but authorities are using an obscenity law as part of the crackdown.

“All of our board members are detained due to the allegations of obscenity,” said Yildiz Tar of Ankara-based KAOS GL, Turkey’s leading LGBTQI+ news portal.

“They look into our social media account, and our news articles are seen as obscene because, for example, there is one picture of two women kissing, and they see that it's obscene. So that is why they have been detained.”

The measures resemble actions taken against LGBTQI+ communities in Russia and Egypt, Tar said.

“It's very similar to Russia and Egypt, like the things they want to do is very similar to anti-gay propaganda laws, and there were huge operations, and people got detained,” Tar said.

“So it's very similar to both countries. And actually, like the Turkish government is very fond of Putin's way of dealing things.”

The crackdown has also drawn condemnation from the European Union and international human rights groups.

“It's an attempt to show LGBTQ+ people as immoral and against the family. But in fact, none of this does anything to protect the family at all,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, who leads Human Rights Watch’s Turkey office.

“It's all about discrediting and stigmatizing people for their sexual orientation or gender identity.”

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Wider crackdown

The arrests form part of a broader crackdown on people regarded as opposing the government, Sinclair-Webb said.

“This operation should be set in the context of a very wide crackdown on anybody who is regarded as oppositional to the government, whether in terms of being politically or in terms of their lifestyle or their outlook… there is a general attempt by the government to impose as well as, you know, ideological conformity on people, lifestyle,” Sinclair-Webb said.

President Erdogan routinely refers to LGBTQI+ people as perverts and has stepped up his rhetoric ahead of much-rumoured early elections. Gurlek has called on prosecutors to increase investigations into the LGBTQI+ community, fuelling fears of further arrests.

The crackdown has also prompted condemnation across Turkish civil society, with trade unions, doctors’ associations and opposition parties voicing their opposition.

For Tar, that support offers some hope amid fears over what could follow for Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community.

“If this attack won't be stopped, it would mean a lot of maltreatment and torture; it can also cause hate crimes; it incites hatred inside the country too,” Tar said. “And it will mean that you cannot be openly queer; if they succeed in their operation, that is a really, really hellish scenario.”

World.title: A doubleheader feast!
World.content:
This week on The Sound Kitchen it’s a doubleheader: you’ll hear the answers to TWO quiz questions, as well as TWO “Listener's Corner" with Paul Myers, and of course, Erwan Rome’s “Music from Erwan”. So sit down, relax, and join the banquet! Just click the “play” button above to join the feast.

Advertising

Hello everyone!

As noted on the show, I am retiring on 1 October. Unfortunately, The Sound Kitchen is retiring too – I will not be replaced.

We’ve had a great time together all these years, haven’t we?

Click here to listen to past Sound Kitchen podcasts.

I know you will all stay loyal to RFI English – our service has so much to offer. We’re small, but my colleagues are firebrands!

For example, we have wonderful podcasts: Spotlight on France, with journalists Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas; Melissa Chemam’s insightful Spotlight on Africa, and our International Report, usually sent to us by one of our foreign correspondents. We also have an award-winning bilingual series – an old-time radio show, with actors (!) – to help you learn French, called Les voisins du 12 bis.

Remember, podcasts are radio, too! As you see, sound is still quite present in the RFI English service. Please keep checking our website for updates on the latest from our team of journalists. You never know what we’ll surprise you with!

To listen to our podcasts from your PC, go to our website; you’ll see “Podcasts” at the top of the page. You can either listen directly or subscribe and receive them directly on your mobile phone.

And don’t forget, in addition to our audio bilingual series, you can also learn French through our website “Le Français facile avec rfi”. In addition to online lessons, there are news broadcasts in slow, simple French, with exercises to practice what you’ve heard.

Go to their website and get started! At the top of the page, click on “Test level”, and you’ll be advised on the best-suited activities for your level, according to your score.

Do not give up! As Lidwien van Dixhoorn, the head of the “Le Français facile” service, told me: “Bathe your ears in the sound of the language, and eventually, you’ll get it”. She should know – Lidwien is Dutch and came to France hardly able to say “bonjour,” and now she heads this key international award-winning RFI department – so stick with it!

For the quiz on 24 January: I asked you a question about the Africa Cup of Nations, and an article sent to us by Paul Myers, who was there. You were to re-read his article “Senegal outwit Morocco to claim 2025 Africa Cup of Nations”, and send in the answer to this question: At the 2026 World Cup, which took place in the United States, Mexico, and Canada in June, in which group did Morocco play, and in which group did Senegal play?

The answer is, to quote Paul’s article: “Morocco will play in Group C against Brazil, Scotland and Haiti.

Senegal will feature in Group I with France, Norway, and the team that emerges from the intercontinental play-off in March.”

In addition to the quiz question, there was the bonus question: “What is your favorite day of the year? Why? What is it about that day that makes it your favorite?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Dipita Chakrabarty from New Delhi, India. Dipita is also the bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners this week are Muhammed Naved, a member of the International DX Radio Listeners Club in West Bengal, India; Muhammad Abdullah, a member of the RFI Online Visitors Club in Sahiwal, Pakistan; RFI Listeners Club member Rodrigo Hunrichse from Bio-Bio, Chile, and last but not least, RFI English listener Sakila Musarrt from Chapainawabganj in Bangladesh.

Congratulations winners!

For the quiz on 31 January: You were to listen to our podcast “Spotlight on France”, the brainchild of my colleagues Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas. I hope you listen to it regularly, it’s really quite good.

On their programme number 138, Alison reported on La Ménardière, an alternative living arrangement for seniors in the village of Bérat, close to the southern French town of Toulouse. The aim of the project is for seniors to live and grow old together, contributing to society for as long as possible, and to delay – or avoid – the moment when people are forced into institutional care.

The answers you were to send in were: How many residents can live at La Ménardière, and what is the selection process?

The answer is, to quote Alison: “La Ménardière can house up to 20 residents. The selection process to become one is rigorous. Candidates stay for trial weekends and, if they decide to join, they must then complete a six-month probation period.”

The bonus question you answered that week – suggested by Murshida Parvin Lata, the co-chairman of the Sonali Badhan Female Listeners Club in Bogura, Bangladesh – was: “Which daytime temperature do you prefer: cold or hot? Why?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Father Steven Wara, who lives and serves in the Cistercian Abbey in Bamenda, Cameroon. Father Steve is also the winner of this week’s bonus question.

There’s long-standing RFI Listeners Club member Zenon Teles, who is also the president of the Christian – Marxist – Leninist – Maoist Association of Listening DX-ERs in Goa, India, as well as another faithful Sound Kitchen listener – and club member – Radhakrishna Pillai from Kerala State, also in India.

Moving over to Bangladesh, Anjana Parvin – she’s the secretary of the very active Shetu RFI Listeners Club in Naogaon. And last but not the least, club member and my fellow dinosaur, Alan Holder, from England’s Isle of Wight.

Congratulations winners!

Here’s the music you heard on this week’s programme: “Take the A Train” by Billy Strayhorn and Duke Ellington, performed by Duke Ellington and his orchestra; the “AFCON 2025 Official Intro Theme – Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025” by Othmane Laaouina; “What a Wonderful World” by Bob Thiele and George David Weiss, sung by Louis Armstrong; “The Cakewalk” from Children’s Corner by Claude Debussy, performed by the composer, and “Étincelles”, Op. 36, No. 6 by Moritz Moszkowski, played by Alexander Zhou.

I’ll talk to you next week, 26 September, for our final Sound Kitchen together. You’ll hear the answers to the questions about the Grammy Awards Lifetime Achievement Awards and the Benin Bronzes, as well as your responses to the bonus questions on "The Listener’s Corner" with Paul Myers, so be sure and tune in.

Until then, fare thee well!

World.title: A city at the crossroads of history: Unearthing Gaza's ancient heritage
World.content:
Before Gaza became synonymous with conflict, it was a place where merchants sold wine from local vineyards, pilgrims crossed continents, fishermen set out before dawn, and generations of families lived between sea and desert. RFI explores its deep history.

Advertising

Sitting on the coastal corridor linking Egypt, the Levant, the Arabian Peninsula and the Mediterranean, the port city has always been a strategic crossroads.

Like many places around the Mediterranean, Gaza's identity wasn't built by a single people or culture. It was shaped by generations of arrivals, departures and exchanges.

As the Mid-East Junction podcast returns from a six-year hiatus, we'll trace the city's history from the age of the Philistines until the creation of Israel in 1948.

In this first episode of season 3, a Gazan archaeologist, a historian, and a professor of contemporary Arab people shed light on Gaza’s little-known yet fascinating ancient history.

Mid-East Junction is produced by RFI's English-language service. This episode was mixed by Vincent Pora.

World.title: German-Russian relations at freezing point
World.content:
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine destroyed the once-close relationship between Moscow and Berlin. Yet the far-right AfD is calling for a normalization of relations.

For many years, Germany and Russia had a perfect partnership.

Russia supplied cheap energy, which helped German industry succeed in exporting its goods worldwide. This partnership began in the early 2000s. On the German side was Chancellor Gerhard Schröder from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), followed later by Chancellor Angela Merkel of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Their counterpart was Vladimir Putin.

Even when Russia annexed the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea in 2014, business continued as usual. It was then that the agreement to build Nord Stream 2, a direct gas pipeline between Russia and Germany designed to bypass Ukraine was signed. At the time, other European countries and the US warned that the pipeline would provide Russia with powerful leverage.

The warnings proved to be correct. On February 24, 2022, Russian tanks rolled into Ukraine. German hopes for a stable European order, the democratization of Russia, and the continuation of its lucrative business model were shattered.

Hundreds of fake posts target German elections To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How could so many German politicians be so wrong?

"Shortly before the invasion, the widespread view was that there were no rational grounds for an attack on Ukraine, because the economic, military, and political costs to Russia of starting a war would be far too high," Russia expert Mario Baumann of the German Council on Foreign Relations told DW. "People [in Germany] had projected their own rationality onto Russia. They underestimated the regime's imperialist and revisionist ambitions."

After that, nothing in the bilateral relationship was ever the same again. Chancellor Olaf Scholz(SPD) spoke of a Zeitenwende (epochal shift) in foreign and security policy, in the days after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine began.

Since then, the German armed forces have expanded. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the following year, "We must become capable of waging war," a statement that critics still say was an escalation of tensions.

Germany ended its decades-long energy dependence on Russia and shut down Nord Stream 2. In September 2022, the pipeline was blown up. The Federal Prosecutor's Office suspects a Ukrainian group was responsible.

A series of EU sanctions have long since reduced Russian-German trade relations to a minimum. Government cooperation in culture, science, and education has also practically ceased to exist.

A new low point

While the German government under Scholz initially hesitated to take dramatic steps on military aid to Ukraine, Friedrich Merz, then the leader of the opposition, stepped up his rhetoric.

"Ukraine must win the war. Russia must lose the war," he said in 2024 as leader of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group in parliament. In 2025, as chancellor, he then spoke of Russia's "economic exhaustion," which the West must "help bring about." But that has yet to materialize. To this day, Russia has shown no serious willingness to compromise.

Why Putin turned to ex‑German chancellor as a peace broker To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Meanwhile, Germany is feeling the consequences of its military support for Ukraine. The German government has long suspected Russia of being behind cyberattacks on government agencies and critical infrastructure.

So when an armed drone was discovered and defused in August 2026 at Leipzig Airport close to Ukrainian transport aircraft — which transport a large portion of the military aid to Ukraine — the government was certain: For the first time, it publicly blamed the Kremlin.

A Russian cultural center in Berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn were closed, which the German government said were being used as espionage centers. Moscow responded by closing the Goethe Institutes and the German consulate in St. Petersburg.

Putin has denied Russian responsibility for the Leipzig incident, calling it a "serious mistake" to blame Moscow, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov even described the accusations as the "beginning of a real war." But Baumann says: "We shouldn't give in to the fears being stoked, because they are part of Russia's strategy to weaken Germany and Europe."

AfD wants to resume relations with Russia

The German government is also facing domestic pressure as the far-right Alternative for Germany(AfD) has made gains in regional elections and is rising in the national polls. The AfD would prefer to end support for Ukraine and normalize relations with Russia, including deals on oil and gas. High fuel prices in Germany have only made the issue more explosive.

"German support for Ukraine worries many people," said Sven Leunig, political scientist at the University of Jena in Thuringia, following the election in the neighboring state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won the September 6 election by a landslide. However, he noted, "it is less a fundamental rejection of the support itself than a reaction born of fear. People want to 'stay out' of the conflict so as not to be drawn into it more deeply themselves."

In the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, 42% of respondents believe military aid to Ukraine has gone too far. "If public support weakens over the long term, the government will eventually have to respond," says Leunig.

Carry on or change course?

So far, the German government is sticking to its course, as Merz made clear once again following the AfD's election victory. But opinions on how to deal with Russia and the war in Ukraine differ not only among politicians but also among political scientists and experts.

Johannes Varwick of Halle University in Saxony-Anhalt believes it is long past time for a change of course: "German and European policy toward Ukraine resembles a mix of platitudes and wishful thinking," Varwick told DW. "It is high time for a course correction, and Germany should exert pressure on Ukraine to move closer to the latest American proposals, which aim for a compromise and could thus possibly bring about a political solution."

Baumann, on the other hand, argues: "Supporting Ukraine remains the best investment for safeguarding German and European interests. The government has recognized this and should stick to this course and continue to communicate it as such." However, it is important that Berlin act in concert with its European partners.

The war in Ukraine has now lasted longer than World War I. And there is no end in sight. Hopes that Russian-German relations will return to the way they used to be seem illusory for the foreseeable future.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Ukraine steps up measures to protect railways
World.content:
As Russia increases its attacks on Ukraine's rail infrastructure, the Ukrainian government has called for help to replace destroyed locomotives and is making plans to keep passengers safe.

Recent months have seen a rise in Russian drone attacks on locomotives, stations, and infrastructure. More than 1,600 attacks were reported in the first eight months of 2026, according to Oleh Holovashchenko from Ukrzaliznytsia, the state rail operator.

On September 16, a train traveling between the capital Kyiv and Mykolaiv in southern Ukraine was struck by a Russian drone. The day before, another train in the Volhynia region was attacked near the Polish border.

Two days earlier, a drone had struck the locomotive of a passenger train at the Yahodyn border crossing, just two kilometers (1.2 miles) from Polish territory. Nobody was injured, as Ukrzaliznytsia's monitoring system had previously detected the drone and the train had been evacuated about 15 minutes before the attack. At the time, CIA Director David Petraeus was on another train at the same station.

A separate train carrying several former European leaders, including ex-British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and security advisers had stopped at the station earlier the same day. The Ukrainian authorities believe that this diplomatic train was the drone's actual target, but the train departed earlier than scheduled.

'Putin's terror' against Ukrainian logistics

Russia has damaged or destroyed more than 500 Ukrainian locomotives since its full-scale invasion of Ukrainebegan in 2022. More than half of these attacks happened this year, according to a post on the social media platform X by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. He said that part of "Putin's terror" was to destabilize Ukraine's logistics system.

The minister called on international partners to tighten sanctions against Russia further and to provide financial assistance to the Ukrainian government so that it can procure more locomotives that are compatible with Ukraine's Soviet-era broad-gauge (1,520 millimeters or almost 5 feet).

"Ukraine's railway keeps the country moving," Sybiha said. "It enables the rapid evacuation of civilians from frontline areas, transports essential cargo, and keeps grain and other critical goods moving across the country."

Russia was specifically targeting locomotives because they were ideal from a technical point of view, said Vasyl Shevchenko, a former Ukrainian deputy transport minister. "A locomotive's thermal signature is very large, and almost impossible to miss," he told DW. "The impact of a strike can be devastating, because 50 kilograms (110 pounds) of explosives in a diesel locomotive can cause several metric tons of fuel to detonate and completely destroy it. A strike on an electric locomotive will cause a fire that can paralyze an entire stretch of track. That's why they are targeting areas where the loss of a single train can bring traffic to a standstill."

Shevchenko also pointed out that locomotives could not be replaced immediately but had to be ordered in advance and this could take years. Ukrzaliznytsia says that negotiations are underway with various international partners and a contract has already been signed with the French company Alstom. These locomotives are scheduled to start arriving next year.

In the meantime, trains are also being repaired. "While our top priorities used to be saving on costs, providing comfort to the train crew and making sure the trains were attractive, these have changed," Holovashchenko said. "What is most important today is that the locomotive is technically sound and ready to transport passengers and freight." But he added that it was difficult to protect trains against Russia's weapons.

Ukrainian authorities are trying to ensure trains are evacuated before a drone strikes Image: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

Zelenskyy intensifies protection of critical infrastructure

On September 15, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a meeting of the staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief to discuss strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure and logistics.

The key issues were contracts for the production of protection systems for critical infrastructure and logistics, but he added that there were plans to expand the electronic warfare component and reorganize the operation of designated mobile fire teams, as well as strengthening air defense lines.

Zelenskyy said that decisions on backup logistics routes in frontline regions were also being made, and he had instructed Ukraine's Finance Ministry of to find additional funding for the logistics sector.

Experts say it is technically very easy to target a locomotive Image: Odesa Regional Military Administration/AFP

Ukrzaliznytsia sets up monitoring centers

According to Holovashchenko, Ukrzaliznytsia is also seeking its own answers to the new challenges and there are plans to develop early detection systems. He said that a monitoring center had been established to track the movement of drones and trains all over Ukraine.

The fact that Russia has started to use jet-powered Shahed-type drones, which are much faster than previous models, has made it more difficult and given less time to respond. "We used to wait longer to stop trains so we could evacuate passengers," Holovashchenko said. "Now, there are more precautionary stops. But in general, we try not to go into areas where there is a potential danger."

Buses are deployed in areas of particularly high risk and the "train plus bus" concept is being expanded in cooperation with military authorities. Passengers are also being given instructions on how to respond in the event of an alarm and advised to try to get further away from a station than previously.

The most difficult question remains where they should be evacuated to. Holovashchenko said that the monitoring centers had access to maps showing all the shelters along train routes and that dispatchers always tried to stop trains near them, but this was not always possible. He said that train personnel were receiving special psychological support to help passengers.

Ukrzaliznytsia is currently preparing for winter, while working with foundations and other donors to ensure that trains will be heated. Evacuations will be even more difficult as temperatures drop. "This is no easy task. We're providing blankets, rain jackets, and equipment so that train staff can supply passengers with at least the bare necessities if their train comes to a standstill in the middle of nowhere because of a snowstorm, Holovashchenko said.

This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

World.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico denied access to White House
World.content:
Three US news outlets said their journalists were blocked from entering the White House grounds, hours after President Donald Trump announced bans on several media outlets.

News outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Saturday signaled they would take legal action after their journalists were denied access to the White House grounds earlier in the day.

It comes a day after US President Donald Trump announced he would ban the three news outlets from 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue in a row over their coverage of his presidency.

Trump has accused the media of "fake news" over their often critical coverage of his second term in office.

Experts say the bans conflict with the United States Constitution's First Amendment protections for free speech and press freedom.

Trump bans media outlets from White House To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did CNN, MS NOW and Politico say?

CNN reported that its journalist Betsy Klein was denied access at the White House on Saturday morning and her press pass was seized.

"CNN’s mission to report on the U.S. government will continue regardless of any attempts to restrict physical access to the White House and other government buildings, or any other attempts to impede our journalism,” a statement from the channel said.

“We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right."



MS NOW White House reporter Akayla Gardner broadcast from outside the White House after she was denied entry on Saturday Image: Jose Luis Magana/AP Photo/picture alliance

Meanwhile, the left-leaning MS NOW, whose journalists were also turned away from the White House grounds on Saturday, said in a statement that it would challenge Trump's ban.

"The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars,” the network said. "MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.”

Politico's global editor-in-chief Jonathan Greenberger, meanwhile, wrote in an email to staff: “A few minutes ago, our colleague Cheyenne Haslett attempted to enter the White House to do her job as a POLITICO reporter."

"Secret Service denied her entry to the complex and confiscated the pass that allows her access to the White House.

"We stand by her and all reporters here covering the White House. As we said yesterday, we will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights,” Greenberger wrote.

Politico White House reporter Cheyenne Haslett was also denied entry to the White House a day after Trump's announcement Image: Jose Luis Magana/AP Photo/picture alliance

What did Trump accuse US media outlets of?

In a post on his Truth Social network, Trump said the media outlets "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the president of the United States."

"Other fake news media outlets to follow," he warned.

Trump said there was no one incident that prompted the ban, telling reporters in the Oval Office, "It's really just cumulative stories over the past few years."

"I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house," he added.

Trump's relationship with the media is often punitive Image: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/picture alliance

It was unclear whether the banned media outlets would also be blocked from flights aboard the presidential plane, Air Force One.

The US is just weeks away from the November 3 midterm elections in which Trump's Republican Party will struggle to defend narrow majorities in Congress.

With the president's approval ratings at 35%, near historic lows, Reuters/Ipsos polls also show Democrats ahead by around 7-9 points.

Trump's war with the press

During his second term, Trump has continued to round on journalists he deems critical to his administration — a tactic he employed when first elected in 2016.

Last year, he banned the Associated Press news agency from the usual pool of journalists that report on the presidency over its refusal to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.

He has, however, given closer access to new, far-right media outlets seen as more sympathetic to his policies.

Trumps say comedian Jimmy Kimmel should be fired To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump has even called on the US media regulator to remove the licenses of several broadcasters, whose comedy or news shows have mocked his policies and family.

The president has also filed several lawsuits against the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times, the BBC and Iowa's Des Moines Register, sometimes costing the media outlets millions in settlements.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

World.title: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania: Will economy shape the vote?
World.content:
Voters in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania head to the polls on Sunday, with the Social Democrats and far-right AfD neck and neck. Here's a look at key economic issues that could influence the election.

The recent election victory of the far-right AfD party in Saxony-Anhalt has shaken up Germany's political landscape. Although Saxony-Anhalt is only a small state, the AfD's landslide win with nearly 44% of the vote has drawn considerable international attention, as it means this would the first time that a far-right party will likely enter a German government since World War II.

That is not expected to happen in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where voters head to the ballot box on Sunday. State Premier Manuela Schwesig of the center-left Social Democrats remains popular, as polls show, though she isn't without her critics.

The latest polls suggest a neck-and-neck race between the Social Democrats and AfD, rather than a landslide victory for any one party. In fact, the Social Democrats' approval ratings have been on the rise and could indicate a successful final push, potentially returning Schwesig to power.

Lower wages, but solid economic growth

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, like Saxony-Anhalt, is in eastern Germany, but its economy is relatively stable, even though unemployment stands at 7.8%, slightly above the national average, and the median gross annual salary is €47,750 ($54,800) — about €6,000 less than the German average. But Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has seen solid economic growth in recent years.

Jochen Schulte, state secretary in the state's Economy Ministry, said Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's economy has expanded by 5% in inflation-adjusted terms since 2020, compared with 4.6% for Germany overall.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has a large agricultural sector, although it employs relatively few people. Back when the state was part of East Germany, farms were consolidated into large, state-run enterprises known as agricultural production cooperatives, rather than privately organized as in West Germany.

Farms in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, once consolidated into large, state-run cooperatives, are still bigger than the German average Image: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

In many instances, these farm sizes have remained the same since reunification. A typical agricultural company in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will control about 280 to 283 hectares (up to 700 acres) of land, whereas the national average is only about 65 hectares.

The state's now private agricultural companies continue to benefit from their large size, ensuring efficient labor use, strong market positioning, greater market power through centralized purchasing, and a strong negotiating position when selling produce.

Many jobs in shipbuilding, tourism

The state's second major industry is shipbuilding and maritime services, which accounts for a significant share of economic output. Being on Germany's Baltic Sea coast, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has also benefited from the recent investment boom in its defense sector. This has brought business — and jobs — to major shipyards in Wismar and Stralsund, at companies like Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems and other shipbuilders.

Hundreds of fake posts target German elections To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Tourism is another key sector in the state. Until 1990, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania was one of the most important travel destinations for East Germans. Since the fall of the Berlin Wall, Germans from east and west have continued to flock to the Baltic coast, and the region is Germany's second-most popular vacation destination.

That said, relatively few people are directly employed in the tourism sector. That is in part merely a statistical quirk, as many tourism jobs overlapping with service jobs, and also because many tourism jobs are seasonal.

According to figures from the Economy Ministry and industry reports, some 150,000 to 160,000 jobs depend on tourism, either directly or indirectly. Water-based tourism, whether on lakes or the Baltic Sea coast, accounts for an estimated 19,000 jobs.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has few large enterprises, such as automakers and chemical companies, which makes its state and civil service branch the region's largest employer.

Rostock-based AIDA Cruises is another major employer. So is Nordex SE, a manufacturer of wind turbines with production facilities in various regions. German rail operator Deutsche Bahn provides many jobs through its service and maintenance hubs, as do the major ports of Rostock and Sassnitz.

5 things you need to know about Nord Stream To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fossil fuels, renewables power regional economy

Another key industry is the energy sector, with large quantities of Germany's fossil fuels brought in via the Baltic Sea.

When imports of Russian gas came to a standstill in 2022 following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Nord Stream gas pipeline connection points near Lubmin lost their significance. However, a large portion of Germany's liquefied natural gas imports are still unloaded, processed and distributed in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

The coastal state has increasingly invested in renewable energy, including wind power Image: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

Energy availability, not only from fossil fuels such as oil and gas, but also from green sources such as wind and solar power, is becoming increasingly important for the state as well.

In August, the Schwarz Group — which operates the Lidl and Kaufland supermarket chains — announced it would invest €5.6 billion ($6.4 billion) in the construction of a data center south of Rostock.

During the project's presentation in the state capital, Schwerin, the company said its investments in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania could reach tens of billions of euros.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Saudi Arabia: Plume of black smoke near Riyadh airport
World.content:
Smoke was seen billowing from a location near the main airport in Riyadh following overnight warnings of an aerial threat.

Black smoke could be seen rising near King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia's capital city, Riyadh, on Saturday.

Earlier, explosions were reported in the vicinity, following overnight warnings of a "hostile aerial threat."

It comes amid an escalation in attacks by Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi militants and just days days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca. The Iran-backed Houthis denied that accusation, calling it a "worn-out lie."

An overnight air raid alert was issued by Saudi authorities, the first since fighting in neighbouring Yemen intensified this month Image: REUTERS

What has being reported

News agency Reuters published video and photos of a large plume of black smoke rising from an area with a highway to the airport, the main terminal building and other buildings in the foreground.

No casualties or damage has been reported after the alerts were lifted and Saudi authorities have not yet said what prompted the alerts or the cause of the audible explosions.

They previously reported intercepting incoming Houthi missiles and drones.

Saudi Arabia short of options against Iran-aligned Houthis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Warnings issued by Saudi Civil Defense advised people to avoid gathering and filming or photography.

"The area is under a hostile aerial threat," a message received before 3:00 a.m. by Riyadh residents, urging them to stay indoors, as reported by the AFP news agency.

AFP journalists then reported hearing two explosions, before the Saudi civil defence agency lifted the alert half an hour later.

Similarly, Reuters reported that overnight warnings were issued in Riyadh and Al-Kharj, east of the capital, before an all-clear was issued.

A Reuters journalist in Riyadh's Olaya area reported hearing booms before the all-clear message was sent.

Tracking website FlightRadar24 reported "major problems" at the King Khalid International Airport, listing it under its maximum disruption index.

Unravelling security situation

The latest developments come amid an escalation between the Houthisand the internationally recognized government in Yemen that is supported by Saudi Arabia.

A 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia fell apart in July after the rebels allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace. As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.

The group has reported dozens of Saudi strikes since its recent offensive to secure control over the coastal areas near the Red Sea's Bab al-Mandab Strait — a vital global shipping route — from government hands.

World.title: Drone sightings briefly shut Luxembourg airport
World.content:
Flights were diverted and hundreds of passengers affected after unauthorized drones appeared near Luxembourg's only international airport.

Luxembourg authorities are investigating drone sightings that forced the country's main airport to temporarily suspend flights overnight, Prime Minister Luc Frieden said on Saturday.

Frieden said Luxembourg was working with its NATO allies following the incident, which comes amid heightened European concern over suspected hybrid attacks linked to Russia.

What happened at Luxembourg airport?

National carrier Luxair said more than 1,800 passengers were affected, with 17 incoming flights diverted to airports including Brussels, Paris and Frankfurt.

Flights resumed on Saturday, although Luxair warned that delays and knock-on disruption could continue.

The airport said the closure was a precautionary measure to protect passengers, airline crews, airport employees and aircraft.

Frieden stressed that it was too early to determine who was responsible.

"We are analyzing the situation," Frieden told a televised press conference after an emergency meeting with the country's defense and interior ministers.

Have other drones been spotted?

Frieden said "potentially larger drones" had also been observed in Luxembourg's airspace in recent days.

"This is new for Luxembourg, but it is not completely new for our neighboring countries," he said.

Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Unauthorized drones have previously been detected near sensitive sites elsewhere in Europe, including Belgium, Germany and Denmark.

"We will ensure, together with our partners, that we can guarantee the security of our populations," Frieden said.

European governments have repeatedly warned of Russian-linked hybrid activities since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Such incidents have included suspected sabotage, cyberattacks and unauthorized drone flights.

There is currently no evidence establishing who was responsible for the Luxembourg sightings.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

World.title: Thousands protest Kennedy Center demolition fears
World.content:
Protesters took part in a "Hands Around the Kennedy Center" human chain. The demonstration comes amid fears the Trump administration could tear the arts hub down.

Thousands of people have demonstrated at the Kennedy Center in Washington D.C. amid fears President Donald Trump's administration could demolish the arts hub.

Crowds of people gathered in the Foggy Bottom area of the US capital city, many carrying signs as they joined in "Hands Around the Kennedy Center."

Some of those gathered held hands and formed a human chain around the center.

Protesters waved placards reading "hands off Kennedy Center" and sang songs close to where workers removed Trump's name from the building in June following a court order.

Actor Lynda Carter, a vocal Trump critics, addressed the rally on Friday Image: Jose Luis Magana/AP Photo/picture alliance

Protesters, residents condemn move to demolish Kennedy Center

"It makes me sick to my stomach," the AFP news agency quoted Neal Racioppo, a Washington resident who runs marketing and communications for a theatre, as saying.

Trump "can't get his name on this cherished building, so he is depriving the world of what it could be."

"He does not have a right to decide that an institution, a living memorial to a past president, can be demolished," another protester told AFP.

"The Kennedy Center is vital to the arts in Washington. We need it. We need this,” said local arts community member Bud Wilkinson.

"This is not just about putting the president's name on the Kennedy Center. It's about censoring the performances and the programming," Wilkinson said.

Trump and the Kennedy Center

The Kennedy Center — inaugurated in 1971 following the assassination of US President John F. Kennedy — has been a focal point of Trump's plans for Washington since 2025.

Trump has been pushing for major renovations and claims the building was left in a severe state of disrepair by those previously in control.

Trump's handpicked Kennedy Center board voted last year to rename the institution the Trump-Kennedy Center.

In May, a judge ruled that his name was illegally added and ordered it removed.

The Kennedy Center board voted last year to rename the institution the Trump-Kennedy Center Image: Cliff Owen/AP Photo/picture alliance

What has Trump said about the Kennedy Center?

On Wednesday, Trump appeared to imply that the Kennedy Center could be torn down if his administration did not receive "recognition."

"For the Trump administration, for me to get involved and to take that on long term and to carry it or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition, because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close," Trump said.

"It'll end up being ripped down. It's in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape," Trump told reporters.

Edited by: Karl Sexton
