World.title: South Ossetia election: as expected, former Moscow official Marat Kambolov becomes new president
World.content:
Kambolov becomes South Ossetia president

As expected, Marat Kambolov, the prime minister and acting president of South Ossetia who previously held senior positions in the Kremlin, is winning the snap presidential election held on 18 September.

According to preliminary results, he is securing a convincing victory over his formal rivals – state security officer Murat Valiev, South Ossetian University rector’s state adviser Kazbek Kodoev, and Unity party chairman Zurab Kokoev.

After 40% of the ballots had been counted, CEC head Emilia Gagieva said Kambolov had received 88.4% of the vote. Valiev had 4.3%, Kodoev 1.1%, and Kokoev 1.0%.

Marat Kambolov is a former Moscow official who first appeared in South Ossetia in May 2026 as an adviser to then-President Alan Gagloev. He was quickly granted South Ossetian citizenship and, within a month, rose from minister to prime minister, and then became acting president after Alan Gagloev resigned.

Polling stations were also open in Russia – in North Ossetia and Moscow. According to Emilia Gagieva, turnout was high at all polling stations and no violations were recorded.

According to the CEC, the election was monitored by 66 observers from 15 countries: Russia, Abkhazia, Nicaragua, Belarus, Armenia, Venezuela, Germany, Zimbabwe, Kenya, Mexico, Serbia, Tanzania, Turkey, Uganda and South Africa.

CEC member Dina Ostaeva said that “no complaints or appeals related to violations of electoral legislation or the organisation of voting” had been received during the day.

After polling stations closed at 8pm, a celebratory concert and lottery were held in the city centre, with household appliances, smartphones, TVs, bicycles, vacuum cleaners and the grand prize – a Russian-made Niva Legend car – raffled off.

As soon as the prizes had been handed out, Marat Kambolov took the stage, thanked the people of South Ossetia for taking part in the election and said that, in terms of voter turnout, the election had broken all records.

“Preliminary data show that we have broken all records. Never before have so many people taken part. More voters participated in this election than in any previous one. Only together can we strengthen our Tskhinvali and our Ossetia,” Kambolov said.

One of the voters who cast his ballot for Marat Kambolov believes that the high turnout and the large share of votes he received were not so much the result of political strategists’ work as of people believing in Kambolov and voting “for his authority, for the authority of Russia”.

Blogger Alik Pukhaev expressed hope that the new president would “finally make South Ossetia a state for all Ossetians”.

By this, he means the possibility for all ethnic Ossetians to obtain a South Ossetian passport.

At present, the law provides for citizenship only for people born in South Ossetia and their descendants. Under previous governments, however, there were repeated scandals over the illegal issuance — and even sale — of passports to residents of Chechnya, Ingushetia and Dagestan.

Russian State Duma MP Kazbek Taisaev, who observed the election, said it had been organised “at the highest level – transparently, fairly and openly”.

He also stressed that Russia would continue to provide South Ossetia with comprehensive support.

And that is almost certainly what will happen, given that Marat Kambolov is a Russian official who was clearly sent by the Kremlin with the specific aim of taking the presidency and governing in Russia’s interests rather than those of local politicians pursuing their own agendas.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: EU does not recognise “presidential election” in Georgia’s Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region
World.content:
EU condemns Russia and South Ossetia election

The European Union does not recognise the so-called “presidential election” held on 18 September in Georgia’s Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia). In a statement, the EU Delegation said the results of the election have no legal effect.

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry also condemned the so-called “presidential election”, calling it a violation of Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

The EU statement says it does not recognise the constitutional and legal framework, including recent amendments, under which the election was held in the Russian-occupied region, which unilaterally declared its secession from Georgia.

“The EU strongly condemns Moscow’s actions aimed at installing a Russian official as the de facto president of South Ossetia, Georgia’s occupied breakaway region,” the statement said.

The EU also expressed concern over the signing of the so-called “Treaty on Deepening Allied Cooperation” on 9 May 2026 and criticised Russia’s attempts to strengthen its control over South Ossetia in the political, military, economic and judicial spheres.

The EU considers these steps contrary to a peaceful resolution of the conflict and paving the way for the future illegal annexation of the Russian-occupied region.

“Such actions systematically deepen divisions, threaten regional security and stability, and constitute a flagrant violation of international law,” the EU statement said.

The bloc reaffirmed its commitment to a peaceful resolution of the conflict in Georgia, including through its co-chairmanship of the Geneva International Discussions and the activities of the European Union Monitoring Mission in Georgia.

The EU called on Russia to respect Georgia’s sovereignty and cease all actions undermining its territorial integrity.

“The European Union reaffirms its unwavering support for Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders,” the statement said.

On 18 September, snap “presidential elections” were held in Russian-occupied “South Ossetia”. Four candidates took part.

However, calling it an “election race” would only be accurate in a very loose sense, as it was clear from the outset that the overwhelming favourite was so-called “acting president” and “prime minister” Marat Kambolov, who arrived in the region from Russia in May 2026.

Unlike Kambolov, the other three candidates were residents of South Ossetia. But that was where their advantage ended. Most experts described them as “technical candidates” — people who were not seriously trying to compete for the presidency:

Zurab Kokoev, leader of the Unity party;

Kazbek Kodoev, an independent candidate and adviser to the rector of South Ossetia University;

Murat Valiev, a candidate nominated by the Patriots of Alania party and an employee of the state security service.

None of them campaigned among the population. They presented their views on the development of so-called South Ossetia only during live televised debates.

World.title: Pashinyan’s salary to nearly double as Armenian civil servants set for pay rises from 2027
World.content:
Salary increases for public officials in Armenia

From 1 January 2027, senior Armenian officials will receive higher salaries. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, for example, will earn 2,662,000 drams ($7,353), up from the current 1.5 million ($4,143). Deputy prime ministers’ salaries will rise to 2,163,000 drams ($5,975), from 1,289,000 ($3,560).

The increases will apply not only to the executive branch, but also to the legislative and judicial branches. The state budget will allocate 25 billion drams ($69 million) for this purpose. The government has already approved the draft. Parliament must now approve it.

“How does this public official live? How does he buy a suit and a watch? We never assess the negative impact [of this factor] on the development of our state. But the effect is highly negative. If we do not solve this problem, it will lead to disasters,” Nikol Pashinyan said during a discussion of the draft.

The ruling party views the decision as a reform. The prime minister said he was confident that failing to implement the project would mean “keeping Armenia stuck in place and continuing to subordinate the logic of the state to the logic of corruption”.

However, the opposition warns that such decisions will further deepen the sense of social injustice.

“Citizens often become disillusioned and leave the country not only because of economic difficulties, but also because of a sense of injustice,” former MP Garnik Danielyan said.

Salary increases in figures

Under the proposed amendments to the law “On remuneration for persons holding public office”:

the president of Armenia will earn 2,662,000 drams ($7,353), up from the current 1,664,000 drams ($4,596);

the speaker of the National Assembly will earn 2,496,000 drams ($6,895), up from 1,497,600 drams ($4,137);

MPs will earn up to 1,497,600 drams ($4,137), up from 832,000 drams ($2,311);

the president of the Constitutional Court will earn 2,412,800 drams ($6,665), up from 1,664,000 drams ($4,596);

the prosecutor general will earn 1,830,400 drams ($5,056), up from 1,248,000 drams ($3,447);

the ombudsman will earn 1,830,400 drams ($5,056), up from 998,400 drams ($2,758).

Governors, deputy ministers and deputy speakers of parliament will also receive higher salaries.

The stated amounts include taxes and other mandatory payments.

Ruling party representative’s assessment and opposition response

Eduard Aghajanyan, an MP from the ruling party, told journalists:

“The public administration system has consistently faced difficulties attracting highly qualified specialists. The issue became particularly acute after the 2018 revolution, when the logic of working within the system changed radically. Systemic corruption was eradicated, and the motivation mechanisms were completely restructured.

At the same time, pay levels made the public administration system unattractive to highly qualified professionals.

We have been at the helm of government for eight years now. I believe that the decision to address this issue is somewhat overdue.

I welcome the government’s decision. I am confident that it will produce the desired results in attracting highly qualified professionals.”

Former MP from the opposition Armenia bloc Garnik Danielyan wrote on his Facebook page:

“According to official data for 2024, Armenia’s poverty rate stands at 21.7%. One in four children lives in poverty, while thousands of families continue to face severe social hardship. People struggle to meet their basic needs. Moreover, in the 21st century, Armenia has recorded cases of people dying from hunger.

In your 2021 election programme, you [addressing the authorities] promised to halve the poverty rate by 2026. Poverty has not declined. But you yourselves are now living better. You no longer buy vacuum cleaners or televisions on instalment plans. Instead, you are accumulating assets.

Of course, no one objects to high salaries for public officials. But given this level of poverty, should the priorities not be addressing social problems, creating new jobs and ensuring decent living conditions for people?

And this is happening while Armenia’s public debt has already exceeded $14 billion. Housing and employment remain critical issues for thousands of Karabakh Armenians. Hundreds of people still live in temporary shelters, and many are forced to buy groceries on credit.

Clearly, political calculations also lie behind this decision — namely, preserving loyalty within the state system.”

Comments from Armenian residents on social media

The decision to raise the salaries of senior public officials has sparked heated discussions on social media. Most users criticised the authorities. Here are some of their comments:

“Of course, raising the salaries of civil servants and public officials is important. But we must not forget a phenomenon that is shameful for Armenia. Librarians receive the lowest salaries [75,000 drams — $208]. Raise them!”

“After spending days and nights thinking about the people, the ‘democratic’ government decided to raise its own salaries by 60–80%. Meanwhile, citizens earning 80,000–150,000 drams ($220–414) can continue entering shops full of goods. As prices rise rapidly, they must painfully choose whether to buy food for their child or shoes for themselves.”

“They are setting their salaries higher than those of members of the British royal family. And they are paying for all this with our taxes. They will bleed us dry. This is only the beginning.”

“The [prime minister] claims that raising his salary and those of other officials is necessary to prevent a catastrophe. According to this passionate speaker, a ‘catastrophe’ is when someone asks where an official got his suit or watch. I wonder who will ask him what he plans to spend those 2,662,000 drams — around $7,400 — a month on, considering how expensive he is for the state. For nine years now, you have paid neither rent nor utility bills, car expenses, petrol or maintenance costs.”

Salary increases for public officials in Armenia

World.title: Tbilisi condemns “presidential election” in Georgia’s Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region
World.content:
Georgia condemns Russia over South Ossetia election

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry condemned the so-called “presidential election” held on 18 September in the Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia), calling it a violation of Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

According to the ministry’s statement, “the opening of polling stations by Russia in the occupied territory without the consent of the Georgian government is a gross violation of Georgia’s sovereignty and another manifestation of Russia’s policy aimed at the de facto annexation of Georgia’s regions.”

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry said that holding the so-called election violates fundamental norms and principles of international law and cannot legitimise the occupation regime in Tskhinvali or change the region’s status under international law as part of Georgia.

“Holding any so-called elections in Georgia’s occupied territories, which are under military occupation and the effective control of the Russian Federation, while internally displaced persons and refugees are not given the opportunity to return to their homes safely and with dignity, is illegal and cannot have any international legal consequences,” the ministry said.

Tbilisi also condemned Russia’s decision to open polling stations for the Russian State Duma election in occupied Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region from 18 to 20 September.

The Foreign Ministry called on the international community to properly assess and condemn Russia’s actions and ensure an appropriate international legal and political response.

“Georgia continues to call on the international community to firmly protect Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders and support a peaceful resolution of the conflict,” the statement said.

World.title: Armenia’s anti-corruption campaign: law on confiscating illicit assets takes effect
World.content:
Armenia’s law on confiscating illicit property

A large-scale anti-corruption campaign is unfolding in Armenia . As part of the campaign, the state is confiscating assets belonging to members of the country’s former financial and political elite.

The authorities say they are moving from high-profile political accusations to a systematic effort to recover illegally acquired property. The list of people accused of corruption whose numerous properties and business assets have been frozen includes former Armenian president Robert Kocharyan , Prosperous Armenia party leader Gagik Tsarukyan, and former finance minister and ex-head of the State Revenue Committee Gagik Khachatryan. Prosecutors accuse those involved in these high-profile cases of money laundering, bribery and abuse of office.

At the same time, the debate in Armenia goes beyond how they managed to amass such wealth. It also concerns whether the process complies with the law, whether the authorities apply the law equally to everyone, and whether the confiscated property is genuinely being returned to the people.

About the law

Armenia’s Law on Confiscation of Property of Illicit Origin has been in force since 2020. The authorities adopted it “to strengthen the fight against corruption and restore social justice”. The law applies to assets worth more than 50 million drams ($132,120). It allows the state to confiscate property if its owner cannot prove that the income used to acquire it came from legal sources.

According to the Prosecutor General’s Office, between 2018 and the first half of 2026, the state and local communities recovered assets worth approximately 304 billion drams (around $840 million). More than two-thirds of that amount — about $562 million — was recovered over the past three and a half years.

Comment from lawyer Aram Orbelyan

“The Law on Confiscation of Property of Illicit Origin contains fundamental contradictions. In international practice, confiscation models are clearly separated. One involves checking declarations: if a person cannot explain their income, the state confiscates the property. The other involves confiscation following proof of a crime. Our lawmakers, however, have mixed everything together into complete confusion.

The grounds for an investigation are chaotic. Half of the provisions are linked to criminal cases, including cases that authorities have suspended or closed on non-exonerating grounds. The other half allows officials to launch confiscation proceedings based simply on ‘operational information’. As soon as any intelligence report appears, law-enforcement agencies immediately begin examining a person’s property, going back as far as 1991.”

The factual vacuum of the 1990s

“What political statements describe as ‘plunder’ is often impossible to prove in court because the circumstances of that era were different. In the 1990s, non-monetary transactions, including agricultural exchanges, were widespread. There was no clear system of tax and customs control. Vehicle databases only appeared in the early 2000s, while electronic tax records emerged in 2013.

Moreover, the law at the time did not require businesses to keep documents for more than five years. This has naturally created an information vacuum today. Young prosecutors fail to take this historical context into account, leading to dead ends in court.”

Intrusion into private life and the political context

“The extent of the intrusion into private life raises serious questions. The law allows investigators to examine years of bank statements belonging to any relatives of a person under investigation. As a result, investigators and prosecutors gain access to strictly personal spending unrelated to corruption: where people went on holiday, what they ordered in cafés and what illnesses they received treatment for.

Society sees this mechanism exclusively as a ‘law to recover what former [authorities] stole’. Legally, however, the law should target corruption as such, rather than individuals. To ensure that anti-corruption tools do not appear politically selective, they must operate universally. They should apply to all elites, regardless of their current political status or affiliation with the ruling camp.

Authorities must examine both the past and the present transparently, without politically motivated cases, while taking limitation periods and the economic realities of earlier years into account. The process should objectively target illicit property, rather than serve as a selectively applied repressive tool.”

Comment from Varuzhan Hoktanian, an expert at Transparency International’s Anti-Corruption Centre

“The law sparked legal disputes from the outset, which led to a review of its constitutionality by the Constitutional Court. The court, in turn, sought an expert opinion from the Venice Commission. International experts offered two key recommendations. First, the confiscation of property for the benefit of the state should take place through separate civil proceedings, rather than criminal prosecution resulting in imprisonment. Second, some responsibility for proving the lawful origin of assets should fall on the owner.

It is often extremely difficult to prove that property has a corrupt origin. For example, Kocharyan’s case involves the signing of government decisions. For the charges to stand, the prosecution must prove that he deliberately approved specific decisions in the expectation that the assets would eventually pass to his family. This is extremely difficult to establish, so the evidence often appears unconvincing. The situation is compounded by the absence of a mandatory declaration system in the 1990s. As a result, it is now virtually impossible to confirm that property was acquired legally.”

Discrimination or fight against corruption?

“Applying legal mechanisms exclusively to one group of people discredits the anti-corruption institution itself, turning the law into a tool of political pressure. Attempts to deprive opponents of financial resources by seizing their property create a risk of completely clearing the political field. If this is combined with double standards during elections — harsh punishment, including arrests, for vote-buying while ignoring the abuse of administrative resources — the system of checks and balances itself collapses. Ignoring any of these abuses leads to dictatorship.”

What happens to confiscated property?

“The legal question is only one side of the problem. The question of what happens to confiscated property after the state receives it is no less important.

I recall a similar confiscation from Soviet history — the dekulakisation campaign of the late 1920s and early 1930s. We later learned about the grave consequences it caused, including the Holodomor. As it turned out, the party nomenklatura ultimately received everything that the authorities had seized. Today, these assets could likewise pass to new wealthy individuals or another nomenklatura. Once again, ordinary people would receive nothing.

When people talk about confiscating property, they mean both financial assets and movable and immovable property. For example, someone may have built a luxurious house and live in it. If we return to the Soviet example, after the October Revolution, the authorities seized property from wealthy people and turned luxury homes into communal apartments. That will not happen in our case. No one plans to move an ordinary citizen into someone else’s mansion. This raises the question: who received the mansion belonging to formerprimeministerformer prime minister Hovik Abrahamyan, or the Golden Palace hotel in Tsaghkadzor?

The situation is also problematic here. Even if a new wealthy owner buys these properties, a change of government could lead to their seizure again, with the authorities claiming that the original confiscation was unlawful.

Moreover, the phrase ‘returning property to the people’ sounds somewhat abstract to me. The trend shows that confiscated real estate goes not to the people, but to another wealthy person close to the authorities. And the public will ask: ‘What do we get out of it?’

Let me give you an example. There used to be a kindergarten in our courtyard. A newly wealthy owner acquired it through an illegal transfer. If the state takes the building back today and restores its former status as a kindergarten, then yes, that would mean ‘returning it to the people’.

In other cases, this could become a vicious circle in which each successive government dispossesses the previous one. This is quite dangerous, especially in the context of investment. Investors should not have to fear that the authorities might dispossess them tomorrow.”

How can confiscated funds be used?

“As for monetary confiscations, the seized funds go into the budget, into what is known as a ‘common pot’. It is unclear how the authorities then spend this money. These are not earmarked revenues, so the authorities decide how to use them.

It would be better to classify these revenues as earmarked funds and regulate them by law, directing the money towards social programmes designed to improve citizens’ welfare.”

Armenia’s law on confiscating illicit property

World.title: Poll: Do Abkhazia residents consider voting in Russia’s State Duma elections important? Video
World.content:
Russia’s State Duma elections will take place on 20 September. As most residents of Abkhazia hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship, they can also take part in the vote. In the republic, which has a population of 250,000, as many as 35 polling stations have opened, and campaigning is in full swing.

Ahead of the election, we asked residents of Sukhum whether they planned to vote and whether they believed doing so would make a real difference.

The poll produced highly contradictory responses. Some people do not want to spend their day off voting in another country. Others consider it very important because, “if things go badly in Russia, things will get very hot here in Abkhazia too”.

Rustam: “For some reason, Russia is placing great importance on Abkhazia at the moment, and they really want all residents to take part in these elections. Perhaps it does not even matter how people vote, because there is no alternative. What matters is showing the turnout — that people are actively and collectively going to the polls, thereby acknowledging the assistance Russia provides to Abkhazia.

Personally, I will not vote because I see no point in it. If the [Yabloko party] had not been barred from the election, I would definitely have voted. Or I would have supported the Communists. As things stand, I do not want to spend my day off that way.”

Eliso: “I will definitely go to the polls and vote.

I will not say whom I will vote for. But as a Russian passport holder, I have the right to influence the composition of the State Duma, because the decisions made there directly affect us.

As a woman and a future mother, I want Abkhazia residents with Russian citizenship to be able to receive child benefits. I believe this bill should be among the first issues considered by the new parliamentary term.”

Timur: “I always vote in every election, both ours and Russia’s. My choice may almost never win, but I want to feel involved and have at least some opportunity to influence events. Russia directly affects us, and by voting I make my small contribution to what is happening in Abkhazia today.”

Almaskhan: “I will not vote. I never take part in elections and I am not interested in politics. I do not even know which parties are currently running or what they decide. Everything is done without us anyway. We live in a reality that we simply have to adapt to. It is impossible to change anything with a ‘tick’ on a ballot — everything has already been decided.”

Liana: “I will see how things go on Sunday, but I am not particularly keen. I do not even know whom to choose. The only party I hear about is United Russia, because its s are everywhere. Everyone says it is the strongest party. And Kiriyenko (the Kremlin’s overseer of Abkhazia — JAMnews) is a member, so apparently everything here is done through them. If I go, I will probably vote for them.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Investigation launched into dozens of children falling ill at Tbilisi nurseries
World.content:
Children poisoned at Tbilisi kindergartens

Fourteen children were taken to hospitals from state-run nurseries in Tbilisi with symptoms of intoxication. The agency responsible for managing the capital’s kindergartens said seven state-run nurseries had suspended operations “to prevent epidemiological risks”.

According to the agency, the children had developed high temperatures, while some also experienced nausea and vomiting.

The Investigation Service of the Ministry of Finance has launched an inquiry into the incident. Searches reportedly continued throughout the night at four kindergartens and three companies supplying food to them. Relevant teams from the Interior Ministry and the Ministry of Environmental Protection and Agriculture also took part in the investigative activities.

At this stage, it is unclear what caused the children’s condition or whether the cases were linked to food served at the nurseries. Some parents said their children had eaten a beef cutlet at the kindergarten. However, doctors say investigators will only be able to establish the exact cause through clinical tests.

The investigation is being conducted under Article 198, Part 2 of the Criminal Code. The provision concerns the production and sale of products that pose a danger to human life or health, where this creates a risk to life or health.

According to the information available so far, 55 children and one staff member from 20 Tbilisi kindergartens have sought medical attention. However, the number of children and staff showing signs of poisoning may be higher, as not all of them have visited medical facilities.

Maya Chkhaidze, director of the Tsitsishvili Children’s Clinic, said 14 children from different kindergartens had been brought to the clinic. They had experienced vomiting, abdominal pain and symptoms typical of gastroenteritis.

“This could be a symptom of a viral infection or intoxication. At this stage, it is impossible to determine the exact cause,” Chkhaidze said.

According to her, none of the patients is in serious condition. Several children have already stabilised and are in satisfactory condition, although they remain in the clinic under medical observation.

Saba Buadze, a former Tbilisi City Council member from the opposition Lelo party, wrote on social media that companies which win tenders supply food products to kindergartens, while staff prepare meals directly on the premises.

According to him, the estimated value of procurement in this sector exceeded 100 million lari (around $40 million) in 2024–2025.

Buadze recalled corruption cases uncovered in the sector, including during the investigation into the case of recently convicted former State Security Service chief Grigol Liluashvili. One of the corruption episodes for which authorities charged him involved allegedly taking kickbacks from commercial organisations when awarding kindergarten food procurement contracts, using his official position.

“During my time on the Tbilisi City Council, we summoned officials accused of corruption to the council several times. But they failed to attend the hearings, violating the law. Recently, the quality of food in kindergartens has improved compared with previous years,” Buadze wrote.

World.title: Council of Europe Committee of Ministers urges Russia to withdraw troops from Georgia’s occupied territories
World.content:
Council of Europe urges Russia to withdraw troops

The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers has again called on Russia to withdraw its troops from Georgia’s occupied regions and end so-called “borderisation” – the installation of border signs along the dividing lines in the Georgian-Ossetian and Georgian-Abkhaz conflict zones.

According to the Georgian Justice Ministry, at its September meeting the Committee of Ministers discussed the implementation of European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) judgments in the interstate case Georgia v Russia.

● The Committee reaffirmed its support for Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders and called on the Russian Federation to fulfil its international obligations.

● Among its demands, the Committee called for the withdrawal of Russian troops from Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region and an end to so-called “borderisation”.

● The Committee also called on Russia to ensure the free and safe movement of the local population, access to property and the opportunity to receive education in the Georgian language in the Russian-occupied regions.

● The Committee of Ministers called for the necessary conditions to be created for the safe, voluntary and dignified return of displaced people to their homes and for an end to killings, abductions, torture, unlawful detention and other serious violations.

The Georgian Justice Ministry said the government had secured rulings in several major interstate cases against Russia at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, including cases concerning Russia’s deportation of Georgian citizens, the August 2008 war and Russia’s continuing occupation of Georgian territories.

According to the ministry, the Georgian authorities continue to work to secure the full implementation of the ECHR judgments through legal and diplomatic mechanisms.

World.title: Weekly review of prices of Azeri Light, Dated Brent, and Urals
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 19. Average prices for Azeri Light (CIF), Azeri Light (FOB Ceyhan), Dated Brent, and Urals rose this week (from September 14 through 18).

According to Trend’s calculations based on data from oil market participants, the average price of Azeri Light (CIF) crude, produced at the “Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli” field in Azerbaijan, increased by $10.51, or 9.2%, compared to the previous week, reaching $124.18.

Based on the data, the highest price for this grade of crude oil during the week was $128.03 per barrel, and the lowest was $121.08.

The average FOB price of Azeri Light crude at the Turkish port of Ceyhan was $118.52 per barrel, which is $8.68, or 7.9%, higher than the previous week’s figure. Over the week, the highest price reached $122.45 per barrel, while the lowest was $115.50.

The price of Urals crude rose by $3.63, or 4.2%, compared to the previous week, reaching $89.82 per barrel. Over the week, the highest price was $96.94, and the lowest was $84.21.

Dated Brent crude averaged $127.76 per barrel, up $14.1, or 12.4%, from the previous week. Over the course of the week, the price per barrel ranged from a high of $132.19 to a low of $125.47.

World.title: Baku meeting important for combating radicalism and extremism – Soltan Mammadov
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 19. The 7th Meeting of the Council of Heads of Muslim Religious Administrations of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) held in Baku is of significant importance in terms of protecting common values, promoting Turkic-Islamic cultural heritage, as well as combating radicalism and extremism, Azerbaijani MP Soltan Mammadov told Trend.

The “Baku Declaration” adopted during the meeting was also an important step toward further expanding future cooperation with both the Turkic world and Islamic countries.

The MP said that the international conference dedicated to prominent figure and thinker Seyid Yahya Bakuvi is of particular importance for further strengthening religious and cultural ties, studying common heritage and passing it on to future generations.

He noted that the 2017 Islamic Solidarity Games in Baku, the organization of various events as part of cooperation with the Organization of Islamic Cooperation and ICESCO, as well as plans to host the OIC Summit in Baku next year demonstrate the continued nature of Azerbaijan’s contribution to strengthening Islamic solidarity.

The MP pointed out that Armenia’s 30-year occupation of Azerbaijani territories was not limited to territorial occupation, as serious damage was also inflicted during this period on the country’s rich historical and cultural heritage, including mosques and other religious monuments.

President Ilham Aliyev noted in his speech that 65 mosques were completely destroyed by Armenians during the occupation, emphasizing that this was an insult directed not only against the Azerbaijani people but against the Islamic world as a whole.

Mammadov noted that large-scale reconstruction and restoration work carried out in the liberated territories is bringing life back to these lands. In line with the policy set by the head of state, the liberated territories are rapidly being rebuilt, while their historical appearance and former pace of life are being restored.

“The fact that the Aghdam Juma Mosque was among the first religious monuments to receive attention as part of the restoration and reconstruction efforts is also of particular importance. The restoration and reopening of 12 mosques destroyed as a result of the occupation is an indication of the importance our state attaches to preserving our religious heritage. These initiatives are also important in terms of passing our historical and cultural heritage on to future generations,” he said.

World.title: Opening ceremony of Grape and Wine Festival held in Shamakhi (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 19. The Grape and Wine Festival, bringing together viticulture and winemaking traditions, national music and a festive atmosphere, began on September 19 in Meysari village of Shamakhi.

The two-day festival is being held in Meysari village of Shamakhi District, organized by the Shamakhi District Executive Authority, Abqora restaurant and the Nasimi Gardens complex.

Festival guests were welcomed with performances by national wind and percussion instrument ensembles. A ceremonial parade of wine producers was held accompanied by a drum show.

Held for the fifth time, the festival aims to promote local grape and wine production, increase the export potential of wine products, inform the general public about the history of viticulture and winemaking in Azerbaijan and the work carried out in this field, and contribute to expanding the region’s tourism opportunities.

Speaking at the opening of the festival, head of the Shamakhi District Executive Authority Tahir Mammadov said that these days are marked by significant events for Shamakhi. According to him, during the visit of President Ilham Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva to Shamakhi, a number of important tourism and cultural facilities, including hotels, recreation centers, creative and cultural venues, were opened. These projects serve to further expand the tourism and cultural potential of the district.

The head of the executive authority emphasized that not only district residents but also all visitors to Shamakhi benefit from the development projects being implemented in the district.

Tahir Mammadov said that the Grape and Wine Festival, which has already become a tradition, makes an important contribution to promoting Shamakhi’s rich viticulture and winemaking traditions, increasing the district’s tourism appeal and supporting the socio-economic development of the region.

Speaking at the event, Minister of Agriculture Majnun Mammadov said that the festival contributes to the development of viticulture and winemaking in Azerbaijan, the formation of wine culture and the promotion of local wines. The minister noted that viticulture and winemaking are sectors with ancient traditions in Azerbaijan. According to him, important achievements have been made in the development of viticulture and winemaking as a result of the attention and support provided by the state to the sector.

Majnun Mammadov particularly highlighted the work of grape growers, noting that farmers make significant efforts to grow high-quality grapes, deliver the produce to processing facilities and ensure the winemaking process. The minister also highly appreciated the work of winemakers and technologists involved in producing high-quality wines.

This was followed by performances of examples of national dances, including the “Grape” dance, which reflects viticulture traditions. Festival participants had an opportunity to learn more about Azerbaijan’s ancient viticulture and winemaking traditions, as well as the country’s rich tourism potential. Various entertainment programs and shows were presented to visitors.

The festival, held on the premises of the Shirvan Wines LLC viticulture and winemaking complex in Meysari village, featured various brands presenting their grape products.

Entertainment activities organized throughout the day for different age groups added to the festival program. Guests took part in various competitions and quizzes.

An interesting program was also prepared for the festival’s youngest guests. In the children’s entertainment zone, they took part in interactive games and various activities and danced and had fun with animators.

On the first day of the festival, which continued until the evening, popular singers Roza Zergerli, Kazim Can and Joseph U.O, as well as DJ Kamon, performed.

The Grape and Wine Festival will continue on September 20.

World.title: Baku Declaration on establishing Turkic Union of Composers signed (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 19. The Baku Declaration on the establishment of the Turkic Union of Composers (TUC) has been signed within the framework of the 1st Congress (Kurultai) of Composers of the Turkic World, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

Besides, the Congress has discussed the draft charter of a new international professional organization.

The establishment of the TUC became one of the key milestones of the Congress (Kurultai). The new organization aims to bring together composers, musicologists, performers, conservatories, music academies and creative unions across the Turkic countries by laying the foundation for international cooperation.

The Baku Declaration has laid a foundation for further professional interaction among representatives of the music sector in Turkic countries. The TUC will prioritize maintenance and development of the common music legacy, support of contemporary schools of composition, fostering creative and academic exchanges, the creation of joint musical works and projects, and promotion of the music of the Turkic peoples on international stage.

“We seek to create a vibrant musical space in which the rich heritage of the Turkic peoples becomes a source of new works, professional cooperation and international cultural dialogue. The First (Congress) Kurultai in Baku and the establishment of the Turkic Union of Composers (TUC) open a new chapter in the history of musical diplomacy of the Turkic world”, said Professor Aktoty Raimkulova, President of the Turkic Culture and Heritage Foundation.

It is particularly symbolic that the TUC was established in Azerbaijan – a country with outstanding musical traditions that has given world culture such great composers as Uzeyir Hajibeyli, Gara Garayev, Fikrat Amirov and many others.

The 1st Kurultai of Composers of the Turkic World is being held on September 18-20, 2026, within the framework of the 18th Uzeyir Hajibeyli International Music Festival organized by the Heydar Aliyev Foundation and the Ministry of Culture of Azerbaijan.

The Kurultai organizers are the Ministry of Culture of Azerbaijan and the Turkic Culture and Heritage Foundation, in cooperation with the ICESCO Regional Office in Baku, the Union of Composers of Azerbaijan, and the Azerbaijan National Conservatory.

The Kurultai is dedicated to the 100th anniversary of the First Turkic Studies Congress, the 885th anniversary of the great Azerbaijani poet and philosopher Nizami Ganjavi, and the 585th anniversary of the outstanding Uzbek poet Alisher Navoi.

Representatives of the musical communities of Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Türkiye, Uzbekistan, Hungary, and Turkmenistan are participating in the event.

The main goal of the Kurultai is to create a unified musical space for the Turkic world and to strengthen professional ties among representatives of the music industry. The event will address issues related to the preservation and development of the shared musical heritage, support for contemporary schools of composition, the creation of collaborative musical works, the development of creative and academic exchanges, and the promotion of the music of the Turkic world on the international stage.

The Kurultai’s program includes sessions, meetings, academic discussions, an international roundtable, thematic exhibitions, as well as concerts featuring symphonic, chamber, and traditional music.

One of the Kurultai’s key outcomes will be the establishment of the Turkic Union of Composers (TUC), which aims to bring together composers, musicologists, performers, and representatives of leading musical organizations from the countries of the Turkic world.

The establishment of the TUC creates a new institutional platform for cooperation among composers and musical organizations of the Turkic world, uniting historical musical heritage with contemporary professional and creative interaction.

World.title: EU urges US to reconsider visa denial to Palestinian UN assembly delegation
World.content:
The European Union says it regrets Washington's decision to deny visas to Palestinian officials seeking to attend the UN General Assembly.

The US State Department said it was refusing to grant visas to Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas and other members of his delegation ahead of next week's meeting in New York.

Spokesman for the EU's diplomatic service, Anouar El Anouni, said the EU had urged the US to rethink the move, referencing the White House's similar decision last year.

The UN is needed now more than ever When Anthony Albanese and Penny Wong attended the UN General Assembly 12 months ago, it felt like something significant might be happening. This year, things feel like they will be a bit more... prosaic.

"In light of its existing headquarters agreements with the UN and its obligations as host state, we urge the United States for this decision to be reconsidered," Mr Anouni said.

US President Donald Trump's administration denied visas for the Palestinian delegation last year, forcing Mr Abbas — a regular at the UN General Assembly — to address the body by video.

The General Assembly voted 152-3 on Thursday for Mr Abbas to be able to appear virtually once again this year.

On Friday, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also expressed regret at Washington's decision, adding he was concerned about its impact "on the ability of the State of Palestine to participate fully in the work of the United Nations".

As it stands, only members of the Palestinian mission to the UN will be able to attend the meeting, which begins on Tuesday.

The General Assembly voted in favour of Mahmoud Abbas appearing virtually again this year. (Reuters: Remo Casilli)

US at odds with UN members recognising Palestinian state

The US and Israel have objected to the Palestinian Authority's (PA) historical payments to families of imprisoned or slain Palestinians, including those who carried out attacks against Israelis.

The PA recently reformed this system, allocating welfare payments to families on a needs basis rather than political affiliation or prisoner status.

Sources say Australia withdrew from West Bank sanctions talks European diplomats say they were surprised and disappointed that Australia baulked at joining a UK-led move to impose trade sanctions on West Bank Israeli businesses.

The State Department said Washington also opposed Palestinian "actions to internationalise the Israeli-Palestinian conflict including through the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ), seeking to bypass negotiations through seeking unilateral recognition".

They accused them of "continuing to pay stipends to terrorists and to glorify acts of terrorism and terrorists in public pronouncements and school textbooks".

The US is at odds with the 142 UN member states that recognised a Palestinian state at the United Nations last year.

The decision to deny Mr Abbas a US entry visa comes as violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians has escalated in recent months in the West Bank.

AFP

World.title: Russia reports cyber attacks on voting system during parliamentary election
World.content:
Russian authorities have reported multiple attacks on voting systems and communication lines across the country, as Russians head to the polls in a three-day parliamentary election.

The online voting system in Moscow was subjected to a strong attack overnight, but the situation remains under control, the Interfax news agency cited the Central Election Commission's head as saying on Saturday.

The attacks were continuing, but all were being successfully repelled, Ella Pamfilova said, according to state media.

A banner of Mr Putin with a quote reading: "Today, our entire country is one team. And that is undoubtedly the reason for the success of all our endeavours." (Reuters: Alexey Pavlishak)

Separately, Russia's digital ministry said it had registered a sabotage attempt on communication lines in the country's Far East, but that the attack had been thwarted and all communication had been restored, state media reported.

President Vladimir Putin earlier accused Ukraine of trying to interfere with the vote, without providing evidence.

Voting in Russia's parliamentary election runs from September 18 to 20.

Election triggers diplomatic row with Moldova

Russia's parliamentary election has triggered a diplomatic row with Moldova over plans to open polling stations for Russian nationals in the separatist Transnistria region.

Moscow says 220,000 residents of pro-Russian Transnistria, a sliver of land which broke away from Moldova in 1990 at the end of Soviet rule, hold Russian passports and are entitled to vote on Sunday in the election for the State Duma.

Moldova's pro-Western government says Russians may vote only in a single polling station in the Russian embassy in the capital Chisinau.

It contests the 220,000 figure and opposes any polling station in Transnistria, where it has no control over procedures.

Moldovan authorities this week denounced the Kremlin's 15 planned polling stations as "unacceptable and hostile".

Putin's new incentives to recruit soldiers in Transnistria The Kremlin is trying to recruit more soldiers for its war in Ukraine but an analyst says at the rate of casualties, "Russia cannot replace recruits fast enough to keep the 'meat grinder' fed."

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova urged Moldova to drop its objections and halt actions that "run against democracy, international law and common sense".

Moldovan Foreign Minister Mihail Popsoi told Moscow "not to interfere with Moldova's plans for peaceful reintegration" of the breakaway territory.

Flags of Transnistria and Russia fly in a square in Moldova's breakaway region of Transnistria. (Reuters: Vladislav Bachev)

Meanwhile, former Russian federal official Marat Kambolov was elected president of South Ossetia, a Russia-backed breakaway region of Georgia, in a vote Moscow hailed on Saturday as a sign of the territory's desire for closer ties with Moscow.

Election shadowed by war

The Kremlin is likely to cite the election result as evidence of widespread public support for Mr Putin's policies, in particular the invasion of Ukraine — Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II, now in its fifth year.

Most anti-war candidates have been barred from participating.

The second day of voting came after a New York Time report this week, citing two people close to the peace talks, that the White House is now considering signing business deals with Russia before it stops fighting in Ukraine.

Democrats probe Trump Jr wedding parties Two lavish post-wedding parties for Donald Trump Jr and his wife, held in the Bahamas in May, were funded by Russian businessman Umar Kremlev, who has strong ties to President Vladimir Putin, according to a report by US media outlet ProPublica.

"I don't know anything about such signals, and it would be strange to receive them, because we still hear exactly the opposite stance, namely, 'Let's agree on Ukraine and move forward, and everything else later,'" Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov told the RIA state news agency on Saturday.

Also on Saturday, Poland said it conducted a preventative military air operation during Russian strikes on Ukraine — though concluded there was no violation of Polish airspace.

Moldova said it suffered an "unacceptable" violation of its airspace, as it suspected an explosion near its capital to be caused by a drone "from Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine".

Russian forces struck a Ukrainian cargo ship and a tanker located in the Black Sea and in one of Ukraine's ports, the Interfax news agency reported on Saturday, citing the Russian Defence Ministry.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Roosters power into prelim as Sharks insist they are not in rebuild mode
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters are 80 minutes away from their first NRL grand final in seven years after fighting past Cronulla in a 46-10 semifinal win.

Trent Robinson's men will play the Dolphins in a preliminary final after being made to work for victory against the Sharks at Sydney Football Stadium.

Halfback Daly Cherry-Evans was placed on report for tripping Cronulla's Teig Wilton on Saturday and, aside from the fitness of Sam Walker, is likely to be the only question mark heading into next Friday's meeting with the Dolphins.

Queensland number seven Walker underwent ankle surgery less than a month ago but coach Trent Robinson said the team is "pretty confident" he will be back to face the Dolphins.

"He hasn't trained with us yet but he's had really good progressions," Robinson said.

Just as everything fell into place for the Roosters, who also welcomed back Angus Crichton from a long injury lay-off on Saturday, just about everything fell apart for Cronulla.

Halfback Nicho Hynes failed a head injury assessment after copping a bang en route to Lindsay Collins' second-minute opening try.

Nicho Hynes was ruled out due to a second-minute head knock. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

And then centre Mawene Hiroti went off with a knee injury after 20 minutes after crashing over the dead-ball line.

It was little wonder the Roosters put a depleted Sharks outfit to the sword, piling on 24 points in the final half an hour.

Cronulla is now one of just two teams in the NRL era to reach five straight finals series without making a grand final, and has not been returned to the last game of the season despite making the top eight in nine of 10 seasons since.

"We've been up for five years now with the same group of guys and a good portion of those are leaving," Sharks coach Craig Fitzgibbon said.

Cameron McInnes, Sione Katoa, Siosifa Talakai, Jesse Ramien and Mawene Hiroti are some of the core members of the team on their way out, but Fitzgibbon said it would not be a complete rebuild for the club.

"Everyone thinks we need a reset or rebuild; we'll just keep going, we've got some guys ready to go," he said.

"We won't be going anywhere."

Look back at all the action in our live blog below and check out all the stats in the full ScoreCentre.

World.title: Broncos blitz Knights to set up derby preliminary final
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Defending NRLW premiers Brisbane have destroyed Newcastle in a 40-16 win to set up a preliminary final against Gold Coast.

The Broncos led 34-0 at half-time at Langlands Park on their way to clinching a fourth straight win.

But there were some concerns for the Broncos, with Bree Spreadborough sustaining an ankle injury.

Lock Lillian Yarrow was also put on report for a lifting tackle.

It took the Knights until the 16th minute to complete a set of six as they were blown off the park by a rampant Broncos outfit.

Raiders end Tigers' NRLW fairytale The Raiders claim a first-ever NRLW finals win, downing the Tigers 6-0 to end Wests' fairytale season.

Broncos trio Tamika Upton, Jesse Southwell and Romy Teitzel tormented their former club in masterclass displays.

Upton, who was given an early mark 20 minutes from full-time, probed and dazzled from fullback.

Southwell was the chief puppeteer at number seven with a pinpoint kicking game, and Teitzel was dominant in the right edge second-row spot.

The Broncos had a dream start with a try after just 56 seconds, brought about by perfect execution in all aspects of play.

Knights fullback Lucy Spain dropped the ball after a Southwell bomb, with Teitzel picking up the scraps to storm over.

Robinson weaved over five minutes later and barnstorming prop Shannon Mato was unstoppable close to the line.

Teitzel's second try was followed by Upton's four-pointer.

Upton laid one on with a crafty grubber for centre Georgia Bartlett to finish, and it was already a cakewalk before the half-time siren.

Broncos prop Brianna Clark crashed over after the break before Knights backs Mercedez Taulelei-Siala, Shanice Parker and Sidney Taylor got the visitors on the board in an improved second-half performance.

AAP

World.title: 'Western values' and 'national pride' underpin Coalition's education reform plans
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The Coalition has unveiled its plan for "root and branch" reform of Australia's education system, that would include subjects on "Western values", and less time spent on Indigenous history.

Speaking in Sydney's west, Shadow Education Minister Julian Leeser said the reforms would also see the Australian flag flown in all schools to foster more national pride.

He declared that the Coalition's policy would "restore excellence" in education, amid plummeting academic standards.

"Our academic performance is worse than ever. Our boys are disengaged and falling behind, our classrooms are disrupted and, in some cases, dangerous," Mr Leeser said.

To address rising classroom disruption, Mr Leeser floated the idea of teaching pathways for military veterans.

"When I think about the need for better classroom behaviour and more discipline in our classrooms, and the need for more support for Australian values, it seems to make sense," he said.

Make Indigenous history 'discrete' subject

Mr Leeser, who is also the shadow minister for Indigenous Australians, said children should learn about Indigenous heritage, "just like they learn about our British foundation and multicultural character".

Global results show Aussie students' struggles Australian students have recorded their lowest-ever scores in maths and reading in international testing, but improved on their science results.

Advocating for a shorter national curriculum that "returns time to teachers", he said the Coalition would remove cross-curricular priorities — which are areas of learning embedded across the curriculum, rather than as separate subjects.

These include Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories and culture, Asia and Australia's engagement with Asia, and sustainability.

"All three topics are important … but that doesn't mean they should be delivered thematically to our children as cross-curricular priorities," he said.

"Teach them as discrete, carefully planned topics that fit properly within geography or history or science classes."

'Western values' to underpin curriculum

The Coalition's curriculum overhaul also calls for students to "specifically learn" about Western values and culture.

"That includes basics like democracy, the rule of law, a fair go, the development by Australians of our system of constitutional monarchy and federation," Mr Leeser said.

"But I would also like to see Australian students taught and exposed to …classical works of literature, art, music and philosophy that underpin and enrich the ideas that have shaped our country."

The shadow minister said the Coalition's "root and branch" reforms would build a sense of national pride, which he said was lacking.

"Let every school have a flag and let every student take pride in it, its history and the values for which it stands."

Faster pathways for teachers

In addition to potentially streamlining teaching pathways for soldiers, a Coalition government would also slash qualification timelines.

Coalition's teacher claims spark backlash A teacher's union has fired back, labelling remarks by Angus Taylor and Matt Canavan "fundamentally incorrect".

Mr Leeser pledged a Coalition government would support a return to a one-year teacher accreditation system.

"Until the early 2010s, teachers in Australia were generally accredited on the basis of one-year teacher training courses," he said.

"In 2023, the NSW Productivity Commission released data showing that the shift to the longer qualification led to 9,000 teachers not entering the profession between 2015 and 2022."

The Coalition's policy would also include a framework to help all Australian schools develop "a clear statement of behavioural expectations" for students, amid rising instances of abuse towards teachers.

World.title: Mother charged over hidden recording device in son's clothing
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A Gippsland mother has been charged by police after allegedly sewing a recording device into her non-verbal son's clothing after he began refusing to go to school.

Skye Cooper says her seven-year-old son came home from school one day last year with what looked like bruises.

He had been attending Churchill Primary School in the state's east since February 2025, but it was only around a month into his time there when he began acting distressed during the morning school run.

"He would not get out of the car. He started screaming, he started begging for me," Ms Cooper said.

"He just got more and more emotionally distressed… [and] would not be left in a room with anyone other than me. He was traumatised."

Her son has severe epilepsy, autism level three, global development delay and severe language delay. He is also non-verbal.

Ms Cooper said she was prompted to act when she noticed bruising on her son's arm. (ABC News: supplied)

Ms Cooper said she had multiple meetings with the school to express her concerns about her son's experience but didn't feel that her concerns were being addressed.

Worried, Ms Cooper approached a disability advocate for advice and was advised to sew a recording device into his clothes.

Each night, she listened back to the audio — until she heard an aide telling her son "you hurt me, I'll hurt you".

"Once I heard her on the recording threatening him, saying that she'll hurt him … I ended up pulling him out [of the school]," Ms Cooper said.

Charges laid over recording device

The alleged use of a recording device was reported to police and Ms Cooper has since been charged with Regulation of Installation, Use and Maintenance of a Listening Device.

She said she is shocked by the turn of events.

"I was trying to protect my child," she said.

"I just couldn't make sense of it, that … the tables have been turned on me."

She said she's been told by police that if she admits to the charges and makes a donation of $300 to a suitable charity, she won't have a criminal record.

Ms Cooper is receiving legal advice over her next steps.

She has also started a petition calling for the aide's removal and for the Education Minister to push for change in the Surveillance Devices Act to protect parents who use covert recording devices in suspected cases of abuse.

Ms Cooper doesn't believe her concerns have been addressed. (ABC News: Danielle Kutchel)

Earlier this year Ms Cooper received a formal written apology from the aide, which said she did "not specifically recall the exchange" but was "extremely remorseful that such a statement was made".

"I take full responsibility for the language used and am using this as an opportunity to reflect on my communication style under stress," the letter said.

"I clearly used words that I should not have used. While they would not have been intended as a threat or a literal statement, I recognise that language expressed that way is inappropriate."

Recording device 'only recourse you've got'

Julie Phillips is the disability advocate who has been assisting Ms Cooper and who recommended placing a recording device in the child's clothes.

She said she would still recommend it to others, while also warning of the possible consequences.

"But if there's no other way of finding out, what else can you do?" Ms Phillips said.

Julie Phillips advised Skye Cooper to use a recording device. (ABC News: supplied)

She said Ms Cooper's descriptions of her son's behaviour during his time at the school immediately raised red flags.

"One of the common issues with kids who can't use speech to communicate is when their behaviour deteriorates and there is bruising, usually something is going on that's traumatic for them," she said.

"Obviously it shouldn't be that [using a recording device] is the only recourse you've got, but with non-verbal people it is the only recourse you've got.

"The consequences have been experienced by a mother whose number one priority is the safety of her child, who can't communicate with her. If that's not completely backwards, I don't know what is."

Ms Phillips said abuse of children with disabilities in schools is extensive.

"When you take away any options that parents have to find out what is going on at school, your children are in a very dangerous position," she said.

She believes Ms Cooper's use of a listening device was justified and could even be legally defended if it can be proven that there was a threat to assault her son.

"If children can't be safe in government schools, it's a sad reflection on our society."

Ms Cooper said the Disability Workers Commission is investigating the issue.

World.title: Victorian Greens MP Tim Read dies aged 64
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Victorian Greens MP Tim Read has died aged 64, following a high-profile battle with metastatic cancer.

Dr Read, who announced his retirement from the Victorian parliament in January, used his final year as the Member for Brunswick to fight against the Allan government's decision to close VicHealth, described as the world's first health promotion foundation.

The former general practitioner told the ABC in January that VicHealth had helped pioneer sun safety messaging that could have helped him reduce his cancer risk if promoted when he was younger.

Mr Read delivered his valedictory speech to the Victorian parliament earlier this year. (AAP: James Ross)

Paying tribute to Dr Read on social media today, Victorian Greens leader Ellen Sandell said the Brunswick MP was the most liked MP in the state parliament.

"Tim was a brilliant local MP, doctor and scientist — but to those who knew him, he was also the kindest, funniest and most fundamentally decent of people," Ms Sandell said.

"Tim never held back from speaking truth to power, whether it was getting arrested for spray-painting health messages on tobacco billboards prior to getting elected or taking it up to the Premier in Question Time.

"Yet, he was also the most liked MP in state parliament, respected across the community for that rarest combination in a politician: conviction, integrity, wit and genuine humility."

Ms Sandell said Dr Read's advocacy led to legislative reforms over pill testing, tobacco licensing, the abolition of public drunkenness laws and a statewide plan to eradicate congenital syphilis and HIV transmission.

She said his work also led to gay men being allowed to donate blood, and a statutory ban on solitary confinement in prisons.

Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said he spoke with Dr Read earlier this week and was "deeply touched by that conversation".

"We spoke about something on which we have always agreed: integrity in public life and the need for reform," Mr Carroll said.

"Despite his health challenges, he was positive and optimistic for a better world.

"I always valued his intelligent and humane contributions to the public debate."

Victorian Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said Dr Read "was a man of conviction and a thoroughly decent person".

"He brought sincerity, compassion and a strong sense of public duty to his work, earning respect across the parliament," she said.

The Greens MP was a doctor before being elected to the Victorian parliament eight years ago. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)

"His commitment to integrity in public life was unwavering. Through his leadership of parliament's Integrity and Oversight Committee and his advocacy for stronger anti-corruption laws, Tim worked to ensure those entrusted with power were held accountable."

Ms Wilson said parliament often required negotiation and compromise.

" I always enjoyed working with Tim. He was an honest broker, someone who listened, engaged in good faith and approached every discussion with respect and integrity. "

Born in 1962, Dr Read completed a PhD while working as a medical practitioner in a public HIV and sexual health clinic.

His research included HIV prevention and treatment and how best to treat antibiotic-resistant sexually transmitted infections.

Dr Read's political activism started in his early 20s, as a participant in the Billboard-Utilising Graffitists Against Unhealthy Promotions group, comically known as BUGA-UP.

Medical students including a young Tim Read took part in a graffiti campaign in the mid-1980s, when cigarette advertising was still legal on public billboards. (Supplied)

The politician first ran for a parliamentary seat at a federal level, running as the Greens candidate at the 2013 election in former prime minister Bob Hawke's seat of Wills, which overlaps with the state electorate of Brunswick.

The following year, he stood as the Greens candidate for Brunswick in the Victorian election before ultimately winning the seat on his second attempt in 2018.

The Greens hold the inner suburban constituency with a two-candidate preferred margin of 13.7 per cent against Labor.

A by-election for the Brunswick electorate will not be necessary as Victoria is already scheduled to go to the polls on November 28.

Last year, Dr Read told the ABC he had noticed his leg was swollen while getting ready for work.

Scans revealed cancer had spread throughout his body. Dr Read first had a melanoma removed from his leg seven years ago.

His initial diagnosis was grim, forcing the Brunswick MP to retire ahead of the November state election.

Victorian Premier John Cain established VicHealth in 1987. (ABC News)

In January, Dr Read said closing VicHealth would create a "false economy" — an apparent saving that would in fact lead to more spending.

"We need to be strengthening health promotion, not weakening it," he told the ABC.

VicHealth was set up in 1987 by Labor premier John Cain and his health minister David White with bipartisan political support.

The policy banned outdoor tobacco advertising and used taxes from cigarette sales to promote health, including warning about the dangers of cigarettes.

Revenue was used to fund the arts and sport, which until then had relied heavily on tobacco sponsorship.

In his valedictory speech, Dr Read called for stronger NSW-style anti-corruption oversight in Victoria and bolstered rental controls, similar to those of the Australian Capital Territory.

"Despite the theatrics, most of us are here for the right reasons," he said.

"Politicians are unfairly maligned, and for me, politics is the work you do to improve people’s circumstances, not just now but in the future.

World.title: Demons claim top spot as Cats maintain winning ways
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Melbourne is the only unbeaten side after six rounds of the AFLW season, producing a statement 34-point win over Carlton at Casey Fields.

But the Demons may count the cost of Saturday's 8.10 (58) to 3.6 (24) win after star forward Georgia Gall limped off in the third quarter with an ankle injury.

A day after Hawthorn manufactured an upset to topple defending premiers North Melbourne, the Demons knew a win over the Blues would lift them into top spot on the ladder and establish a 6-0 (win-loss) start to their campaign.

The Blues were spirited in the opening half, but Melbourne slotted four straight goals in the third quarter to set up the victory.

Midfielder Olivia Purcell (26 disposals) was at the centre of the blitz, slotting two majors, while Jorja Livingstone scored on debut in the final quarter.

Tyla Hanks (32 disposals, one goal) also excelled, but it came as Gall sustained her injury.

It is the second consecutive loss for the Blues (4-2) and dents their top-four aspirations, although midfielder Claudia Whitfort was typically busy with 24 disposals.

Cats in fifth straight win

Aishling Moloney produced a goal-of-the-year contender to help Geelong to a 14.6 (90) to 7.7 (49) triumph over Collingwood at Victoria Park.

Knowing a victory would shore up their position inside the top eight, the Cats (5-1) were given a scare when the winless Magpies levelled scores minutes after the main break.

But the visitors flicked a switch, finding six goals in an electrifying third quarter to take a 31-point lead into the final break.

One of those majors was from Moloney, who booted the ball from halfway before it took a favourable flurry of bounces and crept into the goal.

The Cats tightened the screws in the final quarter, keeping Collingwood goal-less to seal their fifth straight win.

Midfielders Nina Morrison (30 disposals), Mikayla Bowen (29 disposals) and Georgie Prespakis (12 clearances) were prolific for the Cats, while Moloney and Chloe Scheer grabbed three and four majors respectively.

While the loss kept the Magpies (0-6) winless, they enjoyed a highlight when half-forward Olivia Lewis booted a goal on her AFLW debut after shifting from Super Netball's Melbourne Mavericks to the Magpies.

Lewis was a late call-up on Saturday morning because midfielder Bri Davey was ill.

Swans move clear in top four

Chloe Molloy continued her glittering goal-scoring form, spearheading Sydney to a 14-point victory over Port Adelaide.

Chloe Molloy played a starring role for the Swans. (Getty Images: Mark Brake)

The Swans (5-1) knew a win at Alberton Oval would move them four points clear of the fifth-placed Blues.

Molloy was instrumental in helping the visitors secure the precious 5.11 (41) to 3.9 (27) victory, booting three goals.

Her dazzling display came despite the Power keeping Sydney's usually dynamic attack at bay in the first half, with the scores locked at 16-16 at the main break.

The Swans stepped up in the third quarter, with Molloy booting a crucial goal, although a late major by Gemma Houghton kept the Power in the contest.

Leading by four points at three-quarter time, young Swans forward Cynthia Hamilton snagged a settling major, before Molloy kicked another to open up a match-winning advantage.

Swans defender Zippy Fish was typically influential, picking up 26 disposals, while midfielder Montana Ham had 16 possessions.

Midfielder Abbey Dowrick was a shining light for the Power (2-4), racking up a match-high 27 disposals and 415 metres gained.

Triumphant Bulldogs

The Western Bulldogs held firm to claim a 6.4 (40) to 4.6 (30) victory over Fremantle.

Looking to jump into the top eight, the Bulldogs (4-2) were kept scoreless in the opening term in Perth but kicked four unanswered majors in the second quarter to lead by 11 points at half-time.

The Dockers tightened their defence in the third quarter, holding the visitors to just one point as they surged back after Hayley Miller and Kiara Bowers found goals.

But just 17 seconds into the final quarter, a series of slick handballs led to Bulldogs forward Heidi Woodley slotting a major, before Sarah Hartwig nailed a goal to help her team move up to seventh on the ladder.

The Dockers (3-3) missed an opportunity to cement themselves inside the top eight, although Bowers (23 disposals, eight tackles and one goal) was busy, while midfielders Gabrielle Newton and Aisling McCarthy posted 24 possessions each.

Defender Jess Fitzgerald (25 disposals) shone for the Bulldogs, and midfielder Isabelle Pritchard jagged 21 disposals and a goal.

AAP

World.title: Creditors back $850k rescue deal to save iconic Royal Hotel from liquidation
World.content:
PoliticsWACity life Creditors back $850k rescue deal to save iconic Royal Hotel from liquidation Carla Hildebrandt September 20, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An iconic Perth CBD pub has been given a lifeline after creditors accepted an $850,000 deal to save it from liquidation. John Parker is the businessman behind the Parker Group, which operates popular fine dining hospitality venues including The Royal Hotel, Busselton Pavilion and Ciao Dandy in Karrinyup. His pub and restaurant empire was thrown into uncertainty last month when administrators took control of the companies behind all three venues. On Thursday morning, creditors of Wellington Pty Ltd, the company behind the Royal Hotel, approved a rescue proposal put forward by the Parker Group. John Parker owns and manages multiple hospitality ventures in Perth. Holly Thompson



The deal means the central pub, built in 1882 on the corner of William and Wellington Streets, will continue trading. Administrators Jack James and Paula Smith, from Rodgers Reidy, estimate the company owes about $3m. The tax office is the main creditor, with administrators estimating it is owed $2.4m. In a report filed on September 10, James and Smith said creditors would have got nothing if the company was liquidated. Under the new deal, they are expected to receive 22 cents for every dollar they are owed. In the same report, administrators found “there was a strong indicator” the company was insolvent from at least January 2024, with about $2.2m in debt potentially occurring after that month. John Parker spent $13 million restoring the Royal Perth hotel in 2019.



“We consider there may be a claim against the director for insolvent trading available to a liquidator,” the report states. But, they said Parker would likely not have the funds if pursued. “It would indicate that the (Parker) would not have the financial capacity to meet a judgement debt (if successful),” the report said. The report stated a liquidator could have continued the investigation and sought legal advice in pursuing action against Parker. Busselton Pavilion and Ciao Dandy remain in separate voluntary administration. This masthead has contacted Wellington Pty Ltd, The Parker Group and Rodgers Reidy for comment.
