World.title: Wellington firefighters douse flames in Thorndon firetruck
World.content:
A Wellington firetruck has been taken off the road, after its engine caught fire, prompting a response from a fellow crew.

Firefighters responded in the Northland area, where they found a fire inside the Thorndon aerial-ladder truck about 6.10pm Saturday.

The flames are extinguished.

The New Zealand Professional Firefighters Union said the truck was only one of two high-reach heavy aerial-ladder trucks in the capital.

No-one was hurt in the blaze and the fire was extinguished.

World.title: How Resident Evil rebooted a zombie craze to become a billion dollar franchise
World.content: With nine main series numbered video games, dozens of spin-off games, six movies, plenty of novels and comic books, and even a couple of stage plays to its name, the franchise has grossed nearly $US13b (NZ$22.72b) across all media. The horror survival franchise is about to get another face lift thanks to Weapons director Zach Cregger, who is at the helm of the upcoming feature film.

World.title: Country Life: 'Looking for an edge' on a Māori-owned farm
World.content:
In the past 16 years, the Pukepoto Farm Trust near Taumaranui has never not made a profit for its more than a thousand shareholders, descendants of Ngāti Maniapoto.

It's something the trust prides itself on, as it allows them to give back to the community.

"We can't do a lot on 1000 effective hectares, but we can certainly do a little bit," Trustee Weo Maag told Country Life.

Now it's sharing the secrets to its success with other neighbouring farmers as part of Beef and Lamb's Hub Farm Programme.

'Looking for an edge': Data driven decisions on a Māori owned farm Country Life Download MP3 14m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

Meaning 'little hill', Pukepoto was established by the Māori Land Court in 1978.

Trustee Weo Maag inherited his shares from whakapapa on his mother's side.

"I've always maintained that the land should provide to our people."

He said the trust initially started by paying dividends to shareholders, then moved to providing education grants and most recently, kaumātua grants.

Returning a profit to the shareholders comes from careful planning, he added.

Key focus areas for the farm include integrating technology like the new eShepherd virtual fencing collars from Gallagher. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

"We draw up plans production-wise and expectations based on one season from the other, and then we look to what is it we're going to produce, what then can we sell.

"We can't control what the prices are - we're at the mercy of the processors, but we can control what we produce."

Another important part was having a "yardstick to measure our success".

For Maag this meant "benchmarking" to help when explaining farm operations and results to the shareholders.

"It's about managing expectations," Maag said.

Dozens of utes have packed into a paddock next to the wool shed with farmers eager to hear about the key to success at Pukepoto. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

"I can go, 'hey, how come we didn't produce that many [lambs]? What happened? What went wrong? Did you miss a paddock with the ram or something?' You know, whatever it might be. But if you don't have anything in writing, then you're just flying by the seat of your pants."

The Pukepoto Trust farm joined Beef and Lamb's Hub Farm Programme in October 2025. The programme follows a farm business over several years to help farmers see what change looks like over time in a real system.

Maag said he hoped the programme would help with providing more detailed data as part of the trust's own benchmarking processes.

"With the hub farm, we're going to be able to get accurate measurements around grass growth," he said.

"We've got an idea historically because [of] our irrometer (a tool used to measure soil moisture) and knowing how many sheep we've had, 'oh yeah, we'll be right'. We know the rainfall.

Pukepoto Farm Trust farm manager Terry Head speaking with Darren McNae from AgFirst. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

"But this is going to provide real live data that we can then go... yeah, we were pretty accurate."

It's also about providing tested data and information for future generations, he said.

"At some point, someone's going to replace us. I see the hub farm and the learning from the hub farmers, essentially going to be able to provide information [to] the new trustees who come along, who may not have a greater knowledge in farming, but have a lot of understanding in governance and finance."

On the bright autumn day Country Life visited, about 80 farmers, trustees and other rural professionals turned out for the field day where early results were shared.

"It feels really great to be up there amongst top performing farms in the district."

Meaning 'little hill', Pukepoto hides the true nature of this rugged hill country farm. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Trust chairperson Aloma Shearer said there were wider benefits to being part of the programme too.

"It's about bringing other people, sharing knowledge that you have with other farmers about performance and what we do here, what can help others, that sort of thing.

"I'm just hoping that what we've got to share with farmers here today, with the industry, is going to be helpful for what their plans are for the future."

The field day highlighted how the trust was lifting performance through genetics, making better land use decisions, and integrating technology like the new eShepherd virtual fencing collars from Gallagher.

World.title: Thousands of NZ buildings no longer require earthquake strengthening
World.content:
Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown says common sense has prevailed, after the government passed legislation that means thousands of buildings across the country will no longer require earthquake strengthening.

The Earthquake-prone Building Amendment Bill brings an end to quake strengthening rules in Auckland.

It also means the earthquake-prone building system will no longer apply in the Chatham Islands and the low-seismic zone in the upper North Island within a matter of days.

Parts of coastal Otago and Stewart Island that were previously in a low seismic zone will move to a medium seismic zone.

"Auckland is one of the least seismically active regions of New Zealand, with a much lower earthquake hazard than places such as Wellington and much of the South Island," Brown said.

"Despite that, Auckland building owners were being hit with ridiculous seismic assessment and strengthening costs for a risk that is far lower here than in other parts of the country.

"The system became a big earner for consultants and building managers writing reports, preparing estimates and assessments, proposing strengthening work and producing the dreaded earthquake ratings, all at considerable cost to building owners.

"Thankfully, common sense has prevailed.

Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown says the legislation is great news for residents in his city. RNZ / Nick Monro

"Now we need to tackle the equally bad fire rules that hinder the conversion of second-tier office buildings into apartments in the city," Brown said.

On Saturday, Building and Construction Minister Simon Watts hailed the unanimous passing of the legislation, saying the rules would now focus on buildings located in the areas with the greatest earthquake risk.

"Today, we are delivering significant reform that will save Kiwi building owners and the New Zealand economy a staggering $8.2 billion," he said on Saturday.

"Expensive and often unrealistic remediation costs that are disproportionate to risk threaten buildings becoming derelict. Instead, we're enabling that money to be invested elsewhere to grow businesses, jobs and the economy.

"For buildings that remain designated as earthquake-prone, remediation requirements will be more targeted, helping reduce costs and complexity, while ensuring life-safety risks are addressed.

"For many communities, particularly smaller towns, meeting the current requirements has been a significant challenge. The reforms take a more proportionate approach to managing seismic risk, while ensuring high-risk buildings continue to be identified and addressed," Watts said.

World.title: Fire crews contain Canterbury shed blaze
World.content:
Firefighters have contained a fire that engulfed a shed near the Canterbury town of Prebbleton.

The fire at the Ellesmere Road property broke out about 3.10pm Saturday with up to 14 trucks responding.

Large plumes of black smoke were seen across parts of the region.

World.title: Tokomanawa Queens go big by signing WNBA import Hailey Van Lith
World.content:
In a massive coup for this year's Tauihi Basketball Aotearoa league, the Tokomanawa Queens have lured WNBA player Hailey Van Lith as an import player to their already stacked roster.

The Connecticut Sun guard is the team-mate of New Zealander Charlisse Leger-Walker, who last month signed to play with the Tokomanawa Queens following her debut season in the American basketball league.

Leger-Walker is just the second New Zealand woman to reach the WNBA and getting her signature to play in Aotearoa for the first time in six years was already seen as a bold move by the Wellington-based franchise.

But getting Van Lith, who was selected as the No. 11 overall pick in the first round of the 2025 WNBA Draft, would have been beyond the wildest dreams of Tauihi bosses when they launched the league four years ago.

Van Lith is the ninth most-followed WNBA player on Instagram, with 1.3m followers.

She is a massive name and popular face in women's college basketball but has had a challenging start to her professional career.

Van Lith dealt with a serious ankle injury during her rookie season for Chicago Sky, and has been on short-term contracts at the Connecticut Sun.

The pair will join the Queens when their WNBA commitments end later this month.

Charlisse Leger-Walker. AFP

The Queens announced her signing on their Instagram, saying the "relentless playmaker" brings "elite bucket-getting mentality to the Tokomanawa Queens backcourt.

"Combining high-stakes playoff poise with unshakeable competitive fire, she's ready to ignite the court and set the tone for our 2026 title defence."

The 24-year-old Leger-Walker is joining her older sister Krystal at the Queens and brings a vast base of experience in the US, having played six years of college basketball.

She helped steer the University of California to the NCAA championship earlier this year before she was selected 18th overall in the 2026 WNBA Draft by Connecticut, where she has enjoyed a solid rookie campaign.

World.title: 'Yarnarchists' blanket Christchurch for annual yarn bomb festival
World.content:
Central Christchurch has been blanketed with knitted and crocheted installations as a talented band of 'yarnarchists' stitch together the city's annual public art festival Yarnarchy.

The event is in its fourth year and adds a handmade element to the city's post-quake Gap Filler programme, which temporarily transforms vacant downtown lots into vibrant community areas.

Organiser Kate Finnerty says Yarnarchy is a showcase for the depth of talent and creativity in Ōtautahi.

She started the festival in 2022 as part of her work as Gap Filler's urban play coordinator.

"I quite like that title," she told RNZ.

This year the festival will feature a silent disco tour. Participants will wear yarn-bombed headsets and be led on a 1970s musical odyssey through the collection of artworks.

People take part in Yarnarchy 2026, Christchurch's annual yarn bomb festival. RNZ / Supplied

So what is there to see?

"There'll be some stuff up trees," Finnerty said. "There'll be some quite big stuff but then there'll also be some little sneaky things.

"Like, around the outskirts of Cathedral Square you're looking for little puddles that might be creeping out or little creatures or little scenes, and then up high we've got giant spiders and huge lizards and yeah, a whole bunch of different things."

The inspiration was "one of those 3am, that could work" ideas, she said.

"I was just thinking [of] this beautiful new city. There's all these amazing buildings but it's nice to bring a bit of a human element into it.

"What I love about yarn bombs is it's public art but every single piece is made by hand. It takes a lot of creativity and innovation and perseverance ... it's really kind of touched by people."

Yarnarchy, Christchurch's annual yarn bomb festival, brings a splash of colour to the central city. RNZ / Supplied

Collaborating with other artists is a big part of the festival, as is giving a platform to craftspeople who are often hidden from view.

"The first year we did a collaboration with some street artists ... And then last year we did a collaboration with Jolt Dance, who are an inclusive dance company based in Christchurch."

The silent disco is this year's highlight for her. "It's this incredible experience for people who are doing it but it also creates a real scene and a real hive of activity for the people who are watching it."

Another of the festival's colourful downtown artworks. RNZ / Supplied

Guided by Joy Fools performers Clementine, Delphine and Diane, participants will don personalised yarn-bombed headsets and dance their way through Cathedral Square. As the music begins, guests are led on a musical odyssey through the Square's collection of knitted and crochet artworks.

The first silent disco was held on Saturday but those who missed out have another chance next Saturday, 26 September, the first day of the school holidays.

Spaces are limited. Attendees are encouraged to embrace the spirit of the event by wearing their own knitted or crochet outfits.

World.title: Forest and Bird calls for fast-tracked coal mining application to be declined
World.content:
Forest and Bird are calling for a fast-tracked coal mining application to be declined after the Environmental Protection Authority found gaps in its conservation plan.

The EPA has sent a letter to mining company Bathurst asking for more information about its application to mine coal from Buller's Denniston Plateau.

It has asked the company to be more specific about how it would protect the area's wildlife, which includes protected lizards and insects.

RNZ has approached Bathurst for comment.

"There were some shortcomings in their plan for lizards," Forest and Bird's regional conservation manager Scott Burnett said.

"The Department of Conservation's best practice for lizard management is to salvage more than 80 percent of the lizards from a site before development occurs. In Bathurst's application they expect that fewer than one percent of lizards can be feasibly salvaged, so that's a massive scale difference there.

"Likewise, the avatar moth, which recently won bug of the year, it's only found on the Denniston Plateau, and a number of the sites where it has been found are within the mine footprint. The entomologist who discovered the avatar moth, Brian Patrick, feels that if the mine is to go ahead the moth will go extinct."

Burnett said he was pleased that the EPA had gone back to Bathurst to ask for more information.

"Outside of our overarching concerns around the failings of fast-track, this is an example of the process working as intended," he said.

One expert fears this moth will go extinct if the mine goes ahead. CC BY 4.0 Brian Patrick

"We would ultimately like to see the application declined. We know that is not likely, given the permissiveness of the regime, but we would also like to see really robust conditions in place both to protect wildlife and also to ensure New Zealanders don't foot the bill for future cleanup."

Buller District Council mayor Chris Russell said he supported Bathurst's application and believed it should be granted, but also noted it was important to consider the environmental impacts.

"The effects on ecology and water quality, along with acid mine drainage, rehabilitation and the project's long-term obligations, must be properly tested," he said.

"[But] the significant economic and social consequences of closure must be given the same consideration."

He noted the project would maintain jobs for at least 390 people, the vast majority of which lived in Buller.

Burnett disagreed with that argument.

"This is very much pitched as a jobs versus nature argument. The Buller community outwardly support the mine going ahead to protect jobs in Westport," he said.

"This occurring in 2026 in a climate and biodiversity crisis, where people feel like their best recourse is to double down on short term jobs that cause this environmental harm... [that] is a failure of national and local leadership."

Russell said the final decision belonged to the EPA.

World.title: Hawks fans throw bottles at umpires after 'bravest decision' in prelim
World.content:
Furious Hawthorn fans have thrown bottles at the field umpires after Brisbane benefited from a massive late call in their preliminary final epic at the MCG.

After the Hawks had recovered from a 28-point deficit in the early stages of the final quarter, Hugh McCluggage put the Lions back in front from a set shot with 18 seconds remaining on the clock, before Kai Lohmann goalled after the siren to give Brisbane a 20.11 (131) to 19.8 (122) win in front of 97,835 spectators.

McCluggage was awarded a set shot on goal from 30m out on a slight angle after Hawthorn defender Jarman Impey was penalised for holding the ball, a decision that was greeted by deafening boos from the Hawthorn faithful.

The decision, while controversial, appeared to be the correct one, with Impey's left arm free to dispose of the football while being tackled.

"I think this might be the bravest umpiring decision I've seen in my time in footy," Melbourne great Garry Lyon said on Fox Footy's post-game coverage.

McCluggage said he knew the umpires would call holding the ball on Impey after he pinned a single arm.

"I tried to grab a lever [arm] like we're taught," he told Fox Footy.

McCluggage (6) put Brisbane in front after the free kick was awarded against Impey. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

"We've been taught that you have to try and make an effort to get the ball out if you've got an arm free, so I'll take it."

Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell was left deeply emotional, and said his focus was on other umpiring calls, particularly a deliberate out of bounds call against Mitch Lewis and a high contact free kick to Dayne Zorko.

"It's probably not the one I'm focused on. There were a couple leading up to it," Mitchell said when asked about the Impey call.

"I'm sure the umpires will assess how they performed in that game in key moments."

The final moments led to ugly scenes after the match, and Mitchell joined former teammate Luke Hodge in condemning the behaviour from the fans.

"The emotion of sport is why we love it so much," he said.

"At the end of the game, part of me wanted to break down in tears, part of me wanted to scream with rage, part of me wanted to throw chairs.

"When you're in the stands, you need to continue to be feeling that emotion, because that's why we love it, but we shouldn't be throwing things on the field. But the passion of the game is why we love it.

"I hope for the vast majority that it was done responsibly."

Watson was outstanding for Hawthorn in the loss, finishing with a game-high six goals. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

Nick Watson was outstanding for Hawthorn in the loss, finishing with six goals, while Jack Gunston and Mitch Lewis combined for nine goals between them.

Lohmann's five goals led the way for the Lions, while Eric Hipwood, McCluggage and Charlie Cameron kicked three goals apiece.

Brisbane's win means it will contest Fremantle in next weekend's grand final with the hope a second three-peat in club history after doing so between 2001 and 2003 under Leigh Matthews.

Brisbane veteran Lachie Neale will play against his old side after playing in Fremantle's last grand final appearance in 2013 as a 20-year-old.

Follow the live blog below for a recap of all the action from the preliminary final as it happened.

World.title: Alex de Minaur dines out on home cooking as tricky year winds down
World.content:
Some home cooking has proved just what the doctor ordered for Alex de Minaur as a rough year approaches its end.

De Minaur got Australia off to a perfect start in its Davis Cup tie against Poland, with a 6-3, 6-0 win over Maks Kasnikowski, looking refreshed from a surprisingly lengthy rest period after the US Open.

James Duckworth was unable to emulate the performance, losing 2-6, 6-3, 6-3 to Kamil Majchrzak in the second singles rubber to set up a decisive Sunday in Brisbane.

De Minaur's 231st-ranked opponent was right in the fight in a 35-minute opening set, but the temperature was dialled up as he flew to a second-set bagel in just 20 minutes.

On multiple occasions throughout the dominant performance, de Minaur took time out of his celebrations to fire up the packed Pat Rafter Arena crowd.

"We play outside Australia for 10 months of the year, so we don't really get too many chances to play back here in front of a packed crowd," he said.

"It was a great atmosphere and one that I've missed."

While he remains an admirable ninth in the ATP world rankings, 2026 has by almost every measure been one of de Minaur's toughest in recent memory (albeit with a wedding to British player Katie Boulter mixed in) as evidenced by him sitting 13th in the race for the year-end ATP finals.

He only reached the quarters of one major, losing to eventual champion Carlos Alcaraz at the Australian Open, before falling to players ranked lower than him in Paris, London and New York.

His most recent disappointment against 70th-ranked Botic van de Zandschulp at the US Open marked just his second loss in the second round of a grand slam since 2023.

De Minaur fell in the second round at the US Open. (Getty Images: USTA/Manuela Davies)

It came in a major tournament without world number one Jannik Sinner and with seven-time slam winner Carlos Alcaraz returning from a wrist injury.

Not for the first time, de Minaur cut a dejected figure as he lamented an early exit after consistently being a presence in the last eight in the past few years.

The 27-year-old also endured three first-up losses at the Masters and the only time he reached the quarters, his loss to Valentin Vacherot actually saw him lose ranking points due to a semifinal charge in 2025.

But the good thing for de Minaur is all that is in the past, and the jam-packed tennis schedule means there is always a chance to turn things around.

Alex de Minaur was tasked with starting the tie on the right foot. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

After the Davis Cup comes the Laver Cup in London, where de Minaur will lead Team World against Europe, with the Australian hoping this period can "springboard me back to where I wanna be".

"I know the tennis is there, it hasn't gone anywhere. I've just gotta step up and keep doing what I'm doing," he said.

"It's a different environment and I think I thrive in these types on environments, team competitions. It's a little bit different to your day to day on tour.

"The pressure is different. I'd say it's probably more in team events because you're not just playing for yourself, you're playing for the boys around you and I think that brings out the best in me."

Rinky Hijikata and Max Purcell will take on Karol Drzewiecki and Jan Zielinski in the doubles to kick off the decisive second day, before the reverse singles.

World.title: Aussie teen revving to take on world's best in sim racing championships
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Xavier Cain may well be the only teenager looking forward to his alarm going off at 3 o'clock on a Monday morning.

The 16-year-old student from Mount Gambier, in south-eastern South Australia, will be jumping out of bed and into the driver's seat as he competes against some of the world's best simulator racers.

From the comfort of his home, Xavier will take on other sim racers in the 2026 Porsche eSports Super Cup World Championship, with competition getting underway at 4am on Monday.

"I'm not really aiming to finish a certain position, but I definitely just want to learn a lot for this year," Xavier said.

Xavier's set-up at his home will help him take on some of the best simulator drivers in the world. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook)

"I'm hoping I can be back for many years to come, so I'm not too worried about trying to finish well.

"I just really want to learn a lot so I can bring it into the future years to come."

The Porsche Cup prize is a hefty one: $US10,000 and the chance to compete for a real-world development driving spot with the German motorsport giant.

Racing simulators use computer screens, a realistic steering wheel, and pedal set-ups. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook)

"I always had hopes that I could do well," Xavier said.

" About a year ago, I had a conversation with my friend, and it was just a 'what if' conversation, like how good it would be to race in a world championship. "

Talent on show

Simulation racing uses computers and a realistic pedal and steering-wheel system to create a lifelike driving experience.

Racers need to consider real-world variables like tyre wear, vehicle damage and fuel levels as they tear around virtual tracks.

Driving on the simulator program iRacing, Xavier quickly rose through the rankings and joined a professional team, Automoves Racing, just six months ago.

He is now in the top 1 per cent of racers on iRacing.

Co-owner Jordan McDonnell said Xavier's talent was clear and he was fast-tracked from the academy to the main team.

Jordan McDonnell is a sim racer and sprint car driver. (Supplied: Automoves Racing)

"Even though his ranking was a lot lower than what was needed to be in our main team, I spoke to the other owner and made an exception for him to be able to be pushed up," Mr McDonnell said.

" One thing's led to another and now he's in the top 32 in the world for Porsche Cup cars and representing us on a global stage. "

Based in New Zealand, Mr McDonnell was a sprint car racer before founding his e-sport team with the help of a friend in Canada he met online through sim racing.

He said sim racing had helped grow motorsport and allowed more people access to what could be an expensive industry.

Professional Indycar driver Scott McLaughlin is also boosting the sim racing scene. (Supplied: Twitch)

"There was a driver that was in the academy, his name's Nicholas, and we promoted him to the main team not too long ago," Mr McDonnell said.

"It's 2 in the morning in Poland where he's from, and he just starts yelling out of joy, waking his whole family up.

"So hearing that and his reaction and waking his parents up at 2am, getting promoted … that really just makes you feel good and makes you feel part of something bigger."

Making motorsport accessible

Racing simulators have long been used by motorsport teams as a way for drivers to practice their skills, but they remained a niche hobby for amateurs.

In the past decade, however, sim racing has exploded in popularity as the technology has become more accessible and social media has given it a platform.

Big motorsport names like Formula One champion Max Verstappen, who has formed his own sim racing team to compete in global events, have also helped to push the e-sport into the mainstream.

Major events are governed by international motorsport's peak body the FIA.

Formula 1 driver Max Verstappen has formed his own sim racing team to compete in global events. (Getty Images: EYE4IMAGES/NurPhoto, Marcel van Dorst)

Melbourne driver and content creator Emily Jones said the online culture around sim racing enabled her to have a career in motorsport.

"I've raced against Max Verstappen, Shane Van Gisbergen and Scott McLaughlin and all these international fantastic racing drivers," she said.

" That opportunity wouldn't have happened if it wasn't for sim racing. "

Emily Jones turned her real-world racing experience into success in the virtual world. (Supplied: Emily Jones)

Ms Jones now streams her racing to about 38,000 subscribers on Twitch and produces videos for a YouTube channel dedicated to the e-sport.

"I've been lucky enough to travel overseas multiple times to Germany, Poland, Japan, the US and lots of really interesting places to both compete in international competitions and also just to create content around sim racing," she said.

" If I could go back and tell a child version of myself that I get to travel and also get paid to essentially play advanced video games, I would be pretty stoked. "

Early mornings ahead

Back in Mount Gambier, Xavier's early wake-ups will continue for the next six weeks as he starts his world championship campaign.

It won't be easy juggling the high-octane competition with Year 11 classes at school and TAFE, where he is studying automotive service and technology.

But mum Teresa Cain will be cheering him on as he chases a world title and a chance at a dream real-world experience.

Xavier and his mum, Teresa, are bracing for the early morning race starts as part of the world championship. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook)

"That's everyone's dream that's in racing, isn't it?" she said.

"It would be just amazing to see him get from this and get to that level.

"We'll give him the best possible chance we can and tick all the right boxes to hopefully get him there."

World.title: 'Never too old': 83-year-old footballer still getting a kick
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Robert Johnstone has just two rules when he crosses the white line to enter the football field.

"The first rule is don't fall over, because you're out of the game and you look a fool," the 83-year-old says.

"The second rule is get a kick."

Mr Johnstone, affectionately known by his teammates as "Robbie J", lives in South Australia's Riverland, but has also lived in Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland.

Robert Johnstone says he is always trying to improve and is constantly working on his skills. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

He was a latecomer to Aussie Rules football and only picked up the game in his 70s.

And despite his age, he's not ready to give up the sport he's fallen in love with.

"I'd never tried a group sport. I'd been a loner. I did a lot of fun-run walking and stuff," Mr Johnstone says.

"Now I can't walk past a footy without wanting to kick it.

" It's just magic to be out there with like-minded spirits. "

Still quick off the mark

Mr Johnstone plays for his local team, the Riverland Superdogs, who compete in South Australia's AFL Masters league.

The league only allows players age 35 and up, and has competitions across Australia.

The Riverland Superdogs played in the curtain raiser before the 2024 SANFL Russell Ebert Tribute Match. (Supplied: Robert Johnstone)

Mr Johnstone has the title of oldest player in the competition.

"There's an element of danger to it, and I've still got that little bit of ego; I want to be out there," he says.

" You've just got to accept the fact that everyone's quicker than me, but I do have some little wins. "

Riverland Superdogs president Rob Romeo has played alongside Mr Johnstone for almost 10 years.

He says even in his old age "Robbie J" has grown, becoming a better, more refined player.

He might not be a spring chicken, but Robert Johnstone can still kick the ball "almost 30 metres". (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

"He's usually the first one at trainings," Mr Romeo says.

"Things have slowed down slightly over the years, but there was a time when he would put us to shame.

"He's like a little kid, just trying to get a little bit better at kicking, and we'd just say, 'Don't put too much pressure on yourself. Just come out and enjoy yourself.'"

'No-one keeping score'

While there is no finals series or a premier in the AFL Masters, the competitive spirit and camaraderie has brought players back season after season.

Mr Romeo says the Superdogs don't care how good prospective players ae, as long as they are willing to give it a go.

He encourages anyone over 35 looking for community involvement and exercise to consider it.

"As a kid, you go to footy because your mates go, and this is no different," he says.

Robert Johnstone says finding the AFL Masters competition is one of the best things that's ever happened to him. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

"It opens up your friendship web, whether you come from broken relationships or whatever else that may have happened in your life.

"The exercise also helps with mental health."

Inclusivity the key to success

Former AFL Masters and West Adelaide chief executive Conny Wilson also resides in the Riverland.

She has seen "Robbie J" up close on a number of occasions, and says he embodies inclusivity, which AFL Masters is all about.

"As an aging society, these are great opportunities for people to either reconnect with past teammates or for people looking for friendships to come out and try," Ms Wilson says.

"It's also been exceptionally well received by women, who growing up didn't have the opportunity to play football."

Mr Johnstone's passion for the game also extends to his adopted state, seen in his distinctive mullet, transforming from grey to SA's iconic red, blue and yellow for the annual AFL Masters state carnival, which he will play again this year in the over-65s.

Rob Johnstone's hair is ready for the masters state carnival in Newcastle at the end of September. (Supplied: Robert Johnstone)

While the octogenarian doesn't expect to dominate his competition at the carnival, he is confident he can once again make his mark.

" I rarely get pinged for holding the ball, that's a badge of honour. "

World.title: How Jack Gunston became an unlikely key to Hawthorn's flag hopes
World.content:
There are a lot of things that get better with age. Fine wine, cheese and even a good pair of jeans can improve as the clock winds along.

Football players aren't meant to be in this class. They start to break down as they get old. The mind is often willing, but the flesh is weak. The physical game takes its toll, with years of hits adding up.

Players like Jack Gunston, however, are determined to prove this wrong. Turning 35 next month, Gunston has preserved himself but actively gotten better. His last two years have been his most fruitful in front of the big sticks, and his value to Hawthorn never more important.

Gunston failed to top 60 season goals in the first 15 years of his AFL career. Since turning 33, he has done it twice.

Gunston's longevity has already seen him kick more than 35 per cent of his goals since turning 30, the sixth-highest rate among AFL-era players with over 500 goals. By the end of his career he may be on the podium.

Gunston sits at the vanguard of a revival of a slice of old-school footy. The era of the stay-at-home lead-up forward was recently thought to have gone the way of the dodo, but its revival has been largely implemented by a rising young crop, alongside Gunston that is. That's thanks to a somewhat hidden rule change.

In his fourth stint, at a third club, Gunston is set to lead a Hawthorn forward line into a shot at its first grand final in 11 years. In its way stands his old club.

Gunston's fourth coming

It's a well-worn cliche that nobody knows what a player will become when their name is first read out on draft night. While pundits will be quick to offer a comparison to a current player, each develops on their own, at their own pace.

Gunston was tabbed by Adelaide on potential, more than what he had shown to date in junior football. One of the youngest in the 2009 draft class, Gunston was green, slight and seen as a work in progress.

But as would eventually be the story for the rest of his career, Gunston quickly exceeded expectations at West Lakes. While the skinny frame and blond tips make him seem like a completely different player, Gunston's first goal — beating his defender for pace on the end of a full field rebound — bore a striking resemblance to his final evolution.

Gunston has been blessed to never carry his burdens alone. His whole career has been spent forming multi-pronged partnerships with multiple All-Australian quality forwards.

Most famous was his key role as one of five career All Australians in Hawthorn's legendary 2010s dynasty forward line, but before that he cut his teeth with Taylor Walker and Patrick Dangerfield. Most recently, he has partnered dangerous smalls, including current foils Nick Watson and Dylan Moore.

Gunston's stint in Adelaide wasn't long, but was fruitful. As the young Victorian was trialled all over the ground and worked on building fitness, there were more than just hints at the electric nature of his career to come.

Most know what happened next at the Hawks: three premierships and plenty of acclaim.

But the good times didn't last forever, and that boom period was followed by a fallow one. Injuries, and a short-lived move to Brisbane, left Gunston's career at the precipice.

His move back to the Hawks, and a shift in the way footy is played, has more than revived his career.

The connection is made

Over the past two years, Gunston has effectively become a player reborn.

Instead of the high-roaming beast pushing away from his match-up, the veteran now stays anchored closer to goal. Gunston often sits in space light years from the play, wastelands usually ignored by forwards in years past.

Gunston has forged a fast connection with the Hawks' contingent of skilful young midfielders such as Jai Newcombe, Connor Macdonald and Josh Ward. In some ways it resembles past great Jason Dunstall's bond with Platten and Jarman.

Hawthorn's set-up usually preserves this open space for Gunston to operate in. With this amount of grass, the 300 gamer gets the chance to deploy all the time-honoured tricks in his arsenal.

Gunston feigns, feints and baulks his opponent into submission. He'll lead to one side before darting back. Without support, direct defenders can be trapped in the blender of his athleticism. The connection between Gunston and his teammates is such that they know where he is going before his last decisive move.

Gunston is also unafraid to use the pockets. The instinct for most defenders is to hedge towards goal, and to cede the territory towards the boundary line. Over the past two years Gunston has made opposition sides pay for doing so.

Gunston has converted more goals from near the boundary, at a better clip, than anyone in the league in the past two years.

Gunston isn't alone in the depth in which he is deployed. A handful of players and teams across the league are experimenting more with "vertical spacing", or making the once-compressed ground long again.

Intriguingly, many of the other stay-at-home forwards are on the younger side of the league's key position forwards. Part of this influence may be down to the introduction of anti-density rules in junior footy, and the flow-on effects when those players have entered the league.

Marks inside 50 have steadily increased since the introduction of the rule in junior footy that requires a certain number of forwards to stay within the forward half and 50 at resets. This may have influenced younger players to be more patient with movement patterns, and shown coaches the value of space in the modern game.

The Brisbane test

Hawthorn faces a fearsome opponent on the way to the grand final: Gunston's old team, Brisbane.

The move of Gunston to Brisbane was designed to help the Lions get over the top. The veteran was meant to help mentor younger Lions forwards in the dark arts of finding space. In reality, early-season injuries, the tragic death of his father, and natural development meant Brisbane found different pathways to premiership glory.

Now it's Hawthorn that is the upcoming challenger.

Six weeks ago the reigning premiers saw off Hawthorn easily. Gunston held up his end of the bargain, kicking three of the Hawks' eight goals, but they were convincingly beaten all over the park. Despite dominating clearances, they completely lost the transition game and were torn to shreds by the furious Lions attack.

In order for Gunston to have a chance to be a difference maker, the Hawks have to be patient in the middle of the ground, and get the ball forward enough to have a chance.

World.title: History beckons for Fremantle as greatest-ever fightback propels it into grand final
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

When Hayden Young went back and kicked a remarkable goal from the boundary after the three-quarter time siren, he couldn't have known it would spark his side's greatest comeback.

Never, in 753 AFL games across more than 30 years, had the Dockers recovered from more than 18 points down at the final change to win.

But against Sydney, after what can only be described as an underwhelming three quarters of football, Fremantle created yet more history in a season that keeps on giving to turn a 21-point deficit into a 12-point win.

The Dockers had never won while trailing by 18 points or more at three-quarter time. (AAP Image: Dan Himbrechts)

Shai Bolton produced a stunning long set shot, before Patrick Voss fended Dane Rampe into next week and curled home a brilliant goal to cut the margin to nine points.

Isaiah Dudley, in just his second AFL season, then booted the goal that sent Fremantle to just its second Grand Final.

Fremantle's Isaiah Dudley and Shai Bolton were instrumental in the Dockers' fourth-quarter fightback. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

"We were down for so much, we were playing so poorly for it felt like large parts of it, but we hung in there," Dockers captain Alex Pearce told Fox Footy.

"I don't want to say it's a sense of relief; it's a sense of joy and pride for my teammates in how we were able to play our best footy in that last quarter when the pressure was at its highest."

Flicking the switch

Fremantle fans would have been forgiven for giving up on the Premiership dream midway through the third quarter.

Sydney, undermanned as they were, had an answer for every challenge the Dockers threw their way.

Fremantle had more of the ball but struggled on the short SCG, kicking over the head of their forwards time and again.

Josh Treacy struggled to have an impact as the Dockers missed targets inside 50 on numerous occasions. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Voss, Jye Amiss and Josh Treacy combined for just eight disposals in the first half, which was emblematic of the Dockers' struggles.

Sydney's pressure was intense, as it appeared the Dockers would crack as they did against Hawthorn two weeks ago.

But after the final change, they showed the resolve that had made them the best second-half side for the season.

"We put a bit of pressure on them [Sydney], and they probably didn't play with the same dare," Dockers coach Justin Longmuir told Fox Footy.

"It was a game of adjustments. I didn't think our intensity was off early; I think our method was off early."

Swans fairytale ends

With all the personnel missing, it seemed inevitable that at some stage the Swans would run out of legs.

And in the face of the Dockers' onslaught, they wilted.

Errol Gulden was immense with 36 disposals and eight tackles, while Brodie Grundy toiled in the ruck in a salivating contest against Luke Jackson.

Luke Jackson won his battle against Brodie Grundy, kicking two crucial goals. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

But ultimately, the Dockers had too much talent across the ground, and somehow found another gear to run over the top of the Swans.

It brings to an end a season that will forever be remembered for the events in mid-August which saw the Swans suspend five first-choice players.

The Swans produced a stunning win over Brisbane in their qualifying final in which they also lost captain Callum Mills to a serious knee injury, but couldn't repeat the dose.

"We were in a really good position for three-and-a-bit quarters, and to their credit, at this time of the year you can't give a team any momentum, and they took it," Swans coach Dean Cox said.

"They've been the best team all year, and it showed you've got to play a full 120 minutes against those teams to get the result you're after."

Sydney will be pondering what could have been, while Fremantle has an eye on history.

World.title: Wallaroos edge towards their version of the 'Matildas effect'
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Earlier this year, when speaking about the Wallaroos contesting the 2029 World Cup on home soil, Rugby Australia (RA) president Kristy Giteau revealed her dream.

"I envision packed stadiums, girls screaming after a game to get an autograph by one of our Wallaroos players," she said in June.

Giteau and her RA colleagues are hoping the Wallaroos will create a similar buzz to that generated by the Matildas at the 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup, which was co-hosted by Australia and New Zealand.

Many have described this as the "Matildas effect", with the inspiring run to the semifinals triggering a massive spike in female participation numbers and driving record TV audiences.

RA knows the Wallaroos — ranked ninth in the world — must improve on the field to achieve a similar impact, although this relies heavily on the ongoing process of shifting the program to full-time status.

The players and coaches are doing their part, as illustrated in last weekend's encouraging performance against world champions England.

Despite the 48-15 defeat in Salford, the Wallaroos produced an effort suggesting they can be competitive at the World Cup in three years' time.

They led 10-5 at half-time, which was uncharted territory for the England squad.

The Red Roses hadn't trailed at the half-time break since 2020.

This wasn't a fluke, as the Wallaroos played with aggression in both attack and defence, forcing the Red Roses to make uncharacteristic mistakes.

Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona illustrated her side's physical approach against the Red Roses. (Getty images/Rugby Australia: Lewis Storey)

But it wasn't just the Wallaroos' physicality in the first half that was impressive.

The build-up to prop Faliki Pohiva's 31st-minute try showed they'd identified weaknesses in England's defensive formation and line-out.

Test rugby, though, is an 80-minute game and the Red Roses steamrolled the Wallaroos in the second half, scoring seven tries to one.

This was largely due to the fact they're on a full-time program and their superior strength and conditioning shone through against the semi-professional Wallaroos.

Honourable defeats won't count at the World Cup, but given where the Wallaroos are at this stage of their journey, they deservedly took positives from the result against England.

"It was a pretty good outcome for us, that first 40 minutes," Wallaroos scrum half Samantha Wood said.

"I think the confidence was gaining throughout the half, when we defended our line successfully a few times, and then being able to score one try … it gave us a lot of confidence."

'Intent and purpose'

The Wallaroos want to build upon the confidence Wood spoke about as they prepare to face world number four France in Aix-en-Provence on Sunday morning, AEST.

The coaching staff have drilled into the squad the need to maintain an aggressive approach for more than one half of rugby.

Wallaroos fade after strong start vs England The Wallaroos give world champions England a scare in Salford, but the Australians cannot take advantage of a half-time lead as the Roses secure a thumping victory.

"A lot of the momentum that we did build was off the back of our intent and purpose around contact and collision [on] both sides of the ball," Wallaroos assistant coach Mike Ruthven said.

"A lot of our focus [against France] will be making sure we're really consistent in that contact and collision space.

"You take a huge amount of confidence out of that [England Test] but it's our capacity to be able to sustain that and be really consistent over 80 minutes that is ultimately what we're chasing."

Implementing an effective game plan is just one of the Wallaroos' goals during their three-Test European sojourn as part of the WXV Global Series, which also includes a clash with Scotland in Edinburgh on September 27.

With an eye on the World Cup, blooding players to build depth is among their priorities.

Winger Amelia Whitaker started against England in her first Test, while reserve forward Jemma Bemrose was also given a debut.

Piper Flynn has the chance to make her Test debut against France. (Getty Images/Rugby Australia: Lewis Storey)

Another winger, Piper Flynn, has the chance to earn her a Test cap after she was named on the bench to play France.

RA director of women's high performance Tim Walsh, who's essentially caretaker head coach until Sione Fukofuka assumes the role next year, made it clear to 23-year-old Flynn she's not on tour to make up the numbers.

"He's given me a lot of confidence in myself," Flynn said.

"As he said to me, and I'm sure to a lot of the other girls, we've been picked here for a reason."

That reason is to build towards the World Cup.

As RA dreams of enjoying its version of the Matildas effect in 2029, Flynn doesn't want to miss out on the action.

"It's a really exciting target to work towards," Flynn said.

"It gives us all a little bit of fire in our belly to try and build up and grow stronger, and grow our game to push towards winning a home World Cup."

World.title: Canberra ends Wests' NRLW fairytale in finals shut out
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Zahara Temara's big-game experience has driven Canberra to their first NRLW finals win, helping break the heart of Wests Tigers with a low-scoring 6-0 shut out at Campbelltown Stadium.

With both sides playing their maiden finals match after four years in the competition, it was Temara who shone brightest on Friday night.

The former Queensland State of Origin star laid on a bullet cut-out pass for Isabella Waterman for Canberra's first-half try.

With the Raiders holding a slender four-point lead for much of the second half, the Canberra No.7 then broke the line wide open and drew a penalty to go 6-0 up.

Beyond that, the Canberra halfback's management of the game proved the difference, forcing two dropouts and kicking the Tigers into submission.

Temara won a premiership with the Sydney Roosters in the 2021 season and could now come up against her old club next Saturday in a grand-final qualifier.

The Raiders will play the Tricolours if the all-star Brisbane roster beats Newcastle this weekend, otherwise they will face Gold Coast if the Knights win through.

Canberra controlled the majority of Friday night's game, with prop Chloe Saunders laying an immense platform with 173 metres and 73 of them post contact.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

In truth the Tigers did well to hold on as well as they did, forced to make 85 more tackles with the Raiders camped on their line for the majority of the first half.

But they were unable to land a blow at any point in the second half, with a 10-5 penalty count against them stifling the chance for many opportunities.

And when Tigers fullback Caitlin Turnbull put on a last-minute kick and chase to try and pull off a miracle, it was again Temara who was there to clean it up.

The defeat ends what has been a fairytale season for the Tigers, who won only five games combined in their first NRLW three seasons and collected the past two wooden spoons.

The joint venture had been in contention for a top-two spot before a brutal end to the season, as they reached the first top-flight men's or women's finals series in 15 years.

But their momentum was halted when they were flogged 58-0 by the Titans a fortnight ago, before last week's 22-10 loss to Canberra.

The Raiders, meanwhile, have beaten the Broncos and pushed both Gold Coast and the Roosters, making them a genuine threat over the next fortnight.

AAP

Tech.title: Gemini went rogue, hacked three companies, and Google hid it
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In May, Gemini broke containment and hacked three different companies, but Google didn’t disclose the incident until the Wall Street Journal approached the company. The hacks happened during a test of the model’s cybersecurity capabilities run by third-party Irregular, which was also involved in similar incidents involving Meta and OpenAI.

According to WSJ, Google didn’t disclose the hack because it didn’t consider it to be an “example of model misalignment.” The company said that it was an instance of “mistaken identity,” and once the model realized it had brute-forced its way into a real company by guessing a password, it stopped. “In this case, the model acted appropriately,” Google VP of Security Engineering Heather Adkins said.

Adkins told The Verge that “the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test. In all three of these instances, the model stopped.”

Adkins didn’t elaborate on how Gemini taking it upon itself to break containment and target third parties failed to qualify as misalignment. “Our security team has a long track record of reporting issues we find in other people’s software and systems - even if it’s as simple as a weak password,” she said. “We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they’ve now made to their testing processes. These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly.”

But Jack Cable, CEO of AI security firm Corridor, told WSJ that, “the meta problem is, hey, models are going outside the bounds of what they should be doing, and doing actual cyberattacks.” Additionally, security lapses at Irregular may have made these attacks possible. The model wasn’t supposed to have internet access during testing, but Irregular told WSJ it was unintentionally left available.

As incidents like this pile up, calls to rein in AI have only grown.

Tech.title: Anamanaguchi has ‘too goddamn many’ browser tabs open right now
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

They’re also a band that’s terminally online and very plugged into the video game scene as well as the weirder sides of the internet — just listen to Peter and Luke’s guest spot on the Panic World podcast talking about Etsy witches.

Anamanaguchi has a new single, “Yeah I Guess,” continuing in the musical direction of Anyway. And if it’s a precursor to a new album dropping soon, I’m sure I’ll be looping it endlessly just as I did the tracks “Magnet,” “Fall Away,” and “Valley of Silence.” (Seriously, I’ve at times had Anyway set on repeat for hours straight.)

Not only did all four members of Anamanaguchi agree to answer our weekly questionnaire, but they answered all our questions.

What is your most indispensable tool?

Luke Silas: I think my most used tool is Ableton Live Operator, it is simple and powerful and can make basic things happen incredibly quickly. I usually open it up just for writing or getting ideas down, but more often than not the sounds I get with it tend to make it to the final product!

Which is the most underappreciated?

Ary Warnaar: Built-in laptop mic and cellphone mic aren’t exactly slept on, but def underappreciated. They’re great for just getting ideas down fast, but now they sound so good that I find myself not even re-recording what I thought would be “scratch” vocals.

Peter Berkman: Right now it’s the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S. Best mouse I’ve ever had. It has a sideways scroll. It has a button to switch between notched and smooth scroll wheel. The click is satisfying but still really quiet. It’s really sensitive & responsive on whatever surface I happen to have it on. It feels really good in my hand. It charges directly into a USB-C port without external batteries so it gets to look like a mouse with a tail after it’s worked really hard. When I’m at a different computer, or if I’m on a laptop having to use a trackpad, I feel like I’ve lost so much gestural fidelity. I love the keyboard but let’s be real Douglas Engelbart cooked when he invented the mouse. But he didn’t have the recipe of the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S and he didn’t even live to see it. The LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S wasn’t even invented until June 2022. I have seen two friends recently using the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S and I say “Hey man that’s the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S” I use that thing too.

James DeVito: Lately it’s been an app called “Amphetamine” that keeps your computer from going to sleep for a set amount of time. It’s great when starting an export/render or other task that may take a while and then being able to throw my laptop in my bag and have it work while I head elsewhere… Just gotta make sure the laptop doesn’t ’splode in your bag from overheating.

LS: I love metronomes! Strengthening time is so important, and getting more comfortable with a metronome means you get to play around with time more confidently! I would love people to love metronomes the way I do!

What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?

LS: Probably Discord? Let’s say Discord.

What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?

AW: Would kill to get a normal 1/8-inch headphone out again. I’ve been constantly replacing dongles ever since Apple ditched the headphone out. Because they break or or get misplaced. Frustrating and wasteful.

JD: A wise friend of mine once taught me to increase the key-repeat on my computer beyond what is normally allowed via the UI. It feels insane at first but your hand/brain coordination catches up with the speed eventually and then you can tttttttttttttttype and deleeeeeeete things so much quicker.

LS: The only thing I’d like to add to my iPhone SE is a USB port so I can type with a keyboard because I suck at typing on my phone.

What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?

LS: I have never done this before! I probably should!!

PB: There’s a new radio aggregator called vvorldwide.com. It’s amazing. It’s like having a radio dial in your car except it pools the feeds from NTS, The Lot, dublab, KEXP, loads of different places from all over the world. It’s one of those products that’s like: Wow. Why did nobody think to make this before? It’s so useful, lightweight, and beautiful. It’s amazing to me how detached from reality and human use the big companies are (and have been for a long time). It’s one of those refreshing things you see, it reminds me of The Unfinished Revolution by Michael Dertouzos. You can just build things you want to see!

JD: Gmail :(

How many tabs do you have open right now?

PB: Tab grouping from Firefox has become an artform for me. I don’t see tabs anymore just folders of memory I can recall like a PSX save file.

LS: 46 and 31 between two windows. Too goddamn many. Most of them are meant to be shared with others or read/watched, every weekend I do a cleanout but there are truthfully a few that have been sitting for months. I can’t be the only one.

JD: I like when Chrome on my phone stops displaying the number of open tabs and just shows a smiley face :)

Which social media platform do you use the most?

LS: Staying detached from social media tends to be better for my mental health on the day-to-day, but scrolling following on Twitter is the easiest way for me to stay connected to games or news still. Instagram stresses me out lately more than ever before. YouTube definitely counts and I do love it very much, but shorts are a rare treat; I tend to watch long-form stuff mostly or have different content with no dialogue on a second monitor, like either a video game longplay or lots of restoration or cooking videos.

What is your happy place online?

AW: Facebook marketplace. Specifically low-balling “I know what I got” type mfs. No one ever accepts my offers, but I think it’s important to keep people humble, and long term, I’d like to think that I’m contributing to keeping the prices low for the next buyers.

PB: I’ve just discovered clothes. So I’m hunting a lot on places like Grailed or Depop or whatever. It’s a lot like the way I treat musical equipment on Reverb. It’s fun to sell stuff and buy stuff… when it’s equal amounts it feels more like barter and temporary sharing.

LS: Video game speedruns! Twitch streams like GDQ or RPG Limit Break are very comforting to me and a very sweet community of fun personalities.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

JD: 3D printers. I’ve been 3D printing for a long time now, and it’s gotten so so so much more reliable/easy at this point. The fact that I can design a bracket etc. for stage production and have it in hand within an hour really is the future.

LS: I’m going to say my Game Boy counts for this question. I use it less for sound design than I used to, but I bought new flash cartridges recently for the first time in years, and I’m ready to get cooking with it again very soon! It’s a perfect little self-contained workstation.

Which was the most disappointing?

LS: I’ve bought a few different effects plugins that tend to have some distinct effects but end up not giving me what I’m looking for, or feel far too specific to a use case for me to reach for generally speaking. I’ve found more exciting results from stacking and tweaking stock effects than I have reaching for dedicated single-use stuff.

PB: I’m not gonna hate on here… but they exist.

What game do you have the fondest memories of?

PB: Return of the Obra Dinn was so much fun. Any game that feels like detective work is the kinda thing that gets me going, and instantly creates a moment of excitement for me that stays frozen that I can always go back to. I think about playing [the original] Resident Evil for the first time, the first three Phoenix Wright games: I can tell you everything about where I was and what I was feeling when I first played those games. It’s not even a nostalgia based thing. I played Parasite Eve II for the first time two years ago and it was an instant deep love.

LS: I think my favorite video game of all time is Chrono Trigger. It was a world I really wished I could experience in real life and the atmosphere of every place you go is special to me. I have been trying to rip off Yasunori Mitsuda and Nobuo Uematsu every time I write for the last 30 years. It’s the first game I think of when I want to start a new playthrough of something familiar to me!

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

AW: I don’t like forced two step authentication or even worse, the upper case + number + symbol extra long type passwords. Like if I want my password to just be the letter “a,” that’s on me. I’m comfortable with that choice. I’m comfortable with that level of vulnerability. Shit maybe I don’t even want a password sometimes. Just leave it all out there for the people.

LS: Using AI to make music! Blue check accounts on twitter talking about using AI to make music! Write your own fucking music, have fun learning a skill that will continue to give and build and bloom until the day you die!!!

What is one thing you wish you had created?

LS: “Show Me Love” by Robin S. is a perfect song, and every time I hear it I think “God, I wish that could have been mine.” The combination of the M1 organ, that 909 groove, and Robin S.’ top line is like a simple meal where the right ingredients add up to something far greater than the sum of their parts; a perfect BLT, a chocolate/vanilla/peanut butter milkshake, the freshest sushi you’ve ever eaten.

JD: The Black Eyed Peas performed at the 2020 VMAs and they all had light up crotches that sync’d up to the show. Why the f didn’t they call me to do that?

What creation are you most proud of?

PB: Going back and listening to our album Anyway always surprises me. I love it so much. I think it’s the kinda thing that people who didn’t get it will eventually come around on. Sleeper classic even for me ha.

LS: I think the song “Really Like To” from our latest album Anyway is a song that accomplishes a lot of the things I want to when writing for the band! It’s loud and fast, has fun drum parts, fun to sing along to, and I got to do an ambient section at the end; I like showing it to people as an indication of where we’re at right now.

JD: Anyway as well — the entire process was so collaborative throughout. A lot of really great memories writing at the house and recording at Tarbox Road Studios.

Which are you least proud of?

LS: In 2023 I tried to get good at baking cookies, and in the process made a batch of not only the worst cookies I’ve ever had, but some of the worst food I have ever experienced. They looked great, but on a first bite tasted like absolutely nothing and had a texture of chewing damp sand, and on a second bite a bitter taste began to crawl across my tongue that practically gagged me. The only other human who tasted them was my next-door neighbor, just so I could have a witness to the crime that I’d committed. To this day I’m still not sure how I fucked up that bad, and I’ll never forget that taste.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

AW: When I was a kid I met Steve Lukather, the guitarist of Toto, and I told him I wanted to be a guitarist in a band when I grow up. He told me that if I wanted to get the girls I had to either lift weights or get good at guitar solos. I’ve done neither and I’ve been suspicious of all advice ever since.

PB: My dad told me to “never give up” when I was playing Zelda in my basement as a kid. It gave me a big affinity for puzzles, very encouraging. My dad still gives me important advice at all the big moments in my life — I am very grateful to have him.

LS: Progress, not perfection.

What is your current obsession?

PB: Investigating criminal networks of the 1990s! More of a hobby than an obsession.

LS: I’ve unfortunately found myself going further down the rabbit hole of Deltarune theory videos. I don’t buy into the majority of the speculation shared, but I love the game and there is lots of incredible insight shared into the design of it and aspects of it mechanically and narratively that I didn’t even realize I was missing.

What do you do when you need to focus?

AW: Modafinil. Jk lol, I try not to force focusing and just let it be a byproduct of inspiration/motivation. I wait for the focus to come. If I’m having trouble focusing on something then I probably shouldn’t be doing it. Like driving a car. And if you attach rituals to focus it just invites the possibility of not being able to focus without said rituals.

LS: I wait until about 8pm, charge my phone on the other side of my studio, get a large cup of black coffee, put on my second monitor a very long playthrough of a game I’m already familiar with (most recent one was Grandia II), and keep my door shut as long as possible.

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

LS: Take a walk down the Venice boardwalk, get a two-dollar salad from Chairman Mao’s, and eat while listening to music and watching people skate at the Venice bowl.

PB: It’s very important to fuck off for a minute. I will go out to a Smash tournament in the Dallas area. There’s a very lively scene that’s super competitive and full of great people. I can always go back from that feeling fresh.

When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?

PB: My phone’s dead half the time so it’s a moment that can happen anytime.

LS: I legitimately don’t remember and that depresses me!! I don’t like that!!

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

LS: About a month ago I picked up a used copy of Only Theatre of Pain by Christian Death at Headline Records, great shop I’ve been going to since I was a kid!

JD: I recently bought a record of a band called “Schlong” at Permanent Records in LA. I love finding stuff that isn’t available on streaming. It can be really easy to get complacent with what’s available online but there’s so much out there in the real world!!!

What do you think is worth splurging on?

LS: I think the most consistent answer for me is special meals. Something unique in another country, or something really special to which I don’t get to treat myself often. It’s always food!

AW: Vacation/travel/time off/adventure etc... I wish it wasn’t considered so much of a splurge. The same way you wouldn’t really call going on a hike a splurge, but in a world where just existing can be expensive, I think it’s something that’s tremendously good for the ~soul~, and worth regularly “splurging” some time/money on. I want to talk to my friends about what cool missions they went on this summer, not what new shoes they bought or whatever.

PB: Gonna agree 100% with Ary. The value of travel can’t be overemphasized.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

AW: “If you cant handle him at his fastest, you don’t deserve him at his furiousest”

JD: “Better to waste than to have not”

PB: “You know he had to do it to em”

LS: “Life is Hectic.”

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

PB: I’m very GIF-averse. There’s something about it that feels like wearing someone’s skin. But here’s a pic I like.
